Situations requiring specialists input for management and what specialties to be consulted will be addressed. A multidisciplinary team of consultants is required for the care of infants, children, adolescents and adults with PWS with the care coordinator being a specialist, depending on the age and individual needs of the patient, in the field of pediatrics, clinical genetics, endocrinology or neurology with support from learning/behavioral experts and dietitians. Information will include morbidity and mortality, potential for relapse and recurrence and possible disease outcomes. 4.4.1.1 Introduction and Background Prognosis depends on transition from stage 1 (failure to thrive) to stage 2 (hyperphagia and obesity) of clinical course development; monitoring obesity status and managing with food and dietary control, psychological food security and mandatory exercise for calorie expenditure; determining mental capacity and identifying and treating neurological/psychiatric findings ( e.g ., seizures, autism, aberrant behavior, mental illness and psychosis); monitoring the endocrine, orthopedic, cardiopulmonary and gastrointestinal systems to avoid health related complications ( e.g ., diabetes, scoliosis, hypertension and heart failure, apnea, gastric necrosis) and death [ ]. Many complications are common in PWS and will adversely impact morbidity and mortality, such as obesity, heart failure, apnea and diabetes. If left untreated or unresolved, these complications will shorten the life expectancy. Death typically occurs in the fourth decade of life with average age of females of 31 years and 29 years in males; but if weight control is successful, then PWS adults may live into their seventh decade or beyond. Unfortunately, choking-related deaths do occur at an early age [ , , ]. 4.5 Complications 4.5.1 Section Content and Questions to Answer A list and discussion of the most common complications of both disease and treatment for PWS and how complications can affect further management and outcomes will be discussed including common complications of the disease listed with treatments related to PWS. 4.5.2 Complications Seen in Prader-Willi Syndrome PWS is associated with findings related to obesity (if weight is not adequately controlled). Gastrointestinal problems (constipation, delayed gastric emptying, gastroparesis, gastric inflammation, gastric necrosis and rupture, decreased salivary secretions and swallowing difficulty including choking on food and silent aspiration, rumination, bruxism, increased ghrelin production, leading to enhanced reward from eating). Water intoxication from excessive drinking, altered vasopressin secretion and/or use of diuretic medication can lead to abnormal electrolyte levels. Respiratory issues, including a narrow airway passage, low muscle tone and strength and sleep apnea, collectively lead to an increased chance of aspiration pneumonia. Hyperthermia and hypothermia. 4.6 Secondary Prevention/ Patient Education 4.6.1 Section Content and Questions to Answer Measures to prevent recurrent disease or its complications in treated patients with PWS will be listed in a bulleted format and measures advised to prevent relapse or recurrence will be presented, if applicable. Elements of essential information for patients about diagnosis, treatment and follow-up will be provided including web resources appropriate for patient use to know about the disease, treatment, prognosis and other implications. 4.6.1.1 Introduction and Background Family caretakers for patients with PWS should be informed of the following: Infants with PWS should be handled carefully due to their poor muscle tone. Hypotonia is an ongoing risk factor for sensory motor deprivation in infancy that may result in sensory hunger (sensory seeking form of sensory motor processing difficulty) later in development, so ongoing intensive infant stimulation services are required. Decreased arousal and decreased tone in the facial muscles of emotional expression in early infancy can interfere with emotional bonding between infant and parent, so coaching for persistent infant stimulation is necessary. Individuals with PWS must be monitored carefully for weight gain and due to hyperphagia, access to food in the house must be restricted at a later age in early childhood. To avoid complications from obesity, monitoring caloric intake will be a lifelong activity in PWS. In addition to controlled food access, individuals with PWS benefit from psychological food security, best described by the paradigm no doubt, no hope, no disappointment. This means that the person knows with certainty and accepts the conditions surrounding their diet plan, including menu, portion control and meal schedule. This assures that the behavioral manifestations of disappointment will not occur. Exercise is an essential part of the daily plan for a person with PWS. It provides energy expenditure, sensory motor stimulation, deep breathing increased alertness and stress relief. Children with PWS must be monitored with testing for numerous complications of PWS and caretakers must keep up with scheduled testing and outcome results measured. Individuals with Prader-Willi syndrome require specialized care and supervision throughout adulthood and most live in residential care facilities for safety, to avoid complications of obesity and to provide supervised access to appropriate work, leisure skills and socialization with peers. The following websites are recommended to educate families caring for a child with PWS. www.pwsausa.org - Prader-Willi Syndrome Association (USA) is an organization of families and professionals working together to raise awareness, offer support, provide education and advocacy and promote and fund research to enhance the quality of life of those affected by Prader-Willi syndrome. Utah Medical Home Portal - www.medicalhomeportal.org - Review and information about providing care on Prader-Willi syndrome by primary care physicians, other health care providers and parents to address health care needs. 4.7 Practice Performance Measures/Summary of Evidence 4.7.1 Section Content and Questions to Answer Standard performance indicators and a brief statement of the rule by which each is applied, as defined by Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), Joint Commission and others as appropriate will be provided and discussed on measured standards for quality of care. A summary of the EBM entries will be given. 4.7.1.1 Introduction and Background A meta-analysis studying the effect of rhGH therapy on body composition in adults with PWS identified 8 studies that included 134 individuals treated with rhGH for 12 months. Treatment of individuals with PWS with rhGH led to (weighted mean difference (MD) 95% confidence interval (CI)) reduced body fat (MD: -2.9%; CI: -3.90 to -1.910), visceral fat (MD: -32.97 cm 2 ; CI: -55.67 to -10.26), subcutaneous adiposity (MD: -55.24 cm2; CI: -89.05 to -21.22), and increased lean body mass (MD: 2.41 kg; CI: 1.32 to 3.49). Studies of longer duration confirmed the findings for change in body fat (MD: -2.89%, CI: -4.69 to -1.07) and lean body mass (MD: 2.82 kg; CI: 1.31 to 4.33). Individuals treated with rhGH for 12 months did exhibit small increases in fasting glucose (MD: 0.27 mmol/L; 95% CI: 0.05 to 0.49) [ ]. A multicenter prospective trial studied the effects of long-term continuous rhGH treatment on body composition, growth, bone maturation and safety

Studies of longer duration confirmed the findings for change in body fat (MD: -2.89%, CI: -4.69 to -1.07) and lean body mass (MD: 2.82 kg; CI: 1.31 to 4.33). Individuals treated with rhGH for 12 months did exhibit small increases in fasting glucose (MD: 0.27 mmol/L; 95% CI: 0.05 to 0.49) [ ]. A multicenter prospective trial studied the effects of long-term continuous rhGH treatment on body composition, growth, bone maturation and safety parameters in children with PWS. Fifty-five prepubertal children (mean age of 5.9 ± 3.2 years) were followed over 4 years while treated with rhGH (1.0 mg/m2). Body fat percentage (SDS) was significantly lower after 4 years of rhGH treatment (P < 0.0001). Lean body mass SDS significantly increased during the first year of treatment (P = 0.02) but returned to baseline values the second year and remained unchanged thereafter. Mean ± SD height normalized from -2.27 ± 1.2 SDS to -0.24 ± 1.2 SDS (P < 0.0001) after treatment with rhGH. Body mass index SDS significantly decreased. Thus, body composition and height were significantly improved in children with PWS after long-term treatment with rhGH. No adverse effects were noted on bone maturation, blood pressure, glucose homeostasis and serum lipids [ ]. A Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) studied the effects of rhGH treatment on cognitive functioning in 50 prepubertal children (ages 3.5 to 14 yr) with PWS. Cognitive functioning was measured biennially by validated intelligence tests (the Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence-Revised, Dutch version (WPPSI-R) or the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-Revised, Dutch version (WISC-R)). Total Intelligence Quotient (IQ) score was estimated based on two subtest scores. After 4 years of GH treatment, mean standard deviation scores (SDS) on the Similarities and Block design subtests were significantly higher than at baseline (Mean Difference (MD); 95% Confidence Interval (CI)) for Similarities test- MD: +0.4; 95% CI: -0.1 to 0.7; P = 0.01 for Block Design- MD: +0.3; CI: 0.07 to 0.6, P = 0.01. These results indicate that long-term GH treatment significantly improves abstract verbal reasoning and visuospatial skills and reduces the gap between children with PWS and healthy controls on these skills. Thus, during long-term GH treatment, children with PWS developed their vocabulary at the same pace as healthy references. The mean estimated total IQ score improved 4 points during 4 years of GH treatment, but this result did not reach significance (P = 0.2) [ ]. Several clinical trials for treating hyperphagia and/or obesity in PWS have met with limited success [ ] but other trials are proposed or planned for the future. 4.8 Guidelines 4.8.1 Section Content and Questions to Answer Relevant current guideline(s) identified from established organizations/groups will be provided and concordant with screening, prevention, diagnosis and treatment sections. There are at least five established peer-reviewed and textbook sources of information on the treatment of individuals with Prader-Willi syndrome with cited references for recommenda-tions on diagnosis and management and portal home disease specific websites ( e.g ., medicalhomeportal.org). PWS is a genomic imprinting disorder caused by loss of expression of genes from the chromosome 15q11- q13 region that are expressed only on the father’s chromosome 15 usually due to a deletion of the chromosome region from the father. What are the most common features seen in patients with Prader-Willi syndrome? The cardinal features are infantile hypotonia, a poor suck with feeding problems and failure to thrive, growth hormone deficiency with short stature and small hands and feet, hypogonadism/hypogenitalism, hyperphagia and onset of obesity in early childhood if not controlled and learning/behavioral problems. What tests should be ordered to confirm the clinical suspicion of PWS? DNA methylation testing of the chromosome 15q11- q13 region is undertaken to identify the abnormal PWS methylation pattern using methylation-based PCR or MS-MLPA using several probes in this region. Historically, FISH analysis with probes in the 15q11-q13 region was used to identify deletions in the region. MS-MLPA is also used to not only identify the 15q11-q13 methylation status but also to identify deletions. Now, chromosomal microarrays with SNP probes are used to identify the presence or absence of the 15q11-q13 deletions but also to determine whether maternal disomy 15 is present and the subclass (maternal heterodisomy 15, segmental isodisomy 15 or total isodisomy 15. If the 15q11-q13 deletion, segmental isodisomy 15 or total isodisomy 15 are not identified using SNP microarrays, then genotyping with DNA markers from chromosome 15 is performed on the PWS patient and parents. An imprinting defect of chromosome 15 is present if biparental (normal) inheritance of chromosome 15 is found in the PWS child after examining the DNA pattern from the mother, father and child. What is the suggested treatment once the diagnosis is confirmed? Although there is no cure, growth hormone therapy is indicated to treat the growth hormone deficiency and to improve stature, decrease fat mass and increase muscle and strength. Diet intervention with reduced caloric intake and exercise programs to avoid obesity are recommended throughout the lifespan of an individual with PWS. What is the prognosis for a patient with PWS? Prognosis depends on early diagnosis and treatment with growth hormone and other therapies including stimulation programs to maximize learning, potential and diet intervention to control caloric intake and to lessen obesity and its complications thereby improving the quality of life and lifespan. 4.9.3 Parent Questions What causes Prader-Willi syndrome? PWS is a genomic imprinting disorder caused by loss of expression of genes from the chromosome 15q11- q13 region that are expressed only on the father’s chromosome 15 usually due to a deletion of the chromosome region from the father. Was there something that I did that caused Prader-Willi syndrome to occur in my child? PWS is due to errors in genomic imprinting usually due to a deletion of the chromosome 15q11-q13 region which is not from anything that the mother or father did or did not do to cause the condition. PWS is due to a genetic event that occurred at or around the time of conception. Is there a cure or treatment for Prader-Willi syndrome? There is no cure but treatment with growth and other hormones, diet and exercise plans to lessen the likelihood of obesity and gaining access to therapies (physical, occupation, speech) are warranted. Educational and behavioral treatment plans are helpful to improve the quality of life and to increase life expectancy. Consultation with a clinical geneticist and genetic counselor would be encouraged to answer questions and to provide information useful to the family (and patient) would be encouraged. There is no cure but treatment with growth and other hormones, diet and exercise plans to lessen the likelihood of obesity and gaining access to therapies (physical, occupation, speech) are warranted. Educational and behavioral treatment plans are helpful to improve the quality of life and to increase life expectancy. Consultation with a clinical geneticist and genetic counselor would be encouraged to answer questions and to provide information useful to the family (and patient) would be encouraged. What are the chances that it will occur in future children? The recurrence risk is generally less than 1% but in rare cases ( e.g ., imprinting center defect) the risk may be as high as 50%. Therefore, genetic evaluation and counseling are indicated to determine and discuss the chance for recurrence depending on the genetic subtype which should be determined as it may impact not only on the recurrence risk but also for treatment and prognosis. What can I expect from my child with Prader-Willi syndrome (will my child die early, attend school, live independently, have children)? For newly diagnosed infants and children with PWS, the prognosis is improved with better care and treatment with growth and other hormones. Avoidance of obesity and its complications to improve life expectancy is a lifelong goal and if successful the live expectancy approaches normal. Hyperphagia remains a constant problem which lowers the likelihood for independent living. Children with PWS do attend school in regular classroom settings but may require individual educational programs to maximize their learning ability and progress but close supervision (and access) to food sources is required. PWS males are thought to be sterile although there have been a few PWS females who have established and maintained pregnancies giving birth to live born unaffected children. Those PWS females with the 15q11-q13 deletion are at risk ( i.e ., 50%) of having offspring with Angelman syndrome.

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Cryptosporidium spp. is an important pathogen worldwide, causing diarrheal disease in man and animals. Its effect is more pronounced in infants, children, and the immunocompromised. Its zoonotic characteristics allow this parasite to be transmitted through the oral‐fecal route, primarily in water, food, or hands contaminated with oocysts, during direct contact with the host. An important feature of Cryptosporidium spp. is the high resistance of its oocysts to chlorination and the long time for which they can survive in the environment [ ]. This resistance to environmental conditions, when combined with its relatively low infectious dose, emphasizes the real threat imposed by this parasite in a variety of settings and the need for a better comprehensive understanding of the factors affecting infection outcomes [ ]. A notable aspect of the parasite's biology is its unique intracellular but extracytoplasmic location within the intestinal epithelial cells. This particular niche, separated from the host cell's cytoplasm, is thought to contribute to the marked resistance of Cryptosporidium species to both pharmacological treatments and the host's own immune clearance mechanisms [ ]. Symptoms of cryptosporidiosis are generally watery diarrhea, although other symptoms such as abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting, fever, and discomfort might also occur. In immunocompetent individuals, the disease is usually self‐limiting, and symptoms will disappear in 2–3 weeks. Nonetheless, host factors are crucial in the modulation of Cryptosporidium spp. infection. The immune status of a person is the main factor, immunosuppressed patients being at high risk of severe and prolonged disease [ ]. In HIV patients, the CD4 count serves as a key indicator of immune function and disease susceptibility [ ]. Age is another critical factor, with young children, particularly those under 2 years of age, being more vulnerable to infection and severe outcomes [ ]. Susceptibility to infection can also change with age [ ]. Nutritional status significantly impacts the risk and severity of cryptosporidiosis, with malnutrition increasing susceptibility, especially among children. Pregnancy has also been identified as a predisposing factor for cryptosporidiosis [ ]. Furthermore, the presence of co‐infections can influence the outcome of Cryptosporidium spp. infection [ ]. The result of Cryptosporidium spp. infection is determined by an integrated and multifactorial relation involving host, environmental, and pathogen‐specific factors. Assessment of these factors is important to make tailor‐made preventive, diagnostic, and therapeutic intervention strategies for the disease. Several environmental parameters significantly contribute to transmission as well as the potential severity of Cryptosporidium spp. infection. The standard of water and sanitation constitutes significant factors that contribute to the prevalence of the diseases, especially in resource‐poor areas. Climate and season may also modulate the risk of illness, as studies have reported an association between higher temperature and greater rainfall with the risk of infection [ ]. Seasonal changes in the attack rates of cryptosporidiosis have been reported [ ]. Exposure to animals, particularly infected cattle, has been identified as a major risk factor, as Cryptosporidium spp. is a zoonosis [ ]. In addition to exposure to recreational water contaminated with the parasite, such as swimming pools, lakes, and water parks, a well‐documented mode of transmission is [ ]. Machine learning has become a powerful technology for infectious disease analysis in recent years, with the ability to handle complex biological and epidemiological data. Its applications are varied, such as forecasting disease outbreaks in a population, recognizing important risk factors, and modeling disease severity [ ]. Even as they are not all white, panelist jacklets and machine learning algorithms are good at working with large data quantities and detecting non‐linear relationships not recognized by classical statistical methods [ ]. There are multiple machine learning algorithms available to model those factors related to Cryptosporidium spp. ‐associated diarrhea. These approaches can be generally divided into classification, regression, clustering, and time series analysis, which are suitable to tackle different dimensions of the disease. Classification methods are valuable for predictive risk factors, such as the status of C. parvum infection (infected or not infected) or finding individuals at high risk for serious disease [ ]. Classifiers such as logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks are used most frequently. Regression approaches are appropriate for outcomes involving continuous measures (e.g., duration of diarrhea, level of oocyst shedding). Regression techniquesinclude linear regression, random forests, support vector regression, and neural nets [ ]. Machine learning has demonstrated significant promise in obstetrics for predicting critical maternal and neonatal outcomes. Recent studies highlight its clinical utility: [ ] systematically reviewed ML models (e.g., Random Forest, XGBoost) that predict preeclampsia with high accuracy (AUC: 0.860–0.973) using routine prenatal data. Similarly, [ ] developed a Deep Learning model achieving AUROC 0.91 for intrauterine growth restriction prediction, identifying drug addiction, hypertension, and COVID‐19 as key risk factors. Further expanding applications, [ ] used deep learning (AUROC: 0.81) to identify doula support,

Machine learning has demonstrated significant promise in obstetrics for predicting critical maternal and neonatal outcomes. Recent studies highlight its clinical utility: [ ] systematically reviewed ML models (e.g., Random Forest, XGBoost) that predict preeclampsia with high accuracy (AUC: 0.860–0.973) using routine prenatal data. Similarly, [ ] developed a Deep Learning model achieving AUROC 0.91 for intrauterine growth restriction prediction, identifying drug addiction, hypertension, and COVID‐19 as key risk factors. Further expanding applications, [ ] used deep learning (AUROC: 0.81) to identify doula support, neonatal weight, and gestational age as major predictors of postpartum skin‐to‐skin contact. Collectively, these studies underscore ML's capacity to transform risk stratification and personalized care in perinatal medicine. Clustering approaches can also be applied to the detection of patient subgroups who are at similar risk or have similar disease status. The widely used clustering algorithms are K‐Means or Hierarchical Clustering. Time series analysis can also be used to predict the pattern of cryptosporidiosis incidence over time, which is useful for public health preparation. Popular approaches in this direction are ARIMA and neural networks, including recurrent neural networks (RNN) and long short‐term memory (LSTM) networks [ ]. The most suitable machine learning depends on the research question and the characteristics of the available data. For example: If the task is to predict whether or not the person has been infected, then it would go into the classification category, and to predict the duration till which the person will remain sick, then it would tend to the regression category. Machine learning is a flexible tool for modeling heterogeneity associated with Cryptosporidium spp. diarrhea. Variation in disease presentation results partly from differences in factors involving the pathogen. Some species of Cryptosporidium , such as C. parvum , C. hominis , and C. meleagridis , and some genotypes and subtypes within these species, display distinct host ranges and disease severity [ ]. C. parvum , for example, has different genotypes, including the bovine genotype 2 and the human genotype 1, and several subtypes (e.g., IIa and IIc). The existence of particular virulence factors enabling adhesion, invasion, and resistance against the immune response of the host probably also plays a role in the pathogenicity of various strains [ ]. The primary objective of this research is to implement and evaluate advanced machine learning methodologies for modeling and predicting determinants of Cryptosporidium species‐associated diarrhea, thereby contributing to the development of precision public health interventions and evidence‐based disease control strategies. 2 Material and Methods 2.1 Study Design and Data The dataset used includes 1008 children aged 0–168 months. The dataset included information about gender, age, region of residence, number of people living at home, having an animal, presence of HIV, and underweight. Stool samples were collected to diagnose Cryptosporidium spp. that cause infection in children. This study included 597 boys and 410 girls. Sex information for one child could not be obtained. The dataset included 491 children aged 0–11 months, 339 children aged 12–23 months, 123 children aged 24–59 months, and 55 children aged 60–168 months. The minimum sample size required to detect a significant difference using this test should be at least 1001, given a type I error rate (α) of 0.05, statistical power (1‐β) of 0.8, an effect size (Cohen's d ) of 0.14, and a two‐sided alternative hypothesis (H1). 2.1.1 Data Preprocessing The dataset ( n = 1008) underwent preprocessing: (1) removal of the single entry with missing sex information; (2) one‐hot encoding for categorical variables (e.g., province, water source); (3) no feature selection was applied prior to modeling to avoid bias, as variable importance was inherently evaluated via Gini‐based methods. All 10 predictor variables were retained. The dataset was publicly sourced from a multicentric diarrheal disease surveillance program across Mozambique, anonymized to exclude identifiable patient information [ ]. 2.1.2 Data Availability All relevant data set analysis also referenced in ‘Intestinal protozoan infections among children 0–168 months with diarrhea in Mozambique: June 2014–January 2018’. It comprises several decision trees, and individual trees are voted upon to determine the winning class. The classification and regression trees are a popular non‐parametric decision tree method for classifiers. This tree, along with others, is the basis for more complex algorithms such as random forests. It uses binary trees for its algorithm. The CART decision tree approach divides the input into binary pieces before constructing the decision tree. The CART tree uses the Gini index to determine the variables that receive more information for data classification. When categorizing, variables with lower Gini indices are assigned more weights. CART uses the test‐and‐error method to obtain the best separator point value in each dimension or variable with the lowest Gini index [ ]. In decision trees, such as CART, a small change in data might result in distinct classes (these algorithms are also called unstable algorithms). To address this issue, ensemble classifiers that combine many classifiers have been used. Bagging is an ensemble classification method. Bagging is one of the most frequently used ensemble approaches to increase the predictive accuracy of decision trees. In this strategy, each classifier creates and saves its model by classifying a portion of data. Finally, the class with the highest votes is chosen as the final classifier by utilizing the voting procedure among these classifications. 2.3 Data Analysis The dataset was analyzed using both descriptive and inferential statistical methods in order to look for relationships between Cryptosporidium spp. presence/absence and the predictor variables. Categorical variables were described by counting and percentage computation. Pearson's chi‐square test was used for the evaluation of relations between the outcome variable ( Cryptosporidium spp. infection status) and categorical dependent variables, with the Yates's continuity correction applied for small samples. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. IBM SPSS Statistics 26.0 for Windows was used for all statistical calculations. To comprehensively compare differences in accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and composite metrics (e.g., F1‐score) for the models, the following tests are performed: McNemar's test for accuracy, Fisher's exact test for sensitivity/specificity, bootstrapping for F1‐score confidence intervals, and Wilcoxon signed‐rank test for balanced accuracy. 2.4 Modeling Process For doing predictive modeling, two machine learning algorithms were implemented (Random Forest [RF] and Bagged Classification and Regression Trees [CART]). The dataset was split into training (80%, n = 806) and testing (20%, n = 202) sets using stratified random sampling to preserve class distribution to test model generalizability. A strategy for cross‐validation 5 times was used while training in order to best the hyperparameters and reduce overfitting. The following were computed as performance metrics: accuracy, balanced accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and F1 score as a measure of classification efficacy. Using the Gini index for the bagged CART and the mean decrease in impurity for the RF, the variable importance scores were generated post‐modeling and served to recognize important predictors of Cryptosporidium spp. infection. Class imbalance in the outcome variable was recognized; thus, the use of balanced accuracy and F1‐score for stability in assessment was advocated. This was done after results were interpreted against the backdrop of the clinical and environmental relevance to guide public health interventions. The Precision‐Recall curve (Figure ) was generated solely from the holdout test set predictions of the Bagged CART model across probability thresholds. 2.4.1 Error Calculation Model performance was evaluated using standard classification error metrics (e.g., misclassification rate). For the Random Forest (RF) model, the mean decrease in impurity. (Gini index) was used to quantify feature importance. For Bagged CART, the Gini index reduction 1 − ∑ i = 1 C p i 2 was averaged across all bootstrap iterations to compute variable importance. The Gini index for a node is defined as, where pi is the proportion of class i i observations in the node. Splits were optimized to minimize this impurity. 3 Results The results of the analyses of other categorical data in the dataset for the categories of Cryptosporidium spp. presence/absence variables are given in Table . The RF model showed moderate test (testing: 87.7%) and presented significant flaws when identifying Cryptosporidium spp.‐positive cases indicated by its extremely low sensitivity (2.7%) and F1 score (5.1%). Even though the inadequacy of true positives by the model compromised its clinical relevance, even with high precision (PPV: 50.0%) and NPV (88.0%). On the other hand, the bagged CART model produced similar accuracy (testing: benchmarked to blind toxicity evaluation by other approaches (87.2%)) but focused on sensitivity (97.2%) and F1 score (93.0%), demonstrating effective identification of positive infections, despite the sheer number of enzymes concerned. However, its specificity (15.4%) was strikingly low, which meant excessive negative case misclassification. The high reliability observed in positive predictions with high PPV (89.3%) is accompanied by demerits in ruling out negatives with low NPV (42.9%). The balanced accuracy of the Bagged CART (56.3%) surpassed RF (51.2%) and was closer to the objective of the study, which was to identify risk factors for cryptosporidiosis. The given results indicate that Bagged CART is preferable in such scenarios that take detection of Cryptosporidium infections as top priority (i.e., outbreak surveillance) at the expense of specificity otherwise obtained. The comparative performance of the Random Forest (RF) and Bagged CART models was rigorously evaluated using statistical tests tailored for imbalanced datasets. Both models achieved similar testing accuracy (RF: 87.7% vs. Bagged CART: 87.2%), but critical differences emerged in sensitivity and specificity. The bagged CART model significantly outperformed RF in sensitivity (97.2% vs. 2.7%, p < 0.001 via Fisher's exact test) and F1 score (93.0% vs. 5.1%; bootstrapped 95% CI: [89.5, 96.5] vs. [1.2, 9.0]), emphasizing its strength in identifying Cryptosporidium ‐positive cases. Conversely, RF exhibited near‐perfect specificity (99.6% vs. 15.4%, p < 0.001 via Z‐test), highlighting its bias toward correctly classifying negatives at the expense of missing true positives. Balanced accuracy, calculated as the mean of sensitivity and specificity, favored Bagged CART (56.3% vs. 51.2%, p < 0.05 via Wilcoxon signed‐rank test), aligning with its clinical relevance for outbreak detection. Precision‐recall trade‐offs were evident, with Bagged CART achieving higher PPV (89.3% vs. 50.0%, p < 0.001) but lower NPV (42.9% vs. 88.0%), reflecting challenges in ruling out infections. When the performance metrics were examined, it was observed that the successful model for classification was bagged CART. The variable importance values obtained from the model are listed in Table . The variable importance analysis obtained from the bagged CART model identifies important predictors associated with Cryptosporidium spp. infection. The most important factor was household size (members_household ≥ 5, 100% importance), an indication that larger households significantly increase the risk of infection, probably because of person‐to‐person transmission or crowded living conditions. Water sources became major environmental determinants, with water_source public tap water (91.1%) and water_source piped water (87.7%) ranked second and third, indicating waterborne transmission as an important mode of transmission corresponding to the study conclusion on water quality interventions. Remarkably, absent animals (animal no., 81.8%) and younger age groups (age 12–23 months, 81.5%) were also highly predictive of reduced zoonotic exposure in households lacking animals and increased vulnerability in toddlers. Geographical differences remain even when living in the province. Nampula (79.2 = ) highlighted the regional disparities in man infection prevalence. Such variables as underweight severe (65.0%) and child_hivpozitive (61.5%) were markers of host susceptibility factors, but a moderate score of importance indicated a secondary role relative to environmental drivers. On the other hand, water_sourceothers (5.3%) and older age groups (age 60–168 months, 26.5%) proved to have little effect. These findings jointly underscore the multifactorial nature of cryptosporidiosis, with water as well as household dynamics and early childhood exposure as key areas for public health interventions. The precision‐recall (PR) curve in Figure illustrates the trade‐off between precision (y‐axis) and recall (x‐axis) for the Bagged CART model across varying classification thresholds. The PR‐AUC of 0.74 quantifies the model's overall effectiveness. A value above 0.5 (random guessing) indicates meaningful predictive power. The PR‐AUC of 0.74 (95% CI: 0.68–0.79, bootstrapped with 1000 replicates) indicates robust predictive power above random chance (0.5). 4 Discussion Diarrheal diseases are lethal in children under the age of 5 years, and most of these deaths occur in low‐ and middle‐income countries. In high‐income countries, the disease is rarely fatal but is responsible for most emergency room admissions and hospitalizations [ ]. Diarrhea, caused by many types of bacteria and viruses, has a widespread and diverse transmission mechanism. It is generally transmitted from person to person via the fecal‐oral route or by the ingestion of contaminated food or water. Additional symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, fever, and abdominal pain are observed in addition to diarrhea, depending on the incubation period of the transmitted virus or bacteria [ ]. Although viruses are the leading cause in most cases, the relative frequency of viruses and bacteria varies from case to case. In children's diarrhea, viruses account for approximately 70%–90% of cases, while parasites are usually observed in less than 5% of cases. Cryptosporidium , Giardia , and E. histolytica are the main parasites that cause diarrhea in children [ ]. Recent research has increasingly focused on leveraging machine‐learning techniques to understand and model various aspects of diarrheal diseases, including those potentially caused by Cryptosporidium spp. Several studies have aimed to identify risk factors associated with diarrhea in general, which could include factors relevant to Cryptosporidium spp. infection. For example, machine learning algorithms have been applied to demographic and health survey data to pinpoint significant predictors of diarrhea in children under 5 years of age in various regions [ ]. These studies have utilized algorithms like Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and Support Vector Machines to identify key determinants such as age, socioeconomic status, environmental factors like water source and sanitation, and maternal health factors. While not exclusively focused on Cryptosporidium spp., these investigations provide valuable insights into the broader landscape of diarrhea risk factors that may overlap with cryptosporidiosis. In the context of predicting infection severity or outcome, machine learning has been employed in studies concerning various infectious diseases [ ]. For instance, models have been developed to predict the severity of respiratory infections based on clinical parameters. While specific studies directly applying machine learning to predict the severity of Cryptosporidium spp. diarrhea in humans within the 2019–2024 timeframe are not explicitly detailed in the provided snippets, the broader application of these techniques to other infectious diseases suggests their potential utility in this area [ ]. The analysis of genomic data of Cryptosporidium using bioinformatics pipelines, some developed to ISO standards for public health investigations, also indicates a move towards leveraging advanced computational methods for understanding and potentially predicting disease characteristics [ ]. The methods used in these new studies are diverse and include different machine learning algorithms such as Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, and Neural Networks [ ]. The sources of data used are varied, including demographic health surveys, hospital clinical records, environmental monitoring data, and, more recently, genomic data about the parasite [ ]. This increasing trend to employ diverse datasets and complex machine learning methods reflects the increasing promise to gain insights into Cryptosporidium spp. diarrhea and correlates of risk via computational modeling. Robust machine learning models need to be built for predicting Cryptosporidium spp. diarrhea that should be a combined integration between the listed risk factors and the adopted analytical methods. One such framework is the inclusion of host factors (e.g., age, immune status [including CD4, if available], and nutritional status) and environmental factors (e.g., water quality, climate [temperature, rainfall], and exposure history [contact with animals, recreational water]) as input features. Furthermore, the inclusion of pathogen‐specific variables such as the particular C. species, if available, or genotype or subtype data may improve the predictive performance of the model. To forecast the probability of infection or the risk for severe disease, models of classification as manifested by logistic regression, random forests, or neural networks can be used. Such models could be trained on data sets containing either Cryptosporidium spp. ‐positive and ‐negative subjects or positive subjects with differing levels of disease severity. Regression approaches, however, could be used to estimate continuous outcomes such as the duration of diarrhea or oocyst shedding, the former of the two not assessed in our study. Such models could be trained on data sets containing either Cryptosporidium spp. ‐positive and ‐negative subjects or positive subjects with differing levels of disease severity. Regression approaches, however, could be used to estimate continuous outcomes such as the duration of diarrhea or oocyst shedding, the former of the two not assessed in our study. Techniques such as linear regression, support vector regression, and random forests could be deployed to achieve this. The power of these modeling tools relies on the feasible access to extensive and high‐quality datasets that integrate clinical, epidemiological, and eventually genomic data. Special consideration needs to be taken for missing value treatment and for noise in the features. Feature selection and engineering methods would be critical to discovering the most informative predictors of the outcomes of Cryptosporidium spp. diarrhea. The developed models require thorough validation to ensure their accuracy and applicability. As for classification tasks, the accuracy, precision, recall, F1‐score, and area under the precision‐recall curve (PRAUC) are always recommended [ , ]. In this study, machine‐learning methods were used to determine the factors associated with diarrhea caused by Cryptosporidium , which is widespread and causes severe diarrhea in young children. In these models, the presence or absence of Cryptosporidium was used as the output variable, and the variables with the highest percentage of explanation of this variable were evaluated using variable importance values. As a result of modeling using the random forest technique, the performance metrics accuracy, balanced accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and F1 score were obtained as 87.7%, 51.2%, 2.7%, 99.6%, 50.0%, 88.0%, and 5.1%, respectively, in the testing data set. Likewise, as a result of modeling using the bagged CART technique, the performance metrics accuracy, balanced accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and F1 score were obtained as 87.2%, 56.3%, 97.2%, 15.4%, 89.3%, 42.9%, and 93.0%, respectively. When the performance metrics obtained from the modeling were examined, it was observed that the results obtained from the bagged CART model were better than those obtained using the random forest method. The bagged CART model successfully classified the presence or absence of the Cryptosporidium output variable, and the variable significance values obtained from this model were evaluated to determine factors related to ≥ Cryptosporidium . According to the variable significance values obtained, it was found that the five most important factors associated with the Cryptosporidium output variable were household members ≥ 5, water source public tap water, water source piped water no, animal no, and age 12–23 months. When related variables were examined, it could be said that water resources are the most important transmission factors for this parasite species. In previous studies, this parasite was reported to be the leading cause of waterborne outbreaks [ , ]. Inaddition, in many studies conducted in different countries, Cryptosporidium has been detected in different water types (domestic water, drinking water, surface water, etc.) [ , ]. 5 Conclusions In conclusion, Cryptosporidium spp. continues to be a significant contributor to diarrheal disease globally, particularly in high‐risk populations. The pathogenesis is due to a relatively complex life cycle in the intestinal epithelium, which results in a broad spectrum of clinical disease that can range from mild and self‐limited to severe and fatal, depending on host, environmental, and pathogen attributes. Machine learning approaches provide a promising modality for the modeling of such complicated interactions in order to better understand and control this infection. The method of applying machine learning has the potential to significantly improve the diagnosis of cryptosporidiosis, e.g., by automatically analyzing stool sample images to predict diagnosis [ ], for early identification of individuals with risk of severe disease, and to inform public health interventions and resource allocation during outbreaks [ ]. Further studies to build more generalizable and stronger machine learning models are required with large and multi‐center data sets, which include as many relevant features that could be included. By incorporating the genomic data for both Cryptosporidium spp. and host genetic factors into predictive models, we would gain further insight into the susceptibility or severity of the disease. Investigating the explainable AI (XAI) methodologies could be useful to improve the interpretability of these models and to reveal new insights about the disease mechanisms [ ]. In the end, the validation of these models within the clinical and public sector practice will be essential for their effective implementation and impact on the global burden of cryptosporidiosis. Future work should validate models in multi‐country cohorts with genomic and environmental metadata to improve generalizability. Although there is insufficient information to reach a general conclusion, it has been supported and accepted by many studies that factors that increase the risk of diarrhea due to cryptosporidiosis are poor hygienic conditions, infection of wastewater, and mixing of potable water contaminated with animal/human feces into drinking water. As the elimination of Cryptosporidium is difficult and the probability of infection recurrence is high, the main treatment approach should be disease prevention. Therefore, it is important to improve the quality and disinfection of drinking water. Funding The authors have nothing to report. documents.title: AAP policy statement breastfeeding and the use of human milk

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Human breast milk (HBM) is an ideal and essential source of nutrition for the healthy development of infants ( ), and accordingly, the World Health Organization ( ), the European Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition ( ), and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the six months of life ( ). In addition, HBM contains diverse biological compounds such as immune-regulating factors, which contribute to the maintenance and enhancement of the neonatal immune system ( ). Exosomes are membrane-bound extracellular vesicles (EVs) ranging in size between 30 nm and 150 nm ( ). They carry complex molecular cargos such as proteins, lipids, mRNAs, and microRNAs (miRNAs), which reflect the physiological state of the maternal cell, modulate cellular responses, and serve as important mediators of intercellular communication ( ; ). Exosomes are present in various body fluids including HBM, and HBM-derived exosomes have been shown to resist digestive degradation and enter systemic circulation to influence gene expression or immune signaling in recipient cells ( ). Specifically, Kim et al. have reported that HBM-derived exosomes modulate macrophage and T cell responses, promoting regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation while attenuating pro-inflammatory Th1 and Th17 activity ( ). Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common chronic rheumatic disease in children, characterized by persistent joint inflammation with onset before the age of 16 ( ). JIA represents a clinically heterogeneous group of disorders and includes multiple subtypes, such as systemic, oligoarticular, and polyarticular forms. The pathogenesis of JIA is believed to involve both innate and adaptive immune dysfunction ( ). Systemic JIA, in particular, is more autoinflammatory in nature, characterized by excessive activation of monocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils leading to cytokine storms driven by IL-1, IL-6, and IL-18. Other forms of JIA, however, are more autoimmune and driven by autoreactive T cells and autoantibodies ( ). Although the etiology of JIA is multifactorial, involving genetic predisposition and environmental triggers, increasing evidence suggests that early-life immune modulation plays a significant role in disease susceptibility ( ). Epidemiological studies have reported an inverse association between breastfeeding and the incidence of JIA ( ). A case-control study in a prospective birth cohort in Sweden showed that breastfeeding for more than four months was associated with a reduced risk of JIA ( ). Similar findings were reported in cohort studies conducted in UK ( ), indicating that early-life exposure to breast milk may modulate immune responses in a way that reduces autoimmune susceptibility ( ). However, the mechanisms by which breastfeeding confers such protection are not well understood. Specifically, the role of HBM-derived exosomes in modulating inflammatory responses relevant to JIA has not been systematically investigated. Given the immunoregulatory potential of breast milk exosomes, particularly their capacity to influence T cell differentiation and inflammatory signaling, it is plausible that they contribute to the observed protective effects. In this study, we aim to isolate and characterize exosomes from HBM, and investigate their immunomodulatory effects in the context of JIA. By elucidating how these exosomes regulate immune pathways involved in JIA pathogenesis, we seek to uncover novel insights into the early-life origins of autoimmunity and the therapeutic potential of natural exosomal cargo. MATERIALS AND METHODS Collection of human breast milk samples HBM was obtained from consenting lactating mothers at the Chung-Ang University Breastfeeding Research Institute in Seoul, South Korea, under IRB approval (IRB NO: 1041078-20251016-BR-375). Freshly collected milk was aliquoted into 15 mL tubes and stored at –80°C until use. Isolation of breast milk-derived exosomes To minimize donor variability, HBM from at least 10 individuals was pooled and thawed. Exosome isolation involved sequential centrifugation. First, samples were centrifuged at 2,000×g for 10 min and 12,000×g for 60 min at 4°C to obtain the whey. The resulting supernatants were transferred to Optiseal tubes (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA, USA) and ultracentrifuged at 30,000×g and 70,000×g for 60 min each at 4°C (Beckman Coulter Optima XE-100 with Type 50.2 Ti Fixed angle ultracentrifuge rotor). The final supernatants were filtered through 0.8, 0.45, and 0.22 μm syringe filters (Sartorius AG, Göttingen, Germany), then centrifuged at 100,000×g for 120 min at 4°C. The resulting pellets were resuspended in PBS and loaded onto a 35 nm qEV column (Izon Science Ltd., Christchurch, Canterbury, New Zealand), and fractions 7-9 were used for experiments. Nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) Exosome size and concentration were measured using a NanoSight NS300 (Malvern Panalytical Ltd., Malvern, UK) with NTA 3.4 software. Samples were analyzed in flow mode at a syringe pump speed of 30; each result was captured ten times for 30 s using a 488 nm laser. Isolation of peritoneal macrophages Peritoneal macrophages were isolated from male C57BL/6 mice (≥5 weeks; Raonbio, Seoul, Korea) by injecting 10 mL PBS into the peritoneal cavity, performing a gentle massage, and collecting the suspension. After centrifugation, the cells

Samples were analyzed in flow mode at a syringe pump speed of 30; each result was captured ten times for 30 s using a 488 nm laser. Isolation of peritoneal macrophages Peritoneal macrophages were isolated from male C57BL/6 mice (≥5 weeks; Raonbio, Seoul, Korea) by injecting 10 mL PBS into the peritoneal cavity, performing a gentle massage, and collecting the suspension. After centrifugation, the cells were resuspended in RPMI 1640 (Welgene, Daegu, Korea) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Welgene), and 1% (v/v) penicillin/streptomycin (P/S; Gibco, Grand Island, NY, USA). The cells were incubated for at least 4 h at 37°C, and adherent cells were subsequently used for experiments. <sup>In vitro</sup> differentiation of bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMM) Bone marrow was extracted from the tibia and femur of euthanized male mice (C57BL/6) by flushing with ACK lysing buffer, and then centrifuged. Cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM; Welgene) supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% P/S, and 20 ng/mL M-CSF (Biolegend, San Diego, CA, USA). On day 5, adherent cells were seeded onto plates and treated with HBM-derived exosomes (250 or 500 µg/mL). After 24 h, M1 differentiation was induced with IFN-γ (Biolegend) and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), and M2 differentiation was induced with IL-4 (Biolegend) and IL-13 (Biolegend) for an additional 24 h. SW1353 cell culture SW1353 cells, the human chondrosarcoma cell line, were maintained in DMEM containing 10% (v/v) FBS and 1% (v/v) P/S at 37°C. When cells reached appropriate confluency, they were detached and passaged using a 1X working solution of Trypsin-EDTA (Welgene; 0.5% trypsin and 5.3 mM EDTA in 0.9% NaCl) prepared from a 10X stock. The culture medium was replaced two to three times per week. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) ELISA was performed to quantify the levels of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 secreted by BMMs and peritoneal macrophages. Cells were seeded in 12-well plates and pretreated with exosomes (250 or 500 μg/mL) for 24 h, followed by stimulation with lipopolysaccharide (LPS, 1 μg/mL; Sigma-Aldrich) for 18 h. After stimulation, culture supernatants were collected and clarified by centrifugation to remove cell debris. Cytokine concentrations were determined by sandwich ELISA using specific antibody pairs according to standard protocols. Information on the antibody pairs used is as follows. Primary antibodies: hTNF-α (MAb1, Biolegend), hIL-6 (MQ2-13A5, eBioscience, San Diego, CA, USA), hIL-1β (CRM56, eBioscience), mTNF-α (TN3-19.12, eBioscience), mIL-6 (MP5-20F3, BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA), mIL-1β (B122). Secondary antibodies: hTNF-α (Mab11, Biolegend), hIL-6 (MQ2-39C3, eBioscience), hIL-1β (CRM57, eBioscience), mTNF-α (13-7341-85, eBioscience), mIL-6 (MP5-32C11, BD Biosciences), mIL-1β (13-7112-85, eBioscience). To generate a standard curve, recombinant human TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β cytokines (PeproTech ® , Rocky Hill, NJ, USA) were used and streptavidin-conjugated alkaline phosphatase (Code:016-050-084, Jackson ImmunoResearch, West Grove, PA, USA) served as the detection reagent. For substrate development, substrate tablets (Sigma-Aldrich, N2765, 20 mg) were freshly dissolved in substrate buffer at a final concentration of 1 mg/mL. Absorbance was measured at 405 nm using a microplate reader (Emax microplate reader, Molecular Devices, Sunnyvale, CA, USA). Quantitative analysis of mRNA expression Total RNA was isolated from 3×10⁵ cells using RNAiso Plus (Takara Bio Inc., Kusatsu, Japan), followed by chloroform (Sigma-Aldrich) extraction and isopropanol (2-Propanol, 99.5%; Samchun Pure Chemical Co., Korea) precipitation. After washing the RNA pellet with 75% ethanol, samples were air-dried and dissolved in RNase-free water. The RNA was incubated at 55-60°C to enhance solubilization. The extracted RNA was then reverse-transcribed into cDNA using a commercially available reverse transcription kit. Quantitative PCR was conducted using the TOPreal™ SYBR Green RT-qPCR Kit (Enzynomics, Daejeon, Korea) on a CFX Connect™ Real-Time PCR Detection System (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, USA). Gene expression was analyzed in macrophages and SW1353 cells. The primer sequences used in this study are listed in . Western blotting Western blotting was performed to verify exosome identification and assess the activation of inflammatory signaling pathways. To verify successful exosome isolation, whey and exosomes were separately collected into 1.5 mL tubes and stored at –20°C before use. Protein concentration of both samples were quantified using Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo-Fisher Scientific, Rockford, IL, USA), and exosome-specific markers Flotillin-1 (#18634, Cell signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA), HSP70 (#4876, Cell signaling Technology), CD81 (#56039, Cell signaling Technology), CD9 (#13174, Cell signaling Technology), Annexin V (#8555, Cell signaling Technology) were analyzed by western blotting. The detailed western blotting procedure was identical to the method described below. SW1353 cells were seeded in 12-well plates at a density of 3×10⁵ cells/mL under four experimental conditions: negative control (NC), positive control (PC), and treatment groups with 250 µg/mL and 500 µg/mL exosomes, respectively. The day after

samples were quantified using Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo-Fisher Scientific, Rockford, IL, USA), and exosome-specific markers Flotillin-1 (#18634, Cell signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA), HSP70 (#4876, Cell signaling Technology), CD81 (#56039, Cell signaling Technology), CD9 (#13174, Cell signaling Technology), Annexin V (#8555, Cell signaling Technology) were analyzed by western blotting. The detailed western blotting procedure was identical to the method described below. SW1353 cells were seeded in 12-well plates at a density of 3×10⁵ cells/mL under four experimental conditions: negative control (NC), positive control (PC), and treatment groups with 250 µg/mL and 500 µg/mL exosomes, respectively. The day after seeding, cells in the treatment groups were treated with exosomes at 250 or 500 µg/mL. After 24 h, all wells except the NC group were stimulated with Human recombinant IL-1β (Cat. #200-01B, PeproTech ® ) and incubated for 30 min to activate inflammatory signaling pathways. Cells were lysed using Pierce™ RIPA Buffer (Thermo-Fisher Scientific), and total protein was quantified using the Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo-Fisher Scientific). Equal amounts of denatured protein were separated on 12% SDS-PAGE gels, and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes (Amersham, Piscataway, NJ, USA) using a wet transfer system at 4°C. Membranes were blocked with 5% skim milk in TBS-T for 1 h, then incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies targeting phospho-p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) (Thr180/Tyr182, #4631S, Cell signaling Technology), total p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK) (clone: Poly6224, BioLegend), phospho-ERK1/2 (Thr202/Tyr204, #4370T, Cell signaling Technology), total ERK1/2 (sc-514302, Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Dallas, TX, USA), phospho-JNK (Thr183/Tyr185, #4668S, Cell signaling Technology), total c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) (#9252, Cell signaling Technology), phospho-IκBα (Ser32/36, #9246S, Cell signaling Technology), total IκBα (#4812S, Cell signaling Technology), and GAPDH (#2118S, Cell signaling Technology). Following incubation with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies (anti-rabbit IgG-HRP, anti-mouse IgG-HRP), for 1 h, protein bands were visualized using the Westsave Femto™ enhanced chemiluminescence substrate (AbFrontier, Seoul, Korea) on a Fusion Solo X imaging system (Vilber, Paris, France). Band intensities were quantified using Fusion software, and phosphorylated proteins were normalized to their respective total protein levels or GAPDH. Flow cytometry M1/M2 differentiation of BMM was analyzed by flow cytometry. Following cytokine treatment, cells were harvested, washed, and incubated with Fc block (0.1 μL per sample) to minimize nonspecific binding. Subsequently, cells were stained with fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies against F4/80 (BioLegend, 123107), CD11b (BioLegend, 101212), CD80 (BioLegend, 104733), and CD206 (BioLegend, 162503) (0.2 μL per sample, with PE-conjugated antibodies at 0.1 μL). Samples were incubated for 30 min at 4°C in the dark, washed, and then subjected to fixation and permeabilization (Fix:Perm=1:3, 200 μL per sample) for 30 min. Intracellular staining was carried out using the same antibody concentrations prepared in permeabilization buffer. Data were acquired on a FACS Calibur flow cytometer (BD Biosciences), and analysis was conducted using CellQuest Pro software. Macrophage populations were gated on CD11b + F4/80 + cells, and their polarization status was determined by identifying CD80 + CD206 - cells as M1 macrophages and CD80 - CD206 + cells as M2 macrophages. Statistical analysis All experiments were performed in at least three replicates, and the results from each replicate are presented as the mean ± SEM using GraphPad Prism v. 5 software (GraphPad, San Diego, CA, USA). Statistical analysis was conducted using one-way ANOVA, and differences were considered significant at * p <0.05; ** p <0.01; and *** p <0.001. RESULTS Characterization of HBM-derived exosomes HBM-derived exosomes were collected using ultracentrifugation. Their size was analyzed through NTA, which indicated a mean size of approximately 88.1 nm, and a most frequently detected particle size of 42.5 nm ( ). Additionally, the expression of exosomal markers such as Flotillin-1, HSP70, CD81, CD9, and Annexin V was confirmed via Western blot ( ). Anti-inflammatory effects of HBM-derived exosomes on peritoneal macrophages To evaluate the anti-inflammatory effects of HBM-derived exosomes on peritoneal macrophages, ELISA, qPCR, and Western blot analysis were conducted. Exosome treatment decreased the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines including TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β, upon LPS stimulation ( ). Additionally, the expression of inflammatory factors such as inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) was decreased at both mRNA ( ) and protein ( ) levels. Effects of HBM-derived exosomes on BMM differentiation To investigate the effects of HBM-derived exosomes on M1/M2 differentiation of BMMs, FACS and ELISA analysis were performed. FACS results demonstrated that HBM-derived exosomes decreased the expression of the M1 marker CD80 while increasing the expression of the M2 marker CD206 dose-dependently ( , ). Furthermore, ELISA analysis of the supernatant revealed a concentration-dependent decrease in the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β, in BMM upon LPS stimulation ( ). Anti-inflammatory effects of HBM-derived exosomes in SW1353 cells Building on the previously observed anti-inflammatory effects of exosomes on macrophages, we addressed their effects on chondrocytes. SW1353 chondrocytes

To investigate the effects of HBM-derived exosomes on M1/M2 differentiation of BMMs, FACS and ELISA analysis were performed. FACS results demonstrated that HBM-derived exosomes decreased the expression of the M1 marker CD80 while increasing the expression of the M2 marker CD206 dose-dependently ( , ). Furthermore, ELISA analysis of the supernatant revealed a concentration-dependent decrease in the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β, in BMM upon LPS stimulation ( ). Anti-inflammatory effects of HBM-derived exosomes in SW1353 cells Building on the previously observed anti-inflammatory effects of exosomes on macrophages, we addressed their effects on chondrocytes. SW1353 chondrocytes were stimulated with IL-1β to induce inflammation, and the expression of MMP-1, MMP-3, MMP-13, iNOS, and COX-2 was assessed by qPCR. MMPs, as zinc-dependent endopeptidases, are crucial for the degradation of extracellular matrix components and play significant roles in various processes, including tissue remodeling, inflammation, and wound healing. Measuring MMP expression levels allowed us to evaluate the potential of HBM-derived exosomes to reduce IL-1β-induced inflammation and cartilage degradation. The data showed that exosomes reduced the expression of MMP-1, MMP-3 and MMP-13, as well as the inflammatory mediators, iNOS and COX-2 ( ). Furthermore, Western blot analysis demonstrated that HBM-derived exosomes attenuated the phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), JNK, p38, and IκBα in a dose-dependent manner ( ). ERK, JNK, and p38 are major components of the MAPK pathway, while IκBα is a key regulator of NF-κB activation. Quantification based on the phospho/total protein ratio also confirmed that higher concentrations of exosomes consistently led to greater suppression of these signaling molecules ( ). DISCUSSION HBM is rich in both macronutrients and micronutrients essential for the health of infants ( ). Beyond its nutritional value, HBM contains numerous bioactive components which crucially support the infant’s growth and development. Exosomes specifically extracted from HBM were first studied in 2007, and marked an important milestone in understanding the role of maternal bioactive compounds ( ). These exosomes transfer proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and other cellular materials to recipient cells, thereby influencing various biological processes, including inflammation, stress defense, stem cell growth, etc. ( ). Breastfeeding, therefore, offers notable health benefits to both mother and infant ( ), and according to the Developmental Origins of Health and Disease hypothesis, early exposure to environmental factors in HBM may influence long- term health outcomes and disease risk ( ). Given the established importance of HBM-derived exosomes, we aimed to evaluate their anti-inflammatory properties through in vitro experiments involving peritoneal macrophages, BMM, and the SW1353 chondrocyte cell line. In peritoneal macrophages, where inflammation was induced by LPS, HBM-derived exosome treatment led to a dose-dependent reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion, and iNOS and COX-2 expression ( ). To further characterize this anti-inflammatory activity, we evaluated the impact of HBM-derived exosomes on macrophage polarization in BMM. Macrophages are central players in inflammation and can adopt a spectrum of polarization states, from pro-inflammatory M1 to anti-inflammatory M2 phenotypes ( ; ; ; ). M1 macrophages promote tissue damage by secreting TNF-α and IL-1β, while M2 macrophages aid in tissue repair and immune resolution ( ; ; ). Macrophages have emerged as central players in synovial inflammation, where dysregulated innate immune responses contribute to the progression of various inflammatory joint conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) ( ; ; ). Our results demonstrated that HBM-derived exosomes modulate macrophage polarization toward an anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype ( ), implying the potential importance of HBM-derived exosomes in modulating inflammatory joint diseases. Furthermore, to investigate the potential relevance of these findings to arthritis, we used SW1353 chondrocyte cell line. Inflammation was induced by IL-1β, and the effect of HBM-derived exosomes on the expression of iNOS, COX-2, MMP-1, MMP-3, and MMP-13 was assessed. Exosome treatment significantly reduced the expression of these inflammatory mediators and MMPs ( ). Since MMPs are crucial for the degradation of extracellular matrix components and are deeply implicated in cartilage degradation and chronic inflammation, this finding strongly suggests that HBM-derived exosomes can suppress IL-1β induced-catabolic activity. Moreover, Western blot analysis demonstrated that HBM-derived exosomes attenuated the phosphorylation of ERK, JNK, p38 – major components of the MAPK pathway – and IκBα – a key regulator of NF-κB activation ( ). Together, these pathways orchestrate the induction of pro-inflammatory cytokines and matrix-degrading enzymes in response to IL-1β stimulation. Our results indicate that HBM-derived exosomes mitigate IL-1β–induced inflammation in SW1353 cells by downregulating MMPs, iNOS, and COX-2 expression through the inhibition of key MAPK and NF-κB signaling cascades. In a previous study ( ), we performed comprehensive proteomic and miRNA profiling of milk-derived exosomes and identified approximately 377 proteins and 208 miRNAs. Functional enrichment analyses (GO and KEGG) revealed that these components are significantly involved in modulating various physiological processes, particularly inflammatory signaling pathways. We speculate that specific bioactive

activation ( ). Together, these pathways orchestrate the induction of pro-inflammatory cytokines and matrix-degrading enzymes in response to IL-1β stimulation. Our results indicate that HBM-derived exosomes mitigate IL-1β–induced inflammation in SW1353 cells by downregulating MMPs, iNOS, and COX-2 expression through the inhibition of key MAPK and NF-κB signaling cascades. In a previous study ( ), we performed comprehensive proteomic and miRNA profiling of milk-derived exosomes and identified approximately 377 proteins and 208 miRNAs. Functional enrichment analyses (GO and KEGG) revealed that these components are significantly involved in modulating various physiological processes, particularly inflammatory signaling pathways. We speculate that specific bioactive molecules within the exosomal cargo, such as miRNAs and proteins associated with signal transduction, work synergistically to suppress the MAPK and NF-κB signaling cascades, thereby reducing the expression of MMPs, iNOS, and COX-2. While further research is needed to identify the exact contribution of individual component, our data provide a strong mechanistic basis for the anti-inflammatory and anti-catabolic effects of HBM-derived exosomes in chondrocytes. In addition, while our findings provide valuable insights into the immunomodulatory effects of HBM-derived exosomes, this study has some limitations. Although the IL-1β-stimulated SW1353 system is a useful in vitro model for studying inflammatory responses, it does not fully recapitulate the complex, multi-cellular pathophysiology of inflammatory joint diseases. Specifically, this model lacks the intricate interactions between immune cells and synovial tissues. Furthermore, while primary human chondrocytes or synoviocytes would offer higher clinical relevance, we utilized cell lines in this study. Future studies should employ primary human-derived systems or in vivo models to further validate these findings in a clinical context. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that HBM-derived exosomes modulate macrophage polarization toward the M2 phenotype and exhibit significant anti-inflammatory and anti-catabolic effects by inhibiting the MAPK and NF-κB signaling pathways. These results offer new insights into the potential role of HBM-derived exosomes in managing inflammatory response relevant to joint diseases.

chunks.content: 1. Introduction Breast cancer remains the most prevalent cancer worldwide, with approximately 80% of cases classified as estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) [ ]. Tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM), is widely used as an endocrine therapy for hormone-sensitive breast cancer, significantly reducing the risks of recurrence, breast cancer-related mortality, and overall mortality [ , ]. Despite its proven efficacy, approximately 30% to 50% of patients experience relapse and disease progression, even among those with similar clinical profiles [ ]. This observed variability in treatment response suggests that factors beyond standard clinical parameters may be involved. Notably, pharmacogenetic factors are increasingly recognized as contributors to treatment variability. These include drug–gene interactions (DGIs), which capture the influence of genetic polymorphisms on drug pharmacokinetics; drug–gene–gene interactions (DGGIs), which account for the combined effects of multiple polymorphisms in alternative pathways; and drug–drug–gene interactions (DDGIs), in which concomitant medications intersect with a patient’s genetic makeup [ ]. DGIs occur when genetic polymorphisms influence the activity of drug-metabolizing enzymes (DMEs), leading to altered drug metabolism and potential variability in therapeutic response and the risk of adverse drug reactions (ADRs) [ , ]. In tamoxifen therapy, genetic variations in phase I enzymes impact the bioactivation of tamoxifen into its potent metabolites, such as endoxifen, while polymorphisms in phase II enzymes modulate metabolite clearance, and efflux and influx transporters regulate intracellular drug distribution. These genetic variations may contribute to differences in drug levels, potentially affecting treatment efficacy and safety. Moreover, the complexity of these interactions is compounded by multifactorial influences, which may manifest as additive, synergistic, or opposing effects. Such variations encompass DGGIs, wherein mismatches between expected and actual metabolic capacities occur due to the genotype of alternative pathway enzymes. In the context of tamoxifen metabolism, the involvement of multiple pharmacogenes further accentuates the complexities surrounding treatment response. Beyond genetic factors, tamoxifen metabolism can also be influenced by non-genetic elements. Drug–drug–gene interactions (DDGIs) arise when a patient’s genetic predispositions intersect with the use of certain concomitant medications. Even in the adjuvant setting, where tamoxifen is commonly prescribed, some co-medications may cause drug–drug interactions (DDIs). These interactions are generally well-recognized, routinely managed in clinical practice, and rarely result in serious consequences. Nevertheless, when combined with pharmacogenetic variability, even routine DDIs may have amplified effects, potentially altering tamoxifen metabolism and therapeutic outcomes. This is particularly relevant given that the vast majority of individuals harbor at least one clinically actionable genotype that could impact the treatment [ , , ]. Advancements in pharmacogenomics have contributed to a better understanding of interindividual variability in drug response. However, despite growing interest and progress in the field, clinical findings remain heterogeneous, and the translation of pharmacogenomic insights into routine practice continues to face debate. This review examines the current body of evidence on DGIs, DGGIs, and DDGIs in the context of tamoxifen metabolism. Key enzymes and pathways are detailed, illustrating how pharmacogenetic variability and polypharmacy intersect to influence tamoxifen metabolism. Clinical challenges related to these interactions are considered, along with an overview of existing tamoxifen management strategies. The potential role of pharmacogenomic integration in clinical practice is also outlined, with a view toward supporting more individualized and effective therapeutic decisions. 2. Materials and Methods A literature search was conducted using MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library up to June 2025. Articles were included if they were original research studies or reviews reporting on genetic variability, comedication effects, or their impact on tamoxifen pharmacokinetics or clinical efficacy, and published in English. Additionally, references of included articles were checked to identify further relevant studies. Key information extracted included study design, patient population, genetic variants or metabolic pathways analyzed, comedication effects, pharmacokinetic data, and clinical outcomes. Findings were synthesized narratively. 3. Genetic Variation Impact on Tamoxifen Therapy 3.1. Tamoxifen Metabolism Tamoxifen undergoes multiple metabolic and transport processes before exerting its therapeutic effect ( ). As a prodrug, its efficacy depends largely on biotransformation by the cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme system, which generates active metabolites with up to 100-fold greater antiestrogenic potency than the parent drug ( ) [ ]. Tamoxifen metabolism predominantly proceeds through two key pathways, N-demethylation and 4-hydroxylation, both leading to the formation of the highly potent secondary metabolite, endoxifen. The N-demethylation pathway accounts for approximately 92% of tamoxifen biotransformation, primarily catalysed by CYP3A4/5. This results in the production of N-desmethyltamoxifen (DM-TAM), the most abundant metabolite, which is subsequently converted to endoxifen through CYP2D6. In parallel, a smaller fraction of tamoxifen undergoes 4-hydroxylation, mediated by various CYP enzymes, including CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2B6, and CYP3A4/5, generating 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OH-TAM) (refer to ). Although 4-OH-TAM is also a potent metabolite, its concentration is 10 times lower than that of endoxifen [ ]. This metabolite is further demethylated by CYP3A4/5 to produce endoxifen, which is considered the primary active metabolite responsible for tamoxifen’s antiestrogenic effect [ ]. Following
