documents.title: AAP policy statement breastfeeding and the use of human milk

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Human breast milk (HBM) is an ideal and essential source of nutrition for the healthy development of infants ( ), and accordingly, the World Health Organization ( ), the European Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition ( ), and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the six months of life ( ). In addition, HBM contains diverse biological compounds such as immune-regulating factors, which contribute to the maintenance and enhancement of the neonatal immune system ( ). Exosomes are membrane-bound extracellular vesicles (EVs) ranging in size between 30 nm and 150 nm ( ). They carry complex molecular cargos such as proteins, lipids, mRNAs, and microRNAs (miRNAs), which reflect the physiological state of the maternal cell, modulate cellular responses, and serve as important mediators of intercellular communication ( ; ). Exosomes are present in various body fluids including HBM, and HBM-derived exosomes have been shown to resist digestive degradation and enter systemic circulation to influence gene expression or immune signaling in recipient cells ( ). Specifically, Kim et al. have reported that HBM-derived exosomes modulate macrophage and T cell responses, promoting regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation while attenuating pro-inflammatory Th1 and Th17 activity ( ). Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common chronic rheumatic disease in children, characterized by persistent joint inflammation with onset before the age of 16 ( ). JIA represents a clinically heterogeneous group of disorders and includes multiple subtypes, such as systemic, oligoarticular, and polyarticular forms. The pathogenesis of JIA is believed to involve both innate and adaptive immune dysfunction ( ). Systemic JIA, in particular, is more autoinflammatory in nature, characterized by excessive activation of monocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils leading to cytokine storms driven by IL-1, IL-6, and IL-18. Other forms of JIA, however, are more autoimmune and driven by autoreactive T cells and autoantibodies ( ). Although the etiology of JIA is multifactorial, involving genetic predisposition and environmental triggers, increasing evidence suggests that early-life immune modulation plays a significant role in disease susceptibility ( ). Epidemiological studies have reported an inverse association between breastfeeding and the incidence of JIA ( ). A case-control study in a prospective birth cohort in Sweden showed that breastfeeding for more than four months was associated with a reduced risk of JIA ( ). Similar findings were reported in cohort studies conducted in UK ( ), indicating that early-life exposure to breast milk may modulate immune responses in a way that reduces autoimmune susceptibility ( ). However, the mechanisms by which breastfeeding confers such protection are not well understood. Specifically, the role of HBM-derived exosomes in modulating inflammatory responses relevant to JIA has not been systematically investigated. Given the immunoregulatory potential of breast milk exosomes, particularly their capacity to influence T cell differentiation and inflammatory signaling, it is plausible that they contribute to the observed protective effects. In this study, we aim to isolate and characterize exosomes from HBM, and investigate their immunomodulatory effects in the context of JIA. By elucidating how these exosomes regulate immune pathways involved in JIA pathogenesis, we seek to uncover novel insights into the early-life origins of autoimmunity and the therapeutic potential of natural exosomal cargo. MATERIALS AND METHODS Collection of human breast milk samples HBM was obtained from consenting lactating mothers at the Chung-Ang University Breastfeeding Research Institute in Seoul, South Korea, under IRB approval (IRB NO: 1041078-20251016-BR-375). Freshly collected milk was aliquoted into 15 mL tubes and stored at –80°C until use. Isolation of breast milk-derived exosomes To minimize donor variability, HBM from at least 10 individuals was pooled and thawed. Exosome isolation involved sequential centrifugation. First, samples were centrifuged at 2,000×g for 10 min and 12,000×g for 60 min at 4°C to obtain the whey. The resulting supernatants were transferred to Optiseal tubes (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA, USA) and ultracentrifuged at 30,000×g and 70,000×g for 60 min each at 4°C (Beckman Coulter Optima XE-100 with Type 50.2 Ti Fixed angle ultracentrifuge rotor). The final supernatants were filtered through 0.8, 0.45, and 0.22 μm syringe filters (Sartorius AG, Göttingen, Germany), then centrifuged at 100,000×g for 120 min at 4°C. The resulting pellets were resuspended in PBS and loaded onto a 35 nm qEV column (Izon Science Ltd., Christchurch, Canterbury, New Zealand), and fractions 7-9 were used for experiments. Nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) Exosome size and concentration were measured using a NanoSight NS300 (Malvern Panalytical Ltd., Malvern, UK) with NTA 3.4 software. Samples were analyzed in flow mode at a syringe pump speed of 30; each result was captured ten times for 30 s using a 488 nm laser. After centrifugation, the cells

Samples were analyzed in flow mode at a syringe pump speed of 30; each result was captured ten times for 30 s using a 488 nm laser. Isolation of peritoneal macrophages Peritoneal macrophages were isolated from male C57BL/6 mice (≥5 weeks; Raonbio, Seoul, Korea) by injecting 10 mL PBS into the peritoneal cavity, performing a gentle massage, and collecting the suspension. After centrifugation, the cells were resuspended in RPMI 1640 (Welgene, Daegu, Korea) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Welgene), and 1% (v/v) penicillin/streptomycin (P/S; Gibco, Grand Island, NY, USA). The cells were incubated for at least 4 h at 37°C, and adherent cells were subsequently used for experiments. <sup>In vitro</sup> differentiation of bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMM) Bone marrow was extracted from the tibia and femur of euthanized male mice (C57BL/6) by flushing with ACK lysing buffer, and then centrifuged. Cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM; Welgene) supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% P/S, and 20 ng/mL M-CSF (Biolegend, San Diego, CA, USA). On day 5, adherent cells were seeded onto plates and treated with HBM-derived exosomes (250 or 500 µg/mL). After 24 h, M1 differentiation was induced with IFN-γ (Biolegend) and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), and M2 differentiation was induced with IL-4 (Biolegend) and IL-13 (Biolegend) for an additional 24 h. SW1353 cell culture SW1353 cells, the human chondrosarcoma cell line, were maintained in DMEM containing 10% (v/v) FBS and 1% (v/v) P/S at 37°C. When cells reached appropriate confluency, they were detached and passaged using a 1X working solution of Trypsin-EDTA (Welgene; 0.5% trypsin and 5.3 mM EDTA in 0.9% NaCl) prepared from a 10X stock. The culture medium was replaced two to three times per week. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) ELISA was performed to quantify the levels of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 secreted by BMMs and peritoneal macrophages. Cells were seeded in 12-well plates and pretreated with exosomes (250 or 500 μg/mL) for 24 h, followed by stimulation with lipopolysaccharide (LPS, 1 μg/mL; Sigma-Aldrich) for 18 h. After stimulation, culture supernatants were collected and clarified by centrifugation to remove cell debris. Cytokine concentrations were determined by sandwich ELISA using specific antibody pairs according to standard protocols. Information on the antibody pairs used is as follows. Primary antibodies: hTNF-α (MAb1, Biolegend), hIL-6 (MQ2-13A5, eBioscience, San Diego, CA, USA), hIL-1β (CRM56, eBioscience), mTNF-α (TN3-19.12, eBioscience), mIL-6 (MP5-20F3, BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA), mIL-1β (B122). Secondary antibodies: hTNF-α (Mab11, Biolegend), hIL-6 (MQ2-39C3, eBioscience), hIL-1β (CRM57, eBioscience), mTNF-α (13-7341-85, eBioscience), mIL-6 (MP5-32C11, BD Biosciences), mIL-1β (13-7112-85, eBioscience). To generate a standard curve, recombinant human TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β cytokines (PeproTech ® , Rocky Hill, NJ, USA) were used and streptavidin-conjugated alkaline phosphatase (Code:016-050-084, Jackson ImmunoResearch, West Grove, PA, USA) served as the detection reagent. For substrate development, substrate tablets (Sigma-Aldrich, N2765, 20 mg) were freshly dissolved in substrate buffer at a final concentration of 1 mg/mL. Absorbance was measured at 405 nm using a microplate reader (Emax microplate reader, Molecular Devices, Sunnyvale, CA, USA). Quantitative analysis of mRNA expression Total RNA was isolated from 3×10⁵ cells using RNAiso Plus (Takara Bio Inc., Kusatsu, Japan), followed by chloroform (Sigma-Aldrich) extraction and isopropanol (2-Propanol, 99.5%; Samchun Pure Chemical Co., Korea) precipitation. After washing the RNA pellet with 75% ethanol, samples were air-dried and dissolved in RNase-free water. The RNA was incubated at 55-60°C to enhance solubilization. The extracted RNA was then reverse-transcribed into cDNA using a commercially available reverse transcription kit. Quantitative PCR was conducted using the TOPreal™ SYBR Green RT-qPCR Kit (Enzynomics, Daejeon, Korea) on a CFX Connect™ Real-Time PCR Detection System (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, USA). Gene expression was analyzed in macrophages and SW1353 cells. The primer sequences used in this study are listed in . Western blotting Western blotting was performed to verify exosome identification and assess the activation of inflammatory signaling pathways. To verify successful exosome isolation, whey and exosomes were separately collected into 1.5 mL tubes and stored at –20°C before use. Protein concentration of both samples were quantified using Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo-Fisher Scientific, Rockford, IL, USA), and exosome-specific markers Flotillin-1 (#18634, Cell signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA), HSP70 (#4876, Cell signaling Technology), CD81 (#56039, Cell signaling Technology), CD9 (#13174, Cell signaling Technology), Annexin V (#8555, Cell signaling Technology) were analyzed by western blotting. The detailed western blotting procedure was identical to the method described below. SW1353 cells were seeded in 12-well plates at a density of 3×10⁵ cells/mL under four experimental conditions: negative control (NC), positive control (PC), and treatment groups with 250 µg/mL and 500 µg/mL exosomes, respectively. The day after

samples were quantified using Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo-Fisher Scientific, Rockford, IL, USA), and exosome-specific markers Flotillin-1 (#18634, Cell signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA), HSP70 (#4876, Cell signaling Technology), CD81 (#56039, Cell signaling Technology), CD9 (#13174, Cell signaling Technology), Annexin V (#8555, Cell signaling Technology) were analyzed by western blotting. The detailed western blotting procedure was identical to the method described below. SW1353 cells were seeded in 12-well plates at a density of 3×10⁵ cells/mL under four experimental conditions: negative control (NC), positive control (PC), and treatment groups with 250 µg/mL and 500 µg/mL exosomes, respectively. The day after seeding, cells in the treatment groups were treated with exosomes at 250 or 500 µg/mL. After 24 h, all wells except the NC group were stimulated with Human recombinant IL-1β (Cat. #200-01B, PeproTech ® ) and incubated for 30 min to activate inflammatory signaling pathways. Cells were lysed using Pierce™ RIPA Buffer (Thermo-Fisher Scientific), and total protein was quantified using the Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo-Fisher Scientific). Equal amounts of denatured protein were separated on 12% SDS-PAGE gels, and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes (Amersham, Piscataway, NJ, USA) using a wet transfer system at 4°C. Membranes were blocked with 5% skim milk in TBS-T for 1 h, then incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies targeting phospho-p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) (Thr180/Tyr182, #4631S, Cell signaling Technology), total p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK) (clone: Poly6224, BioLegend), phospho-ERK1/2 (Thr202/Tyr204, #4370T, Cell signaling Technology), total ERK1/2 (sc-514302, Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Dallas, TX, USA), phospho-JNK (Thr183/Tyr185, #4668S, Cell signaling Technology), total c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) (#9252, Cell signaling Technology), phospho-IκBα (Ser32/36, #9246S, Cell signaling Technology), total IκBα (#4812S, Cell signaling Technology), and GAPDH (#2118S, Cell signaling Technology). Following incubation with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies (anti-rabbit IgG-HRP, anti-mouse IgG-HRP), for 1 h, protein bands were visualized using the Westsave Femto™ enhanced chemiluminescence substrate (AbFrontier, Seoul, Korea) on a Fusion Solo X imaging system (Vilber, Paris, France). Band intensities were quantified using Fusion software, and phosphorylated proteins were normalized to their respective total protein levels or GAPDH. Flow cytometry M1/M2 differentiation of BMM was analyzed by flow cytometry. Following cytokine treatment, cells were harvested, washed, and incubated with Fc block (0.1 μL per sample) to minimize nonspecific binding. Subsequently, cells were stained with fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies against F4/80 (BioLegend, 123107), CD11b (BioLegend, 101212), CD80 (BioLegend, 104733), and CD206 (BioLegend, 162503) (0.2 μL per sample, with PE-conjugated antibodies at 0.1 μL). Samples were incubated for 30 min at 4°C in the dark, washed, and then subjected to fixation and permeabilization (Fix:Perm=1:3, 200 μL per sample) for 30 min. Intracellular staining was carried out using the same antibody concentrations prepared in permeabilization buffer. Data were acquired on a FACS Calibur flow cytometer (BD Biosciences), and analysis was conducted using CellQuest Pro software. Macrophage populations were gated on CD11b + F4/80 + cells, and their polarization status was determined by identifying CD80 + CD206 - cells as M1 macrophages and CD80 - CD206 + cells as M2 macrophages. Statistical analysis All experiments were performed in at least three replicates, and the results from each replicate are presented as the mean ± SEM using GraphPad Prism v. 5 software (GraphPad, San Diego, CA, USA). Statistical analysis was conducted using one-way ANOVA, and differences were considered significant at * p <0.05; ** p <0.01; and *** p <0.001. RESULTS Characterization of HBM-derived exosomes HBM-derived exosomes were collected using ultracentrifugation. Their size was analyzed through NTA, which indicated a mean size of approximately 88.1 nm, and a most frequently detected particle size of 42.5 nm ( ). Additionally, the expression of exosomal markers such as Flotillin-1, HSP70, CD81, CD9, and Annexin V was confirmed via Western blot ( ). Anti-inflammatory effects of HBM-derived exosomes on peritoneal macrophages To evaluate the anti-inflammatory effects of HBM-derived exosomes on peritoneal macrophages, ELISA, qPCR, and Western blot analysis were conducted. Exosome treatment decreased the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines including TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β, upon LPS stimulation ( ). Additionally, the expression of inflammatory factors such as inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) was decreased at both mRNA ( ) and protein ( ) levels. Effects of HBM-derived exosomes on BMM differentiation To investigate the effects of HBM-derived exosomes on M1/M2 differentiation of BMMs, FACS and ELISA analysis were performed. FACS results demonstrated that HBM-derived exosomes decreased the expression of the M1 marker CD80 while increasing the expression of the M2 marker CD206 dose-dependently ( , ). Furthermore, ELISA analysis of the supernatant revealed a concentration-dependent decrease in the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β, in BMM upon LPS stimulation ( ). Anti-inflammatory effects of HBM-derived exosomes in SW1353 cells Building on the previously observed anti-inflammatory effects of exosomes on macrophages, we addressed their effects on chondrocytes. SW1353 chondrocytes

To investigate the effects of HBM-derived exosomes on M1/M2 differentiation of BMMs, FACS and ELISA analysis were performed. FACS results demonstrated that HBM-derived exosomes decreased the expression of the M1 marker CD80 while increasing the expression of the M2 marker CD206 dose-dependently ( , ). Furthermore, ELISA analysis of the supernatant revealed a concentration-dependent decrease in the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β, in BMM upon LPS stimulation ( ). Anti-inflammatory effects of HBM-derived exosomes in SW1353 cells Building on the previously observed anti-inflammatory effects of exosomes on macrophages, we addressed their effects on chondrocytes. SW1353 chondrocytes were stimulated with IL-1β to induce inflammation, and the expression of MMP-1, MMP-3, MMP-13, iNOS, and COX-2 was assessed by qPCR. MMPs, as zinc-dependent endopeptidases, are crucial for the degradation of extracellular matrix components and play significant roles in various processes, including tissue remodeling, inflammation, and wound healing. Measuring MMP expression levels allowed us to evaluate the potential of HBM-derived exosomes to reduce IL-1β-induced inflammation and cartilage degradation. The data showed that exosomes reduced the expression of MMP-1, MMP-3 and MMP-13, as well as the inflammatory mediators, iNOS and COX-2 ( ). Furthermore, Western blot analysis demonstrated that HBM-derived exosomes attenuated the phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), JNK, p38, and IκBα in a dose-dependent manner ( ). ERK, JNK, and p38 are major components of the MAPK pathway, while IκBα is a key regulator of NF-κB activation. Quantification based on the phospho/total protein ratio also confirmed that higher concentrations of exosomes consistently led to greater suppression of these signaling molecules ( ). DISCUSSION HBM is rich in both macronutrients and micronutrients essential for the health of infants ( ). Beyond its nutritional value, HBM contains numerous bioactive components which crucially support the infant’s growth and development. Exosomes specifically extracted from HBM were first studied in 2007, and marked an important milestone in understanding the role of maternal bioactive compounds ( ). These exosomes transfer proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and other cellular materials to recipient cells, thereby influencing various biological processes, including inflammation, stress defense, stem cell growth, etc. ( ). Breastfeeding, therefore, offers notable health benefits to both mother and infant ( ), and according to the Developmental Origins of Health and Disease hypothesis, early exposure to environmental factors in HBM may influence long- term health outcomes and disease risk ( ). Given the established importance of HBM-derived exosomes, we aimed to evaluate their anti-inflammatory properties through in vitro experiments involving peritoneal macrophages, BMM, and the SW1353 chondrocyte cell line. In peritoneal macrophages, where inflammation was induced by LPS, HBM-derived exosome treatment led to a dose-dependent reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion, and iNOS and COX-2 expression ( ). To further characterize this anti-inflammatory activity, we evaluated the impact of HBM-derived exosomes on macrophage polarization in BMM. Macrophages are central players in inflammation and can adopt a spectrum of polarization states, from pro-inflammatory M1 to anti-inflammatory M2 phenotypes ( ; ; ; ). M1 macrophages promote tissue damage by secreting TNF-α and IL-1β, while M2 macrophages aid in tissue repair and immune resolution ( ; ; ). Macrophages have emerged as central players in synovial inflammation, where dysregulated innate immune responses contribute to the progression of various inflammatory joint conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) ( ; ; ). Our results demonstrated that HBM-derived exosomes modulate macrophage polarization toward an anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype ( ), implying the potential importance of HBM-derived exosomes in modulating inflammatory joint diseases. Furthermore, to investigate the potential relevance of these findings to arthritis, we used SW1353 chondrocyte cell line. Inflammation was induced by IL-1β, and the effect of HBM-derived exosomes on the expression of iNOS, COX-2, MMP-1, MMP-3, and MMP-13 was assessed. Exosome treatment significantly reduced the expression of these inflammatory mediators and MMPs ( ). Since MMPs are crucial for the degradation of extracellular matrix components and are deeply implicated in cartilage degradation and chronic inflammation, this finding strongly suggests that HBM-derived exosomes can suppress IL-1β induced-catabolic activity. Moreover, Western blot analysis demonstrated that HBM-derived exosomes attenuated the phosphorylation of ERK, JNK, p38 – major components of the MAPK pathway – and IκBα – a key regulator of NF-κB activation ( ). Together, these pathways orchestrate the induction of pro-inflammatory cytokines and matrix-degrading enzymes in response to IL-1β stimulation. Our results indicate that HBM-derived exosomes mitigate IL-1β–induced inflammation in SW1353 cells by downregulating MMPs, iNOS, and COX-2 expression through the inhibition of key MAPK and NF-κB signaling cascades. In a previous study ( ), we performed comprehensive proteomic and miRNA profiling of milk-derived exosomes and identified approximately 377 proteins and 208 miRNAs. Functional enrichment analyses (GO and KEGG) revealed that these components are significantly involved in modulating various physiological processes, particularly inflammatory signaling pathways. We speculate that specific bioactive

activation ( ). Together, these pathways orchestrate the induction of pro-inflammatory cytokines and matrix-degrading enzymes in response to IL-1β stimulation. Our results indicate that HBM-derived exosomes mitigate IL-1β–induced inflammation in SW1353 cells by downregulating MMPs, iNOS, and COX-2 expression through the inhibition of key MAPK and NF-κB signaling cascades. In a previous study ( ), we performed comprehensive proteomic and miRNA profiling of milk-derived exosomes and identified approximately 377 proteins and 208 miRNAs. Functional enrichment analyses (GO and KEGG) revealed that these components are significantly involved in modulating various physiological processes, particularly inflammatory signaling pathways. We speculate that specific bioactive molecules within the exosomal cargo, such as miRNAs and proteins associated with signal transduction, work synergistically to suppress the MAPK and NF-κB signaling cascades, thereby reducing the expression of MMPs, iNOS, and COX-2. While further research is needed to identify the exact contribution of individual component, our data provide a strong mechanistic basis for the anti-inflammatory and anti-catabolic effects of HBM-derived exosomes in chondrocytes. In addition, while our findings provide valuable insights into the immunomodulatory effects of HBM-derived exosomes, this study has some limitations. Although the IL-1β-stimulated SW1353 system is a useful in vitro model for studying inflammatory responses, it does not fully recapitulate the complex, multi-cellular pathophysiology of inflammatory joint diseases. Specifically, this model lacks the intricate interactions between immune cells and synovial tissues. Furthermore, while primary human chondrocytes or synoviocytes would offer higher clinical relevance, we utilized cell lines in this study. Future studies should employ primary human-derived systems or in vivo models to further validate these findings in a clinical context. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that HBM-derived exosomes modulate macrophage polarization toward the M2 phenotype and exhibit significant anti-inflammatory and anti-catabolic effects by inhibiting the MAPK and NF-κB signaling pathways. These results offer new insights into the potential role of HBM-derived exosomes in managing inflammatory response relevant to joint diseases.

chunks.content: Injury has been the leading cause of death and a cause of disability in children in the United States for decades. , Injury leads to more years of potential life lost than cancer, congenital anomalies, and perinatal health issues combined. , Survivors of childhood injury frequently suffer mental and behavioral health sequelae and physical disabilities, sometimes with long-term consequences. , Improving outcomes requires an approach that recognizes childhood injury as a significant public health problem. Using the continuum of care model for trauma system development and planning provides a framework to integrate care and optimize outcomes. This continuum of care includes injury prevention, prehospital care, emergency department (ED) care, interfacility transport, acute and critical inpatient care, inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation, and reintegration into the community and primary care medical home (Fig. ). A systems-based approach requires distinct elements of structure and function to perform together in an interrelated and cohesive manner. , A functional trauma system is represented by a sequential practice of evidence-based evaluation and management along the continuum of care and needs to be team-based, cohesive, and seamless to improve care quality in an efficient and effective manner. Current pediatric trauma care lacks cohesion and has notable gaps in pediatric readiness across the nation, leading to preventable death and inferior outcomes. Recent data have highlighted disparities in care and outcomes after pediatric injury, lack of equitable access to resources, and the importance of the relationship between injury and poor mental health outcomes and quality of life. , – Systems-based approaches to pediatric trauma readiness, child abuse, head injury, and imaging practices have also been developed and/or updated. – TRAUMA SYSTEMS Children are injured in a variety of geographic locations, and involvement of emergency medical services (EMS) and both local and regional hospital systems is paramount to optimizing care. Pediatric trauma care refers to the care received in any setting by a child who has suffered a traumatic injury, and a trauma center is a hospital-based setting specifically designated or verified to provide trauma care. , Trauma care is provided in a variety of settings including in the field, at nontrauma hospitals or centers, and at adult and/or pediatric trauma centers (PTCs). Additionally, in addition to the ED, minor trauma care may be provided at urgent care and private practice clinics. Ideally, a comprehensive pediatric trauma system incorporates prehospital and hospital-based care capable of initial stabilization of children of any age and their transfer, when needed, to centers providing advanced pediatric trauma care. A cohesive system allows for prompt communication and coordination, with tiered care concordant with patient needs. A trauma system focuses not only on survival but also survivorship, following the patient through discharge to a rehabilitation or home environment. Integration of disaster response systems at the local, state, regional, and national levels is an essential component of any functional trauma system. Coordination of trauma system development generally includes physicians and nonphysician clinicians (e.g., nurses, nurse practitioners, or physician assistants) and their professional organizations; hospital, state, and regional emergency management teams; the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response Hospital Preparedness Program; state hospital associations; local and state departments of health; state and regional trauma advisory councils; state legislatures; and local community leaders, among others (Table ). Effectiveness of state or regional pediatric trauma systems across the country has not traditionally been assessed. However, a state-based scoring system was created in 2022, called the Pediatric Trauma System Assessment Score (PTSAS), to measure each state's pediatric trauma capacity within the context of their trauma system (Fig. ). Through a Delphi process, six domains were chosen (injury prevention and recognition, access to care, quality improvement and trauma registry, disaster, legislation, and funding), each of which included three to five seminal parameters reflecting a state's pediatric trauma capabilities. A PTSAS summary score ranging from 0 to 100 was computed based on the weighted averages of each domain (with a score of 100 being the highest capabilities). The PTSAS score has been associated with both out-of-hospital and in-hospital deaths, and every 1-point increase in PTSAS has been associated with a decrease in overall state-based mortality of 0.12 (95% confidence interval [CI], −0.22 to −0.02) deaths per 100,000 children (Fig. ). Because of regional geography and the limited number of PTCs, timely access to pediatric trauma care varies significantly across the nation. , , A 2017 US Government Accountability Office report found that only 57% of children in the United States lived within 30 miles of an American College of Surgeons (ACS)– and/or state-designated PTC, defined as centers able to treat children of all ages and all injuries regardless of severity. Considerable variation existed by state, with 15 states having less than a quarter of children living within 30 miles of a PTC. In 2023, Burdick et al. reported that the percentage of US

geography and the limited number of PTCs, timely access to pediatric trauma care varies significantly across the nation. , , A 2017 US Government Accountability Office report found that only 57% of children in the United States lived within 30 miles of an American College of Surgeons (ACS)– and/or state-designated PTC, defined as centers able to treat children of all ages and all injuries regardless of severity. Considerable variation existed by state, with 15 states having less than a quarter of children living within 30 miles of a PTC. In 2023, Burdick et al. reported that the percentage of US children younger than 15 years who could not reach a level I, II, or III PTC within an hour of injury was 45.5% by ground and 25.9% by air transport. Non-PTCs within the trauma system, including adult trauma centers (ATCs), community hospitals, rural or critical access hospitals, and adult regional hospitals, among others, are relied on to safely provide stabilization and initial management of an injured child. This phenomenon is particularly true in rural and underserved areas of the country (Fig. ). Hence, it is essential that any hospital, health care center, or urgent care site that may treat injured children has the necessary training and resources to provide pediatric-specific care (see section Pediatric Readiness). Collaborative efforts are important, as are novel approaches to improve care for children without immediate access to a trauma center (e.g., teleconsultation/telemedicine). INJURY PREVENTION Injury prevention is the cornerstone of pediatric trauma care. The field of injury prevention uses scientific principles to identify areas for intervention and best practices. The Haddon matrix is a popular systematic approach to injury prevention, analyzing injuries by considering how the host (i.e., child) is susceptible to or injured by an agent (e.g., motor vehicle, firearm) in a specific environment (e.g., physical, social, economic) and in three different temporal phases: preinjury, during the injury event, and postinjury. , Building on the Haddon matrix, an injury equity framework was recently designed to “provide clinicians, researchers, public health professionals, and policy-makers a theoretical basis for identifying and analyzing factors that influence who is injured, the severity of the injury, and the injury outcome using an equity lens.” The framework highlights the intersectionality between historical and current societal factors and community, family, and individual factors within the Haddon matrix structure. Overall, a multipronged approach to injury prevention is essential and may include legislation, advancing safety technology, improving the built environment (e.g., parks, roadways), addressing risk factors related to a child's environment (e.g., home, school), anticipatory guidance, and education of caregivers. Furthermore, interventions should be evidence based and equity focused. Mechanism- and community-specific injury prevention initiatives have a long history of success, including the traffic safety, safe storage of firearms, window falls, and car seat programs, to name a few. , – More than 20 years ago, Dr. Maureen Durkin and colleagues studied the incidence of severe traffic injuries before and after a community-based intervention involving the creation of safe and accessible play areas, traffic safety education, and supervised activities for school-aged children. During the intervention period, a 36% unadjusted reduction in the incidence of traffic injuries to school-aged children was observed (rate ratio [RR], 0.64; 95% CI, 0.58–0.72). Comparable reductions in traffic-related injuries were not identified in younger children (aged 0–4 years) or school-aged children who were not targeted by the program or for traffic fatalities involving school-aged residents in other communities in the city. Policy-based injury prevention efforts that were legislated to become state or federal statutes have proven some of the most effective, including seat belt and child passenger safety legislation. , Often, a combination of approaches is essential. Dr. Barbara Barlow was instrumental in identifying, describing, and promoting regulatory changes related to window falls by children in New York City. After Dr. Barlow's work in Washington Heights led to a 1979 ordinance requiring landlords to install window guards, the number of injuries children sustained from falling out of windows decreased in the neighborhood by 96%. Effective public health messaging through the “Children Don't Fly” campaign helped solidify and disseminate her pivotal work. More recently, Dr. Lois Lee and colleagues summarized the evidence regarding firearm injury prevention and harm reduction, describing safe firearm storage, anticipatory guidance, lethal means counseling, and legislation through an American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) policy statement. Policy statements endorsed by national organizations like the AAP have wide distribution and often guide advocacy efforts nationwide. The AAP has published a number of policy statements, clinical reports, technical reports, and other resources related to injury prevention in childhood. These include drowning prevention, pedestrian safety, child passenger safety, helmet use, and more. – More resources can be found on the AAP website at https://www.aap.org/en/policy/ and for families at healthchildren.org . The AAP also designed The Injury Prevention Program, which helps

safe firearm storage, anticipatory guidance, lethal means counseling, and legislation through an American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) policy statement. Policy statements endorsed by national organizations like the AAP have wide distribution and often guide advocacy efforts nationwide. The AAP has published a number of policy statements, clinical reports, technical reports, and other resources related to injury prevention in childhood. These include drowning prevention, pedestrian safety, child passenger safety, helmet use, and more. – More resources can be found on the AAP website at https://www.aap.org/en/policy/ and for families at healthchildren.org . The AAP also designed The Injury Prevention Program, which helps pediatricians provide injury-related anticipatory guidance using a developmentally based schedule and supports pediatricians by providing a standardized resource about injury prevention for parents and caregivers. The Injury Prevention Program has recently been shown in a cluster randomized controlled trial to result in a reduction of parent-reported injuries in children. This highlights the important role of pediatric physicians and nonphysician clinicians (e.g., nurses, nurse practitioners, or physician assistants) in injury prevention and supports emphasize of age-appropriate safety topics during well-child visits and other health care encounters to educate families on injury prevention using available resources from the AAP and other organizations. , The Consumer Product Safety Commission has been instrumental in industry-specific injury prevention initiatives, including but not limited to baby walker-related injuries, furniture safety, and more. Federal agencies like the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have routinely contributed to injury prevention efforts. One example is sports-related injury prevention with resources, education, and guidance for health care staff, coaches, and parents regarding concussions and protective equipment. The CDC also provides research and resources related to child abuse and neglect. The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA)'s National Fetal, Infant, and Child Death Review Program and local child death review programs have traditionally helped with outreach messaging. There are now child death review teams in all 50 states and most US territories, which generally incorporate multidisciplinary approaches to the community's death review process. , Finally, nonprofit organizations have, and continue to, contribute to injury prevention. Safe Kids, Prevent Child Injury, Charlie's House, Prevent Child Abuse America, and the Injury Free Coalition for Kids have addressed injury risks related to drowning, television and furniture tip overs, child abuse, and all-terrain vehicle use, to name a few. Many of these organizations promote risk reduction behaviors such as bike helmet use and safe teen driving. Both Safe Kids and the Injury Free Coalition for Kids have been instrumental in research, education, and advocacy for childhood injury prevention nationwide, and Prevent Child Injury provides multimedia toolkits on injury prevention topics, including information for families and providers, reports and data, and social media materials for outreach. – Despite incredible efforts in the injury prevention space, it is important to note that many causes of injury to children have not changed over the past decade. Aside from deaths due to motor vehicle collisions and pedestrian injuries, which have declined substantially, many injury-related causes of deaths have not changed for 20 years. , This highlights the importance of continued focus on injury prevention initiatives at local, regional, and national levels. PEDIATRIC READINESS The 2006 Institute of Medicine report evaluating the US emergency care system described care for children as uneven and found that many of the country's EDs lacked the necessary equipment, drugs, and supplies to care for children adequately. The National Pediatric Readiness Project works to address these gaps with strategies to improve children's care including standardized guidelines and checklists. This includes the recommendation that there be a pediatric emergency care coordinator (PECC) position established in every ED in the nation. The PECC is tasked with providing education and training, ensuring maintenance of equipment and supplies, and completing quality improvement related to all types of pediatric trauma care and has been associated with improved ED pediatric readiness. The HRSA-funded Emergency Medical Services for Children (EMSC) Program has incorporated the National Pediatric Readiness Project performance measures for assessment of state-based programs (Table ). Prehospital and ED pediatric readiness across the country is an essential component of pediatric trauma systems. New studies have validated the effectiveness of pediatric readiness in reducing in-hospital mortality after injury and critical illness. , , Emergency department pediatric readiness is also independently associated with long-term survival among injured children. , This makes pediatric readiness of all EDs across the country an essential component of health care safety and quality. , – Because of its success, the program has also been extended to the prehospital care environment. , The ACS Committee on Trauma is a partner in pediatric readiness and has outlined a blueprint along with recommendations for incorporating pediatric readiness into trauma system development. PREHOSPITAL AND INTERFACILITY PEDIATRIC TRAUMA CARE Prehospital Care Prehospital care may be provided by a variety of emergency health care clinicians, including emergency medical technicians, advanced emergency medical technicians, emergency medical responders, and paramedics. Police and/or fire departments, private or third-party ambulance services, and public agencies all play a role in parts of the country. Aside from specialty units associated with large children's hospitals, individual prehospital nonphysician clinicians infrequently care for critically ill or injured children, particularly those who volunteer or work in rural or underserved areas. Limited knowledge and experience with pediatric trauma patients are addressed by continuing education efforts through established courses supported by the AAP, American College of Emergency Physicians, American Heart Association, National Association of Emergency Medical Technicians, National Association of EMS Educators, and National Association of EMS Physicians, among others. Local and regional EMS-based pediatric-specific educational initiatives and practical experience at children's hospitals have been used to optimize competency and comfort with care of the injured child. Additional methods for skill maintenance include simulation and online and remote training. – Simulation-based training for prehospital personnel in the management of pediatric emergencies is associated with improvement in some skills (i.e., choosing the correct airway equipment and use of Broselow tape), and data suggest that low-fidelity simulation training is more effective than high-fidelity simulation at improving pediatric resuscitation skills. However, limited exposure of any training (whether simulation-based, lecture, or online self-study) may not be sufficient to substantially improve skills, highlighting the need for iterative and varied approaches to capacity building and skill maintenance. The EMSC Program has introduced pediatric readiness to EMS systems, using collaborative approaches and promoting a PECC for each EMS service. The PECC is responsible for pediatric quality improvement to make sure that pediatric equipment is up to date and working and that all emergency health care clinicians know how to use the equipment and use periodic simulation to refresh skills. Individual states have the responsibility of regulating their own EMS system. In some states, EMS agencies are required to submit practice guidelines and protocols to the state medical director for approval and other states require a standardized state protocol. Evidence-based and standardized pediatric-specific protocols for prehospital care are an essential component. In all states, licensure of EMS agencies requires an approved number of education hours and/or experience dependent on the level of service provided, although these hours may or may not include pediatric education. Direct feedback from trauma centers can assist with continued process improvement for EMS teams and agencies. Feedback can be provided in real-time by including EMS teams in trauma quality improvement meetings, in case reviews, and/or in written or oral feedback through direct communication after a child's injury-related encounter is complete. Examples of follow-up guidelines and communications are included in the EMSC Inter-facility Toolkit. Although evidence guiding prehospital care is limited, there are increasing data regarding best practices for pediatric resuscitation in out-of-hospital traumatic cardiac arrest; fluid, drug, and product administration; cervical spine stabilization; and airway management. – Field triage criteria are updated regularly by the ACS Committee on Trauma and the CDC. – These criteria include anatomic and physiologic parameters that indicate whether transport to the highest level trauma center available within the geographic constraints of a regional trauma system is indicated. Additional parameters, including mechanism of injury and other considerations (including young age and concerns for child abuse), suggest transfer to a trauma center, although not necessarily the highest level. In general, trauma systems have a goal of undertriaging no more than 5% and overtriaging between 25% and 35%. Iterative review of field criteria is essential and guides updates to national field triage guidelines. , Community Care and Interfacility Transport More than 27% of injury- and poison-related ED visits in the United States in 2020 were for children younger than 18 years. Although young and/or critically injured children may need transfer to a higher level of pediatric trauma care, many children are effectively and safely cared for at facilities that are not PTCs. For centers that evaluate and transfer injured children, there are national or multi-institutional guidelines that can guide pediatric care (e.g., Image Gently using “as low as reasonably achievable” principles). , , Nearly 25% of EDs do not have reduced-dose radiation protocols for computed tomography and radiographic imaging. Partnering with trauma centers that care for children for advice on appropriate workup before transfer is ideal. For centers that routinely care for and admit children, other guidelines are accessible through national organizations. For example, the Pediatric Trauma Society (PTS) Hub provides updated and vetted guidelines for the acute management of injuries by body system and is readily accessible to the public on the PTS website. The EMSC Inter-facility Toolkit provides guidance on specific components associated with interfacility transfer, including templates and examples of guidelines and agreements for public use, summaries of standards and regulations, and family considerations. Interhospital transfer guidelines, policies, and procedures facilitate patient transfer, often through multidisciplinary centralized “transfer centers.” Transfer centers allow hospitals that initially treat children to efficiently initiate transfer to higher levels of care with a single call. These calls can facilitate guidance on when and how a child should be transferred on the basis of their physiology and injuries, what diagnostic and therapeutic interventions are indicated prior to transfer, and what method of transport is most appropriate (e.g., ground vs. aeromedical, one-way vs. two-way with a specialized team, advanced life support vs. basic life support). Pediatric transport teams may be the best resource for severely injured children because of their specific expertise in pediatric resuscitation and trauma care. – Generally, as soon as it is recognized that a child will likely need transfer to a higher level of care, further diagnostic tests beyond basic laboratory tests can be limited to those that will inform the need for intervention prior to transfer or those that dictate the need for transfer after consultation with PTC personnel. Only necessary imaging studies should be completed to minimize radiation and to avoid the need for repeat imaging after transfer. , Transport decisions are a collaborative effort between referring and accepting physicians to determine mode (air vs. ground), the appropriate level of expertise of transport team members, and the necessary equipment to ensure a safe transport to optimize patient care, all while considering the cost and time for the mobilization of each transport type and the respective travel times. Although the patient's health is the utmost priority to guide interfacility transport decisions, recognizing the impact of transport on the child and family (e.g., separation of child and parent) is important. Telemedicine and Teleradiology The use of technology to support clinical care decision making has increased over the past decade. Telehealth services have the potential to enhance the reach of tertiary trauma care for children in rural and underserved areas where pediatric specialty care is not readily available. Services can include education, protocol sharing, “as low as reasonably achievable”–based guidelines, and administrative oversight. As a consequence of the COVID-19 pandemic, teleradiology has been progressively used around the nation. Data suggest that efficient cloud-based imaging may lead to decreased repeat imaging, lower costs, and fewer delays in care for pediatric trauma patients. With the growth of telehealth opportunities to improve care, appropriate and commensurate payment models must be developed to support telehealth services. TRAUMA CENTERS In 2006, the National Study on Costs and Outcomes of Trauma found that trauma center care was associated with decreased mortality, particularly for the most critically injured patients. In general, trauma centers are described by their ability to provide trauma-specific care, with level I being the highest, most comprehensive level of care (Table ). Trauma centers can be self-described, state designated, and/or ACS verified. They can be classified as PTCs, ATCs, or combined adult/PTCs. The ACS verifies ATCs as levels I, II, and III and pediatric centers as level I or II, with level I as the highest level. Verification by the ACS is a process that is integrated into their quality programs and involves four components: adherence to standards, comprehensive infrastructure, rigorous data to guide quality improvement, and external peer review. State criteria for trauma level designation may differ from or be identical to ACS verification criteria and may include as many as four or five levels. State criteria for trauma level designation may differ from or be identical to ACS verification criteria and may include as many as four or five levels. American College of Surgeons verification criteria are reviewed and updated at regular intervals and published as “Resources for the Optimal Care of the Injured Patient,” which provides a comprehensive description of the necessary resources to provide optimal care for injured adults and children (Table ). A 2022 standard for ACS verification at all levels of trauma centers addresses the pediatric readiness of the hospital ED: “In all trauma centers, the emergency department must evaluate its pediatric readiness and have a plan to address any deficiencies.” This standard aims to raise awareness of the importance of pediatric readiness, include the trauma surgeon as part of the team, and begin to optimize resources for pediatric care in all settings. Injured children, including adolescents, may have improved outcomes at PTCs, although the data are mixed. , – For example, a 2019 analysis of Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project data for injured children 16 years and younger demonstrated improved mortality for children who were treated at a level I PTC compared with a level I trauma centers with no pediatric verification (adjusted odds, 0.6; 95% CI, 0.4–0.9). Similarly, a 2024 Trauma Quality Improvement Program (TQIP) analysis of injured children 15 years and younger with severe injury found treatment at a level I or level II PTC was associated with decreased mortality (adjusted odds, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.61–0.85) compared with centers without pediatric verification. In firearm-specific injury data from the 2010–2016 National Trauma Databank files in children 13 to 16 years of age, odds of mortality were 2.88 times higher at ATCs compared with PTCs (95% CI, 1.55–5.36; p < 0.001). However, using a 1:1 propensity score matching model, no difference in mortality was found by trauma center type. Perhaps most importantly, recent data suggest that risk-adjusted benchmarking in adults is not a reliable surrogate for pediatric outcomes. Hence, it is imperative that pediatric-specific metrics are measured and targeted for quality improvement. Pediatric trauma centers are generally capable of providing a broad range of pediatric services delivered by pediatric-focused staff, including physicians and nonphysician clinicians trained in pediatric emergency medicine, nurses with demonstrated competency in the care of injured children, pediatric anesthesia providers, and pediatric medical subspecialists and surgical specialists. Resources at PTCs required by the ACS include readily available/on-site interventional radiology, pediatric anesthesiology, pediatric surgery, pediatric orthopedic and neurosurgical care, and pediatric critical care, among others. A protocol for screening patients at high risk for psychological sequelae from their injury is also required, along with a process for referral to a mental health clinician trained in trauma-informed care. For the appropriately trained clinician, examples of evidence based therapies may include Trauma-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and Alternatives for Families: A Cognitive Behavioral Therapy. To help guide trauma centers, the ACS Committee on Trauma has published best practice guidelines to guide screening and intervention for mental health disorders in the acute trauma patient, including pediatric-specific resources. Pediatric trauma centers also often have certified child life specialists, and the 2023 standard for ACS verification requires all PTCs to have a child life program. In addition, PTCs often have child abuse physicians; pediatric registered dietitians and pharmacists; pediatric physiatrists; pediatric occupational, physical, and speech therapists; pediatric pain medicine specialists; and pediatric palliative care services. Many of these specialized services can be offered through consultation and, in some cases, telemedicine. ED at the Trauma Center Once a child arrives at the ED of the PTC, care continues by initiating or continuing resuscitation and identification of injuries, regardless of whether the child arrives from the field or is transferred from a referral center. Transferred patients meeting triage criteria are evaluated in the same manner as patients who have not been evaluated elsewhere. The ACS requires all trauma centers to have clearly defined tiered activation criteria to efficiently and expeditiously mobilize the appropriate staff and resources as a team. These criteria are used to ensure that the resources and personnel that are commensurate with the needs of the patient are available. The ACS defines patient criteria and trauma surgeons response times for the highest level of activation. Some critically injured patients may need to transition directly to the operating room or interventional radiology suite. These criteria are used to ensure that the resources and personnel that are commensurate with the needs of the patient are available. The ACS defines patient criteria and trauma surgeons response times for the highest level of activation. Some critically injured patients may need to transition directly to the operating room or interventional radiology suite. Protocols for massive transfusion, management of noncompressible hemorrhage, replants, vascular injuries/critical limb ischemia, spine and neurological trauma, and others are critical to provide prompt limb and lifesaving care. – Special consideration should be taken to formalize systems for optimal and efficient care for injuries that may require coordination with an adult center (i.e., vascular injury/compromise, replants, complex pelvic trauma). Additionally, guidelines for body region-specific imaging are critical to limit radiation and the need for repeat studies. , , – Critical Care, Acute Care, and Operative Resources at the Trauma Center A well-equipped and staffed pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) is essential for optimal care of the injured child, and the availability of PICU beds within a region may improve survival in pediatric trauma. Pediatric intensive care units offer a setting with necessary equipment and advanced technology to support physiologically unstable or intubated patients who need advanced monitoring. Pediatric intensive care units are staffed by physicians and nonphysician clinicians with pediatric critical care training or expertise. Pediatric intensive care unit resources are essential for the management of severe traumatic brain injury and advanced burn resuscitation. , In the PICU, attention is paid not only to physiologic stability but also to minimizing secondary harm (e.g., preventable delirium, decubitus ulcers, hospital acquired infections). The ACS recommends that surgeons be the primary physicians and/or involved on all patients admitted with traumatic injuries; however, notable variability exists in the structure and care processes in place for critically injured children. Critically injured children likely benefit from collaborative care by both the trauma and PICU services. Likewise, comanagement with medical teams on acute care floors is often beneficial and/or essential depending on hospital-specific resources and processes (i.e., which teams are in house, relative expertise, etc.) and patient age and comorbid diagnoses (i.e., uncontrolled diabetes, prematurity, psychosis, complex care needs, etc.). The acute care hospitalization at a PTC frequently incorporates a multidisciplinary team, including physical therapists, occupational therapists, speech therapists, and mental and behavioral health specialists (among others) concordant with each child's needs. Readily available access to the operating room at all times is critical, and the ACS requires an operating room to be staffed and available within 15 minutes of notification for levels I and II centers for cases that are considered to be emergencies. Urgent cases include the timely fixation of orthopedic fractures, and levels I and II trauma centers must have a dedicated operating room prioritized for fracture care in nonemergent orthopedic trauma. SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS Issues unique to management of children, irrespective of where they receive definitive care, include reducing diagnostic radiation exposure; addressing pain during invasive procedures; weight-based fluid, drug, and electrolyte management and blood transfusions; family-centered care; and child life specialty care, among others. Careful consideration of the extent of diagnostic radiation for trauma evaluation is important because of the risk of radiation-related malignancies over the lifetime of a child. , , Patterns of injury and pathology in children are different than those of adult patients, and much of the imaging protocols in adult trauma patients do not apply to pediatric trauma patient. Knowledge of incidental findings and normal variations of pediatric anatomy may mitigate false-positive diagnoses. The ability to provide a full range of safe but effective pain management strategies for children is important, including nonpharmacologic techniques. , A child- and family-centered environment facilitates family presence during care that may range from wound debridement, suturing and dressings, fracture reduction, or postarrest resuscitations and optimizes communication and education between the treatment team and family. The presence of child life specialists before, during, and/or after invasive procedures has been associated with improved care-experiences. Family presence during trauma resuscitations requires a designated team member to be with the family at all times, when possible, to support the family and help them understand and process the events. Overall, trauma-informed care from the time of injury and throughout the care continuum, including rehabilitation, is critical. Child Abuse A unique aspect of pediatric trauma care is the need for awareness and recognition of signs of child abuse and neglect. Various historical factors, examination findings, and diagnostic testing results are associated with child physical abuse. – A combination of these findings is often included in institution-specific screening tools. It is important to note that multiple reports have identified disparities in child abuse reporting, with children from historically marginalized racial or ethnic groups disproportionately identified as potential victims of abuse and more likely to be investigated, to be subject to unnecessary tests, and to have a change of caregiver at discharge. – Minimizing disparities in reporting (and unnecessary tests) requires a multipronged approach, including clinical pathways/guidelines and staff education on bias reduction. Multidisciplinary teams that care for children with suspected child abuse often include social work and pediatricians with expertise in child abuse recognition and management, if available. The use of telemedicine or remote consultation may help expand the reach of trained child abuse pediatricians and their expertise. The ACS, EMSC Innovation and Improvement Center, and American Pediatric Surgical Association have all published resources and/or guidelines for assessment of child abuse. For children with suspected physical abuse, the ACS recommends consultation with a surgical trauma service, in addition to a child abuse physician and social worker. , , Diagnostic studies beyond what would typically be pursued for the injury of presentation may be required, including imaging to detect previous occult injuries and specific laboratory studies. Commonly used clinical decision rules (e.g., Pediatric Emergency Care and Research Network tools for traumatic brain injury and intra-abdominal injury) do not apply in child abuse. – Although there is variability in state statutes, all health care workers in all states are mandated by law to report concern for child maltreatment. The AAP Council on Child Abuse and Neglect has resources, including clinical reports, policy statements, technical reports, and educational offerings for physicians, patients, and families pertaining to child abuse and neglect, including special populations and situations (e.g., children with disabilities, sex trafficking, abusive head trauma, child abuse fatalities, and long-term sequelae and management of abuse). – Injury Trends Historically, the leading cause of injury-related death in children, adolescents, and young adults 1 to 19 years of age was motor vehicle collisions. In 2019, firearm injury became the leading cause of death in this population. Both the ACS and the AAP have published resources for health care workers, patients, and families regarding firearm injury prevention and safe storage. , The ACS, AAP, and American College of Emergency Physicians have all published position statements, policy statements, and/or technical reports on firearm safety and firearm-related injury prevention. , , – There has also been an increase in suicide among adolescents and young adults in recent decades, highlighting the need for evidence-based suicide prevention strategies and suicide screening. – The AAP Blueprint on Youth Suicide Prevention is a free online education resource to support pediatric health clinicians “identify equitable youth suicide prevention strategies” ( https://www.aap.org/suicideprevention ). Overall, since 2010, trauma-related ED visits have been increasing, although with fewer hospitalizations. The COVID-19 pandemic was associated with further shifts in injury epidemiology among children and adolescents. , – REHABILITATION AND REINTEGRATION INTO THE COMMUNITY Injury during childhood has been associated with poor educational outcomes, functional status, and quality of life. , – The trauma community has more recently emphasized survivorship and recovery given the potential long-term physical and mental health effects of trauma on the child, family, and community. To this end, postinjury trauma-informed care, along with recovery and resiliency programs, are becoming more common. – The goal of a trauma system is to return children to full, age-appropriate function with the ability to reach maximum adult potential. This process includes reintegration into the community, school or educational environment, and primary care medical home. The primary care pediatrician is an essential navigator in this postinjury phase of care, supporting children and adolescents with short- and long-term sequelae, in addition to assisting in the transition to adult trauma-informed care clinicians. Crisis intervention and ongoing support can be offered through hospital-based violence intervention programs to youth who are injured through interpersonal violence and are at risk of reinjury and psychosocial trauma. – For injured children with extensive care needs after the acute injury, the availability of both inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation resources specifically for children is a scarce yet vital component of trauma care. Physical, occupational, cognitive, speech, and play therapies, along with psychological and social support, are essential elements of a comprehensive rehabilitation effort for the injured child and family. Physical, occupational, cognitive, speech, and play therapies, along with psychological and social support, are essential elements of a comprehensive rehabilitation effort for the injured child and family. The ability to begin early rehabilitation during the acute hospitalization, particularly for children with traumatic brain injury and cognitive challenges or with fractures and mobility requirements, is inherent to recovery and reintegration. – There are many areas of the country with no inpatient pediatric rehabilitation resources and limited outpatient resources that are barriers to optimal or expeditious recovery. Novel approaches to care, such as telehealth and mobile or wearable health technologies, may help increase access to pediatric-specific care to meet the needs of all children, despite where they live, grow, and play. Mental Health The impact of injury on a child goes well beyond the initial hospital encounter. Mental health sequelae, such as posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression, are common after pediatric injury. An estimated 20% of children report posttraumatic stress symptoms after injury, and previous injury is also associated with anxiety and depressive symptoms. , , In a managed Medicaid population (using the MarketScan database), an estimated 25% of children 0 to 17 years of age with nonfatal firearm injury were diagnosed with a new mental health condition. In another MarketScan study, documented mental health diagnoses increased by 63% in the 12 months after unintentional injury, from 95.9/1000 person-years preinjury to 156.7/1000 person-years postinjury (RR, 1.63; 95% CI, 1.39–1.92). The rate of psychotropic prescriptions also increased from 121.7/1000 person-years preinjury to 310.9/1000 person-years postinjury (RR, 2.55; 95% CI, 2.26–2.89). Similar trends have been identified in injury-specific pediatric populations, particularly among children and youth with firearm injuries. , Estimates do vary, as yet another MarketScan study looking at and evaluating children 6 to 17 years of age admitted for traumatic injury found that only 3.3% developed a subsequent mental health diagnosis (i.e., PTSD, depression, anxiety, or adjustment disorder) and only 1.6% developed PTSD, presumably because of suboptimal recognition of these symptoms. Despite variability in estimates, there is widespread understanding that injury is intricately related to mental health and quality of life after injury and also affects families, parents, and caregivers. , , Resources including screening tools for children and adolescents can be found in the ACS “Best Practice Guidelines: Screening and Intervention for Mental Health Disorders and Substance Use and Misuse in the Acute Trauma Patient.” PERFORMANCE IMPROVEMENT, EDUCATION, AND OUTREACH Effective clinical performance and quality improvement are integral components of trauma programs and indirectly for trauma systems as a whole. Performance improvement efforts often focus on patient safety and harm prevention, reporting of delays in diagnosis or care, near misses, trends in morbidity across service lines, mortality review to recognize opportunities for improvement, and/or communication issues. Review of trauma care provided to children is facilitated by comprehensive chart review. Collaborative reviews between transferring and receiving institutions and transport teams are important for children transferred for additional care. Each dedicated trauma center has an institutional trauma registry, which exports data to state and (often) national databases so that outcomes can be risk adjusted and benchmarked to allow for evaluation of care quality across institutions and inform opportunities for improvement. Quality review generally adopts the Donabedian framework of structure, process, and outcomes, with selection of performance improvement initiatives based on performance indicators that fall below a specific threshold based on benchmarking. , Quality indicators should be remeasured after implementation, with reassessment of outcomes. Outcomes are compared through programs like the ACS Pediatric TQIP, the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival, and the National EMS Information System. Data systems, however, continue to be disjointed and lack the ability to link across data sets to fully understand the continuum of care and the connection between processes and outcomes. One consideration is to create a National Unique Identifier for each trauma patient that starts from the initial encounter (e.g., EMS, urgent care, or other) and is added to all centers (and their data set), at which the patient is treated. This identifier would follow a child from initial evaluation through acute treatment, rehabilitation, and postdischarge follow-up. This is an important step to obtain comprehensive understanding of the impact of a pediatric trauma system on long-term outcomes. At all institutions that treat injured children, systematic child mortality and morbidity review processes help identify variations in standard of care, trends in outcomes, and systematic risk factors for which interventions can be developed, evaluated, and improved.

PEDIATRIC DISASTER PREPAREDNESS AND SURGE Disaster preparedness for adults and children in the United States has improved significantly since Hurricane Katrina in 2005. Hospital accreditation programs including The Joint Commission have strengthened their disaster preparedness requirements for institutions. There is considerable federal support through the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response Hospital Preparedness Program and the HRSA Regional Pediatric Pandemic Network (PPN) to improve pediatric disaster care nationally. – As of 2022, there were 10 children's hospitals partnering with professional associations, nonprofit organizations, government agencies, and others through the PPN to improve the pediatric readiness of health care systems and ensure high-quality, equitable pediatric care in emergencies, disasters, and pandemics. Children have unique needs for health care in mass casualty incidents involving trauma and burns. Along with physiologic considerations unique to the trauma management of children, additional issues of triage, identification, decontamination, tracking, and reunification are considered. Support services including child life, social work, child and adolescent psychologists, and bereavement counselors, among others, are important to recovery. Children and youth with special health care needs (CYSHCN) are a vulnerable population during disasters because of mobility challenges, language impairment, executive functioning and sensory difficulties, medical conditions with and without technology dependence, and other trauma exposure. Even with disaster planning, households with individuals with disabilities are less likely to be prepared, and very few studies have examined the optimal methods of disaster communication tailored for families of CYSHCN. , The AAP has resources available for patients, families, and physicians related to CYSHCN to prepare before, help during, and recover after disasters. , A process for recruiting pediatric health care professionals when a surge response is needed is a mainstay of institutional disaster plans. Although the needs of children in disasters can be anticipated, the capability of a trauma system to meet these needs requires frequent simulation practice and mock disaster drills, including multi-institutional, state, and regional planning. State, regional, and federal agencies manage the legal, operational, and information systems to provide effective pediatric mass casualty care through the following: (1) predisaster/mass casualty planning, management, and assessment with input from child health professionals; (2) close cooperation, agreements, public-private partnerships, and unique delivery systems; and (3) use of existing public health data to assess pediatric populations at risk and to model graded response plans on the basis of increasing patient volume and acuity. Regional Medical Operations Coordinating Centers can coordinate care across EMS agencies, hospitals, public health, and emergency management leadership. They can effectively load balance a trauma system ensuring that each child receives optimal care at the appropriate facility. Pediatric trauma systems may play a role in supporting adult centers during crisis, such as occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic, during which surgeons boarded in trauma and critical care provided intensive care services for adults.
