Development of critical care subspecialties Developing critical care subspecialties optimizes resource allocation and improves efficiency and quality of care. Attending physicians and higher-rank specialists are encouraged to pursue subspecialty training according to institutional and disciplinary needs. Areas such as respiratory, cardiovascular, and neurocritical care should be prioritized, with gradual expansion into other fields. Training should cover clinical care, education, and research, including subspecialty techniques, teaching curricula, and both basic and clinical research capacity, to ensure high-level competence. Establishing a subspecialty-specific quality control system is recommended to regularly assess care quality, patient outcomes, and complication rates, thereby ensuring safety and continuous improvement. ICU Equipment Configuration ICU equipment configuration requirements by hospital tier ICU equipment configuration for secondary general hospitals The ICU equipment configuration for secondary general hospitals should include the following items: (1) An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system, with a power capacity sufficient to meet the emergency needs of ward lighting and medical equipment for at least 1 h; (2) Beds equipped with a comprehensive functional equipment rail or rack. Each hospital bed should be provided with ≥12 power outlets and two interfaces each for oxygen, compressed air, and negative pressure suction, to ensure functional support for electricity, medical oxygen, compressed air, and negative pressure suction; (3) Hospital beds suitable for ICU use, along with anti-decubitus mattresses; (4) Monitoring equipment. Each bed should be equipped with a bedside monitoring system capable of ECG monitoring, blood pressure monitoring, pulse oximetry, and invasive pressure monitoring; (5) Respiratory support equipment. Each bed should have a manual resuscitator (bag-valve-mask). An appropriate number of ventilators and portable ventilators may be installed based on actual needs; (6) Infusion equipment. Each bed should be equipped with an infusion pump and micro-infusion pumps. Each bed should have ≥4 micro-infusion pumps, along with an appropriate number of enteral nutrition infusion pumps; (7) Blood purification devices. An appropriate number of blood purification devices may be installed according to actual needs; (8) Other essential equipment, consisting of an electrocardiograph, blood gas analyzer, defibrillator, CPR rescue cart, and therapeutic hypothermia/normothermia devices. ICU equipment configuration for tertiary hospitals The ICU equipment configuration for tertiary general hospitals should be comprehensive, specifically the following: (1) A UPS system with a sufficient power capacity to meet the emergency needs of ward lighting and medical equipment for at least 1 h; (2) Beds with a comprehensive functional equipment rail or rack. Each hospital bed should be provided with ≥18 power outlets, six wired data transmission ports, and two interfaces each for oxygen, compressed air, and negative pressure suction, thereby ensuring functional support for electricity, medical oxygen, compressed air, and negative pressure suction; (3) Hospital beds suitable for ICU use, along with anti-decubitus mattresses; (4) Monitoring equipment. A central monitoring system should be equipped in the ward area. Each bed should have a bedside monitoring system for monitoring basic vital signs, ECG, blood pressure, pulse oximetry, and invasive pressure. Pulse indicator continuous cardiac output monitors should be installed as needed. Each ICU ward should be equipped with at least 1 portable monitor to facilitate the safe transfer of patients; (5) Respiratory support equipment. A sufficient number of invasive ventilators should be installed based on demand. Each ICU ward should be additionally equipped with at least 1–2 conventional ventilators for backup use. A manual resuscitator (bag-valve-mask) should be installed for each bed. Up to two portable ventilators should be provided for every 20 beds to facilitate the safe transfer of patients. High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) oxygen therapy devices and noninvasive ventilators should also be installed as needed; (6) Beds with an infusion pump, ≥4 micro-infusion pumps, and an enteral nutrition infusion pump; (7) Blood purification devices as needed; (8) A sufficient number of mobile ultrasound machines; (9) A sufficient number of bronchoscopes according to the number of beds. Where feasible, ICUs may be equipped with disposable electronic bronchoscope systems and an adequate supply of consumables (for special patients); (10) ECMO. ICUs with the required qualifications should be equipped with ECMO devices based on the bed demand and activated clotting time detectors to meet clinical use requirements; (11) Other equipment. The specific quantity of equipment such as electrocardiographs, blood gas analyzers, defibrillators, continuous hemodynamic monitoring equipment, CPR rescue carts (equipped with video laryngoscopes, endotracheal tubes, cricothyrotomy kits, various connectors, emergency drugs, and other rescue tools), temporary external pacemakers, airway clearance devices,

of bronchoscopes according to the number of beds. Where feasible, ICUs may be equipped with disposable electronic bronchoscope systems and an adequate supply of consumables (for special patients); (10) ECMO. ICUs with the required qualifications should be equipped with ECMO devices based on the bed demand and activated clotting time detectors to meet clinical use requirements; (11) Other equipment. The specific quantity of equipment such as electrocardiographs, blood gas analyzers, defibrillators, continuous hemodynamic monitoring equipment, CPR rescue carts (equipped with video laryngoscopes, endotracheal tubes, cricothyrotomy kits, various connectors, emergency drugs, and other rescue tools), temporary external pacemakers, airway clearance devices, therapeutic hypothermia/normothermia devices, mobile X-ray machines, and pneumatic compression pumps for thrombosis prevention should be provided based on clinical requirements; (12) Additional equipment. Qualified institutions with the necessary capabilities are recommended to be equipped with intracranial pressure monitoring devices, EEG monitoring devices, cerebral oxygen monitoring devices, IABP devices, ECCO₂R devices, sublingual microcirculation monitoring devices, POCT devices (for detecting myocardial enzymes, coagulation function, inflammatory factors, acute kidney injury markers, etc.), and ventilator internal circuit disinfection machines. Equipment configuration requirements for sub-ICU The equipment configuration for sub-ICU should refer to the ICU standards, mainly including the following: (1) Monitoring equipment. A standard monitor should be installed for each bed, as well as portable monitors; (2) Respiratory support equipment. Necessary ventilators and manual resuscitators should be installed for each bed; (3) Infusion equipment. Each bed should be equipped with infusion and micro-infusion pumps; (4) Rehabilitation-related equipment, such as patient transfer devices, bedside exercise bikes, walking aids, and limb function trainers; (5) Portable oxygen supply devices; (6) Other essential equipment, including an electrocardiograph, multi-functional defibrillator, blood gas analyzer, enteral nutrition pump, electric suction device, CPR rescue cart, and therapeutic hypothermia/normothermia devices. Equipment configuration requirements for convertible ICU bed units Convertible ICU bed units should function as ICU beds, with their equipment configuration following the ICU standards. Specifically, the equipment configuration requirements for convertible ICU bed units include the following: (1) Oxygen source. The hospital should be equipped with a dual-channel oxygen supply system to ensure the continuous supply of oxygen under any circumstances. The calculation of the medical oxygen source flow rate should be based on the patient’s needs and comprehensively consider the maximum oxygen flow rate required when using equipment such as invasive ventilators, noninvasive ventilators, and HFNC oxygen therapy devices. The recommended flow rate for each high-flow oxygen delivery terminal is 40–60 L/min. The recommended simultaneous usage coefficient for oxygen terminals in convertible ICUs is 40; (2) The air supply is capable of providing compressed air; (3) Power supply. Dual-channel and emergency power supplies should be installed to ensure the normal operation of equipment under any circumstances. Each bed should be equipped with at least 12 power outlets; (4) Universal equipment interfaces. Each bed should be installed with ICU-standard oxygen interfaces, compressed air interfaces, and two negative pressure suction interfaces. The oxygen supply, air supply, power supply, suction equipment, and interfaces should all meet ICU requirements to ensure safe and convenient equipment connection. Quality Management Medical quality and safety represent the core components of the Healthy China initiative, being essential to the high-quality development of healthcare services. Quality control in CCM is vital to build a high-quality and efficient healthcare service system and safeguard people’s lives and health (the Quality Control Indicators for Critical Care Medicine in Supplementary material). [ ] Establishment of medical quality management systems ICUs should implement quality management standards and quality control indicator systems mandated by health authorities at all levels and their affiliated hospitals. Establishing and improving comprehensive regulations, job responsibilities, technical standards, and operational procedures are recommended. Annual quality control implementation plans and improvement programs should be developed based on local conditions, with regular audits and revisions to ensure compliance. These will promote the high-quality development of ICUs. Each ICU should establish a medical quality management team, in which the department director serves as the principal person responsible for quality management. Collection and reporting of quality control Indicators ICUs should implement principal quality management and self-assessments according to quality control indicators and monitoring standards related to key technologies and major conditions in CCM. Medical quality management tools and digital platforms should be fully utilized to collect indicators related to patient safety and quality of care, thereby forming a foundation of institutional quality data. ICUs must report quality control data accurately and promptly to the relevant health authorities as required. Continuous improvement of medical quality ICUs should regularly evaluate compliance with quality management requirements, analyze and provide feedback on collected quality data, and establish goal-oriented, refined strategies for continuous quality improvement. Assessing the effectiveness of these interventions is also needed to ensure continuous enhancement of medical quality. Professional Training and Continuing Education Standardized residency training in CCM Resident physicians in Department of Critical Care Medicine at all

indicators related to patient safety and quality of care, thereby forming a foundation of institutional quality data. ICUs must report quality control data accurately and promptly to the relevant health authorities as required. Continuous improvement of medical quality ICUs should regularly evaluate compliance with quality management requirements, analyze and provide feedback on collected quality data, and establish goal-oriented, refined strategies for continuous quality improvement. Assessing the effectiveness of these interventions is also needed to ensure continuous enhancement of medical quality. Professional Training and Continuing Education Standardized residency training in CCM Resident physicians in Department of Critical Care Medicine at all hospital levels are required to complete SRT. Requirements for SRT in CCM Resident physicians under a standardized CCM training must complete a 3-year phased training program. The program aims to cultivate professional integrity, clinical competence, patient management skills, communication and teamwork abilities, teaching capacity, and learning capabilities of clinical physicians, enabling them to independently establish fundamental diagnoses and provide treatment within the discipline. The detailed requirements can be found in the ``Content and Standards for Standardized Residency Training (2022 Edition) — Detailed Rules for Critical Care Medicine Training.'' [ ] Enhancing the development of SRT Bases for CCM (1) Tertiary hospitals, particularly teaching hospitals affiliated with medical schools already accredited as SRT bases for internal medicine and surgery, are recommended to actively fulfill the requirements for and apply to become SRT bases for CCM. Specific requirements are outlined in the “Standard for Standardized Residency Training Bases (2022 Edition) – Detailed Rules for Critical Care Medicine Training Bases.” [ ] (2) Strengthening faculty training within the CCM training bases is recommended. Eligible supervising physicians and directors of specialized training bases are encouraged to participate in key faculty training programs for SRT in CCM. Additionally, residents should be encouraged to evaluate and provide feedback on their instructors to enhance the quality of clinical teaching. (3) The teaching requirements and training capacity of specialized training bases must comply with the “Standard for Standardized Residency Training Bases (2022 Edition) – Detailed Rules for Critical Care Medicine Training Bases.” [ ] Standardized subspecialty training in CCM Intensivists, who have completed SRT, with further career aspirations should undergo standardized subspecialty training in CCM. The specific requirements can be found in the “Content and Standards for Standardized Subspecialty Training (2019 Edition).” [ ] Chinese critical care certified course (5C) and core skill training programs All practicing intensivists in hospitals at various levels should participate in the ``Chinese Critical Care Certified Course'' (abbreviated as 5C) and obtain the ``Certification of Completion.'' Additionally, intensivists should actively engage in core technical skill training programs organized by the CSCCM and obtain the corresponding certification upon passing the assessments. Standardized training for CCM specialist nurses Nurses in Department of Critical Care Medicine should undergo standardized training to become specialist nurses in CCM. Specific requirements: The program aims to equip participants with the multifaceted competencies required for clinical practice, teaching, and research in CCM through comprehensive, systematic, and standardized training. Trainees should acquire solid clinical nursing practice skills, nursing quality management capabilities, education and consultation abilities, teamwork skills, and foundational teaching and research competencies. Thereby, the program cultivates highly qualified specialist nurses capable of working independently in clinical nursing within CCM. Enhancing the development of training bases for CCM specialist nurses: (1) Tertiary hospitals, particularly teaching hospitals affiliated with medical schools, are recommended to actively work toward meeting the criteria for establishing standardized training bases for CCM specialist nursing and apply for accreditation. The comprehensive strength of the hospital, departmental scale, range of critical care nursing techniques performed, medical equipment, and clinical workload must comply with the “Accreditation Standards for Clinical Training Bases of Critical Care Specialist Nurses by the Chinese Nursing Association”; [ ] (2) Strengthening faculty training at CCM specialist nurse training bases is advised. Eligible nurses should be encouraged to participate in key faculty training programs for standardized specialist nurse training in CCM. Staffing allocations, qualifications of supervising instructors, and requirements for base directors must adhere to the “Accreditation Standards for Clinical Training Bases of Critical Care Specialist Nurses by the Chinese Nursing Association”. [ ] Scientific Research in CCM Construction of research platforms and scientific research systems for CCM Department of CCM in affiliated hospitals of medical colleges, teaching hospitals, and provincial tertiary grade A hospitals should establish the following research platforms to meet basic and clinical research needs as possible [ ] : (1) Complete GCP certification and institutional filing for medical device clinical trials; (2) Disease-specific databases (such as sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, or acute kidney injury), annotated disease-specific datasets, and biobanks in units with appropriate conditions; (3) Laboratories or research institutes for CCM at all levels in units with appropriate conditions; (4) An intelligent healthcare support system for critical care in units with appropriate conditions.

Department of CCM in affiliated hospitals of medical colleges, teaching hospitals, and provincial tertiary grade A hospitals should establish the following research platforms to meet basic and clinical research needs as possible [ ] : (1) Complete GCP certification and institutional filing for medical device clinical trials; (2) Disease-specific databases (such as sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, or acute kidney injury), annotated disease-specific datasets, and biobanks in units with appropriate conditions; (3) Laboratories or research institutes for CCM at all levels in units with appropriate conditions; (4) An intelligent healthcare support system for critical care in units with appropriate conditions. Based on disease-specific databases, algorithms such as large language models, artificial neural networks, and machine learning models should be integrated to support early warning, subtype classification, and decision-making for various critical illnesses; (5) A deep international cooperation in Department of Critical Care Medicine in affiliated hospitals of medical colleges, teaching hospitals, and provincial tertiary grade A hospitals, such as joint graduate training and international multicenter clinical research. Competency training and research directions in CCM Intensivists are encouraged to be actively engaged in competency training for clinical and basic scientific research, including research topic selection, study design, drug clinical trials, literature retrieval and review, experimental skills, data analysis and visualization, and academic writing. Intensivists are also encouraged to actively apply for research projects and talent programs, including various projects at the hospital, university, county (bureau), city (department), province (ministry), and national levels. Recommended priority research directions for departments of CCM [ ] are (1) construction of big data centers and information management platforms for CCM; (2) acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS); (3) shock and hemodynamic monitoring and treatment; (4) infection and sepsis diagnosis and treatment; (5) acute kidney injury and blood purification; (6) analgesia and sedation; (7) gastrointestinal dysfunction and nutritional support strategies; (8) organ dysfunction and repair; (9) epidemiology of critical care-related diseases; and (10) cerebral function monitoring and brain protection. Construction and requirements for scientific talent teams by hospital tier Department of Critical Care Medicine should optimize the talent development environment to stimulate the innovative drive of scientific talents, improve talent training mechanisms to support high-quality development, promote talent introduction and aggregation to build talent teams and innovation hubs, deepen the ``diversified'' development reform of talents, and improve talent training, employment, evaluation, and incentive mechanisms. Furthermore, strengthening industry-university-research integration is essential to facilitate the efficient transformation of scientific research achievements by scientific talents, focus on talent incentive and security mechanisms to address concerns in talent development, and encourage applications for talent programs to build multi-level critical care scientific talent echelons. [ ] Department of Critical Care Medicine in secondary hospitals with conditions should also strengthen the cultivation of critical care scientific talents by participating in scientific research training, establishing support relationships with research institutes, engaging in multicenter studies and research projects, and introducing talents. GCP filing and qualification requirements for clinical research on drugs and medical devices Clinical trials of drugs and medical devices in CCM should be conducted in clinical trial organizations meeting the corresponding conditions according to the Drug Administration Law of the People’s Republic of China , the Announcement of the National Medical Products Administration and the National Health Commission on Issuing the Provisions for the Management of Drug Clinical Trial Institutions (no. 101 [2019]) , the Good Clinical Practice for Medical Device Trials , and the Measures for the Administration of Qualification Requirements and Record-filing for Medical Device Clinical Trial Institutions . Clinical Trial Organizations for drugs and medical devices must be filed and managed according to national requirements. [ , ] Response to Public Health Emergencies Formulation of emergency response strategies ICUs should respond promptly to public health emergencies by improving bed management and patient triage, implementing the principle of centralized treatment for critically ill and injured patients, and optimizing the allocation of medical resources. They should establish a hierarchical reporting and information-sharing mechanism, along with stratified treatment approaches and individualized “one patient, one plan” management. Multidisciplinary collaboration and teleconsultation systems are recommended to comprehensively improve both emergency response capacity and routine clinical care, including critical illness prevention and complication control. Team building in emergency situations During public health emergencies, ICU teams should mobilize expert resources, clearly define staff responsibilities at different levels within emergency plans, and form an MDT. A tiered personnel training mechanism is recommended, along with standardized handover systems and emergency response protocols. Additionally, strengthening infection prevention and control training, as well as personal protection skills, is advised. Furthermore, mechanisms for multidisciplinary collaboration, regional resource sharing, psychological support, and incentive systems should be implemented. Integration of emergency plans with routine drills Medical emergency response plans should be formulated based on risk assessments of potential public health emergencies, with regular drills to test their effectiveness. Plans should be revised promptly based on

expert resources, clearly define staff responsibilities at different levels within emergency plans, and form an MDT. A tiered personnel training mechanism is recommended, along with standardized handover systems and emergency response protocols. Additionally, strengthening infection prevention and control training, as well as personal protection skills, is advised. Furthermore, mechanisms for multidisciplinary collaboration, regional resource sharing, psychological support, and incentive systems should be implemented. Integration of emergency plans with routine drills Medical emergency response plans should be formulated based on risk assessments of potential public health emergencies, with regular drills to test their effectiveness. Plans should be revised promptly based on changing circumstances, implementation experiences, and lessons learned from drills. Training should focus on emergency organization and management, rapid response, technical protocols, material reserves, departmental coordination, and media communication. Practical exercises should emphasize multidisciplinary teamwork and the use of telemedicine platforms. A scientific evaluation system is required to continuously assess and improve the effectiveness of training. Enhancement and Optimization of ICU Service Models Early rehabilitation in the ICU Once the critically ill patient’s condition is fully assessed and medical safety is ensured, initiating early bedside rehabilitation within 3–4 days of admission is recommended to improve outcomes. Several recent studies have shown that early bedside rehabilitation can improve the prognosis of critically ill patients in multiple dimensions, such as reducing the duration of mechanical ventilation and delirium and promoting physical function recovery. [ , , , ] Furthermore, multiple international guidelines recommend early mobilization and rehabilitation in the ICU. [ ] The Department of Critical Care Medicine should establish a rehabilitation team comprising intensivists, rehabilitation therapists (including physical, occupational, and speech therapists), nurses, and other relevant healthcare professionals. Multidisciplinary collaboration is essential in early rehabilitation and requires the CCM leadership. Moreover, patient and family cooperation also influences rehabilitation outcomes. [ ] Including family members should be considered according to the specific setup of each ICU. Rehabilitation measures in ICUs include, but are not limited to, early mobilization, respiratory function training, and airway clearance techniques. Rehabilitation for critically ill respiratory patients aims at reducing physiological and psychological dysfunction, improving ventilation, preserving existing function, and promoting early recovery of the physical function. [ ] For ICU patients on mechanical ventilation, exercise includes positioning management with active and passive movements. [ ] Treating respiratory dysfunction is also important for early rehabilitation, aiming to improve ventilation and lung compliance, reduce the work of breathing, and clear airway secretions. Airway clearance techniques can be applied to mechanically ventilated patients for the prompt removal of secretions and maintenance of airway patency. Respiratory muscle strength training aims to enhance the strength and endurance of respiratory muscles, typically using incentive spirometers, pressure threshold devices, and resistance devices. [ , , ] Providing rehabilitation therapy that covers the entire disease course for critically ill patients and addressing the challenge of chronic critical illness by establishing and improving sub-ICU facilities are recommended. After surviving the acute critical phase, some patients enter a state of chronic critical illness, requiring a certain level of monitoring and rehabilitation therapy. [ ] For these patients, rehabilitation primarily includes functional recovery training, such as cognitive, swallowing, and motor rehabilitation, to help them regain daily living abilities as soon as possible. Patients receiving physical rehabilitation in well-managed step-down units after the acute phase demonstrate improvements in physical and cognitive function with favorable safety profiles. [ , , ] Therefore, establishing step-down units under the management of the ICU and providing targeted functional training are recommended to accelerate patient recovery. MDT on the critical care platform The Department of Critical Care Medicine should organize an MDT for collaborative diagnosis and treatment of complex and critical cases. Diagnosis and treatment in the MDT is a patient-centered, disease-oriented approach when experts from multiple disciplines collaboratively develop personalized and comprehensive diagnosis and treatment plans through joint discussion. [ , ] MDT provides a platform for academic exchange and clinical collaboration across different disciplines, enhances the comprehensive capabilities of the medical team, optimizes diagnostic and therapeutic methods, and strengthens scientific research and innovation, playing a positive role in hospital development. Telemedicine Regional tertiary critical care centers should actively collaborate with primary ICUs to establish tele-critical care systems. Telemedicine in CCM, also known as ICU telemedicine programs (tele-ICU), is a care delivery model providing continuous critical care interventions through telemedicine. It aims to expand or supplement ICU capacity, [ ] thereby addressing ICU resource shortages and variability in treatment quality and ultimately improving clinical outcomes of ICU patients. Tele-ICU implementation is associated with shorter hospitalization and lower mortality. Furthermore, tele-ICU may reduce ICU operational costs through optimized resource allocation. ICU telemedicine programs (tele-ICU), is a care delivery model providing continuous critical care interventions through telemedicine. It aims to expand or supplement ICU capacity, [ ] thereby addressing ICU resource shortages and variability in treatment quality and ultimately improving clinical outcomes of ICU patients. Tele-ICU implementation is associated with shorter hospitalization and lower mortality. Furthermore, tele-ICU may reduce ICU operational costs through optimized resource allocation. [ ] The construction of CCM and critical care capacity in China has advanced rapidly in recent years. However, significant challenges remain, including uneven regional development and disparities in treatment quality. The provincial-municipal-county three-tier tele-ICU system, which was established under national policies such as the development of medical consortia and the Thousand Counties Project, can standardize diagnosis and treatment practices in primary hospital ICUs, strengthen quality control management, and promote homogeneous and standardized medical care in CCM, ultimately reducing mortality. During public health emergencies or scenarios when many ICU patients or injured people need urgent rescue, the tele-ICU system optimizes the utilization of critical care expert resources, overcoming limitations such as physical distance, geographical barriers, and operational constraints. This ensures that all patients have access to the most optimal diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. The establishment of a three-tier tele-ICU system requires the prior implementation of bilateral ICU platforms and foundational infrastructure development. The operationalization of the tele-ICU system necessitates the refinement of institutional protocols, division of responsibilities, workflow procedures, and performance incentives and accountability mechanisms. Team members operating within the tele-ICU framework must complete cross-regional practice registration filing in advance to secure legal credentials. Hierarchical diagnosis and treatment system and two-way referral mechanism Advancing the development of hierarchical diagnosis and treatment systems and two-way referral mechanisms in CCM through the framework of medical consortia is recommended. The two-way referral mechanism serves as a critical measure for effectively allocating medical service resources between regional higher- and lower-tier healthcare institutions and establishing a rational hierarchical care system. [ ] Imbalances in critical care capabilities and resource distribution across regions have become increasingly evident with the recent rapid advancements. Thus, ICUs in university-affiliated hospitals, teaching hospitals, and provincial tertiary hospitals must accelerate ICU bed turnover by transferring stabilized patients to primary ICUs for continued care to address the growing demand for treating critically ill patients. Conversely, primary ICUs, which are constrained by limited resources and capabilities, need to transfer patients that exceed their treatment capacity to university-affiliated hospitals, teaching hospitals, or provincial tertiary hospitals. This process fulfills the essential requirements of hierarchical diagnosis and treatment of critically ill patients, together with the two-way referral. The development of medical consortia serves as a key platform and service carrier for advancing the hierarchical diagnosis and treatment system at the current stage. [ ] The hierarchical diagnosis and treatment system, as well as the two-way referral mechanism, in CCM should actively seek government support and top-level hospital management planning. Efforts should be focused on strengthening talent cultivation and implementing grassroots ward rounds and training programs to build homogeneous disciplines within medical consortia. [ ] Furthermore, establishing bidirectional referral and resource-sharing platforms, clarifying incentive and oversight mechanisms, and refining the referral system are mandatory. Operational charters, capability demarcation, and bidirectional referral criteria must be defined in the development of CCM consortia to ensure that healthcare institutions at all levels leverage their respective strengths, coordinate across tiers, and optimize resource utilization. In summary, this guideline provides a comprehensive roadmap for the construction and high-quality development of CCM in China. It focuses on nine key domains related to foundational development (standardization of ICU ward construction, staffing and technical requirements, and equipment allocation), quality improvement measures (optimization of medical quality management and control systems, promotion of multidisciplinary collaboration, and the development of telemedicine and tiered diagnosis and treatment systems), capacity building (strengthening standardized training and continuing education, and enhancing emergency response capacity for major public health events), and research and future development priorities (advancing scientific research capacity in critical care, promoting technological innovation, cultivating high-level leading talents, and expanding international influence). This guideline aims to enhance the overall capacity for comprehensive critical care, improve the quality of services and the level of CCM nationwide, and strengthen the establishment of an efficient, collaborative, and sustainable critical care system. Furthermore, it seeks to drive scientific innovation and breakthroughs in international competitiveness, thereby continuously advancing the progress and development of CCM in China. chunks.content: Introduction Children who share a care environment with an abused child—referred to as contact children—face an increased risk of physical abuse ( ; ; ; ; ). Injury testing of contact children, including skeletal surveys (SS) —a standardized series of radiographs used to identify fractures—and neuroimaging, has been recommended by some experts to detect injuries that may not be apparent on history or physical examination alone ( ; ; ). However, precise indications for when such testing should be performed remain uncertain ( ), underscoring the need for additional data to inform evidence-based guidelines. Prior research examining injury testing among contact children is limited and has yielded variable results. A multicenter study of children evaluated by Child Abuse Pediatricians (CAPs)—physicians with subspecialty training in the evaluation of suspected child abuse—between 2010 and 2011 identified fractures in 16 of 134 (12%) contact children under two years of age, with twins at particularly elevated risk ( ). Despite skeletal survey being considered the standard of care at participating centers, only 76% of high-risk contacts underwent this evaluation ( ). More recently, a single-center study reported abnormal skeletal survey findings in 9 of 97 (9%) contact children, while none of the 34 neuroimaging studies performed in contact infants identified occult injuries ( ). Of note, in this context, occult injuries refer to injuries that are not apparent based on history or physical examination alone and are identified only through imaging or other diagnostic testing, a term that is widely used in the child abuse and pediatric trauma literature ( ; ). Guidelines from the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), published in 2015 and reaffirmed in 2021, recommend skeletal survey for household contacts under two years of age but provide no age-specific guidance on neuroimaging ( ). In other pediatric contexts, neuroimaging decisions are often guided by the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) decision rule; however, PECARN was not developed for suspected child abuse or contact children, where injuries lacking clinical significance may still have forensic relevance. Reflecting this uncertainty, recommendations vary, with one group advocating MRI for all contacts under 12 months ( ), while the ExSTRA multicenter study suggested neuroimaging for contacts under six months but identified no occult injuries in 19 asymptomatic infants ( ). Together, these shortcomings highlight a critical gap in the literature: the lack of contemporary, multicenter data on injury testing practices and diagnostic yield among contact children. This gap is particularly important given that testing decisions require substantial clinical coordination and resources and have meaningful implications for children’s health and clinical management. The objective of the present study was to determine rates of injury testing and diagnostic yield among contact children evaluated within the Child Abuse Pediatrics Research Network (CAPNET), a U.S.A-based, multicenter observational research network. By leveraging contemporary data from multiple pediatric referral centers, this study aims to provide empirical evidence to inform clinical decision-making regarding injury testing for contact children. Methods This was a cross-sectional study using CAPNET, a U.S.A-based, multicenter observational research network of children <10 years (120 months) old who underwent subspecialty evaluation for concerns of physical abuse at 10 participating pediatric centers. The methods of CAPNET and demographics of the patient sample have been previously published, and CAPNET’s core definitions and data dictionary are publicly available ( ; .; ). Participating CAPNET centers obtained approval or exemption from their local Institutional Review Board to collect, share, and analyze data. Participants and Settings CAPNET includes 10 US quaternary pediatric hospitals with dedicated child protection teams with at least 2 board-certified Child Abuse Pediatricians (CAPs). Data were abstracted from the medical record for children <10 years (120 months) old if they received care at the participating center and were evaluated by a CAP for recent concerns for physical abuse between February 1, 2021, and December 31, 2022. Evaluations were included whether the child was seen in person by the CAP or recommendations were given by telephone or telehealth. Data were abstracted by CAPs or trained data operators from the electronic medical record into an encrypted database using the Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) platform and subject to published quality assurance processes ( ; ). Contacts Contacts were defined as children who shared a care environment (including a home, daycare, etc.) where there was suspected physical abuse. As an observational network, CAPNET collects different data for contacts depending on the information available to the clinical team ( ). In some cases, CAPs are aware of contact children but make no testing recommendations and perform no evaluation of the contact children. In other cases, CAPs recommend testing for contacts, who may be evaluated at the hospital where the CAP practices or at a different center. This means that, for some contacts, only partial information is available and entered into the CAPNET database; for these

a care environment (including a home, daycare, etc.) where there was suspected physical abuse. As an observational network, CAPNET collects different data for contacts depending on the information available to the clinical team ( ). In some cases, CAPs are aware of contact children but make no testing recommendations and perform no evaluation of the contact children. In other cases, CAPs recommend testing for contacts, who may be evaluated at the hospital where the CAP practices or at a different center. This means that, for some contacts, only partial information is available and entered into the CAPNET database; for these contacts, CAPNET collects the contact’s age, sex, relationship to the index child, the tests that were recommended by the CAP, and any test results that are known. Some contacts meet CAPNET eligibility and have a full evaluation by the CAP, either because they present for their own concerns of abuse or due to concerns raised for another child. When multiple children from the same environment are identified and their information is entered into CAPNET, subjects are grouped together into family groups. Decisions regarding testing or whether to perform evaluation by the CAP are at the discretion of the clinical team and may depend on clinical factors such as a child’s age, symptoms, perceived likelihood of abuse in the index child, or on practice variability by center or CAP. For children who receive CAP evaluations, CAPNET records whether the child presented due to exposure to family violence (e.g., suspicion of abuse in another child, intimate partner violence [IPV], elder abuse, or animal abuse). We sought to identify contacts who received an evaluation because of concern for abuse in another child. We therefore excluded contacts with CAP evaluations if concern for exposure to child abuse in another child was not listed among the reasons for presentation. Injury Testing Participating centers conducted skeletal surveys according to AAP/American College of Radiology (ACR) guidelines ( ). Neuroimaging included computed tomography (CT), standard magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or Fast MRI, but not cranial ultrasound alone ( ; ). CAPs assessed abuse likelihood using a previously published 7-point scale ranging from 1-Definitely Not Physical Abuse to 7-Definite Physical Abuse ( ). We considered skeletal survey to be recommended by AAP guidelines for contacts who were <24 months old if the index child had a high likelihood of abuse (6 or 7 on the 7-point scale) ( ; ). We determined imaging rates and injury identification for contacts of index children with high likelihood of abuse using age thresholds of <6 months and <12 months. Diagnostic yield was defined as the proportion of studies that identified previously unrecognized injuries. For skeletal imaging, the yield reflected the sum of findings on initial and, if obtained, follow-up skeletal survey. For neuroimaging, injuries included intracranial hemorrhage, parenchymal injury, and cranial fractures not previously identified, but not isolated scalp injuries ( ). We used descriptive statistics to describe injury testing rates and diagnostic yield. We used odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) to measure differences between groups. Results Participating CAPNET centers evaluated 7202 children for concerns of physical abuse during the study period. Of these, 6256 (87%) were index children who received CAP evaluations and 946 were contacts with CAP evaluations ( ). Among the contacts, 152 (16%) presented for reasons other than exposure to abuse in another child, leaving 794 contacts for analysis ( ). More than half of these contacts (530, 67%) had a normal physical exam. Among the 3917 other identified contacts who did not have CAP evaluations, 1005 received some testing recommendations from a CAP, and 2912 received no recommendations. Skeletal Surveys According to AAP guidelines, skeletal survey (SS) would have been indicated for 316 identified contacts (<24 months of age and associated with an index child with a high level of concern for abuse). Among these, 196 (62%) were known to have received an initial SS. Of the 196 completed SS, 20 identified new fractures ( ). Eleven contacts whose skeletal survey identified new fractures also received a Follow-Up Skeletal Survey (FUSS). Of these, 5 identified additional fractures and 1 confirmed the presence of a fracture that was suggested on the initial SS. Additionally, 283 contacts received a SS even though they were older than 24 months of age (n=110) and/or were associated with an index child who had a lower level of concern for abuse (n=230). Of these, 10 had fractures identified ( ). Among the 30 contacts with additional fractures identified on SS, 11 (37%) had findings on physical examination, 14 (47%) had at least 1 rib fracture identified and 14 (47%) were twins. Among the 316 contacts <24 months old with an index child with high level of concern, 50 were twins, 123 were <12 months, and 39 had findings on physical

contacts received a SS even though they were older than 24 months of age (n=110) and/or were associated with an index child who had a lower level of concern for abuse (n=230). Of these, 10 had fractures identified ( ). Among the 30 contacts with additional fractures identified on SS, 11 (37%) had findings on physical examination, 14 (47%) had at least 1 rib fracture identified and 14 (47%) were twins. Among the 316 contacts <24 months old with an index child with high level of concern, 50 were twins, 123 were <12 months, and 39 had findings on physical exam. SS were completed for 37/50 twins compared to 124/266 non-twins (OR 3.26, 95%CI 1.66–6.41) and were positive for 11/36 twins compared to 9/124 non-twins (OR 5.41 95%CI 2.03–14.36). SS were completed for 76/123 contacts under 12 months vs. 85/193 contacts 12–24 months old (OR 2.05, 95% CI 1.29–3.26) and were positive for 14/76 contacts <12 months old vs. 6/85 contacts 12–24 months old (OR 2.97, 95% CI 1.08–8.19). SS was completed for 35/39 contacts with findings on physical exam (OR 10.49, 95% CI 3.63–30.30) and was positive for 7/35 contacts with physical exam findings vs. 13/126 without findings (OR 2.51, 95% CI 1.09–5.80). Neuroimaging A total of 123 contacts were younger than 12 months of age and associated with an index child with high concern for abuse. Among these, neuroimaging was recommended by the CAP or medical team for 56 (46%) and results were available for 49 contacts. Of the 38 children with neuroimaging modality reported (because they received a CAP evaluation), 30 (79%) had a head CT, 9 (24%) had Fast MRI, and 6 (16%) had full brain MRI. Overall, neuroimaging identified injuries in 7 of these cases – 5 with intracranial hemorrhage and 2 with skull fractures ( ). All but one contact with positive neuroimaging findings was <6 months old and all were twins. Injuries (one subarachnoid hemorrhage and one fracture) were also identified in 2 of 49 contacts who had neuroimaging despite being older than 12 months (n=23) or with lower concern for abuse in the index child (n=33). Of the 123 infant contacts, 84 (68%) were <6 months old, 38 (31%) were twins and 63 (51%) were documented to have a normal physical examination after a CAP evaluation (n=46) or by other clinicians (n=17). Neuroimaging was performed in 39/84 infants 0–6 months old, compared to 10/39 contacts 6–12 months old (OR 2.51, 95%CI 1.09–5.80). Neuroimaging was performed in 30/38 twins compared to 19/85 non-twins (OR 13.03, 95%CI 5.13–33.08). In all but two cases where the contact had neuroimaging, the index child had intracranial injuries identified. All but one of the contacts with new injuries on neuroimaging were twins of the index child. Two contacts with new injuries on neuroimaging had cutaneous findings on physical examination and one had macrocephaly. Among the 63 with documented normal physical examinations, neuroimaging was completed in 36 (57%) and injury was identified in five. Discussion This study contributes to understanding physical abuse and neglect by characterizing injury testing practices and diagnostic yield among children who share a care environment with an abused child. Although primarily intended to inform clinicians who evaluate children for possible physical abuse, the findings also highlight the substantial clinical effort and coordination required to implement recommended injury testing for contact children. Decisions to pursue testing often require CAPs and frontline providers to engage hospital systems, caregivers, and child welfare agencies, particularly when children are asymptomatic. Our findings reinforce existing recommendations for higher-risk groups—especially younger children and twins—and provide contemporary, multicenter data to inform future efforts to refine injury screening strategies and resource allocation. Injuries were identified in a modest proportion of contacts in this large cohort. Imaging was more often completed, and injuries were more common, in younger contacts, twins, and those with signs of injury on physical examination. Because testing was more likely to be completed in contacts with the highest perceived risk, the true yield of universal testing likely falls between the assumption that all untested children had no injuries and the observed yield among tested children (6–12% for SS; 6–14% for neuroimaging). There is currently no widely accepted yield threshold at which routine testing should be recommended or avoided in cases of suspected physical abuse. The PECARN decision rule for neuroimaging in children younger than two years recommends imaging for those with high-risk features (4.4% risk of clinically important traumatic brain injury) and observation for lower-risk children (0.9% risk) ( ; ; ). However, PECARN is based on clinically significant outcomes, whereas some injuries identified in this study, although not clinically significant, may still carry forensic relevance. At these pediatric referral centers, skeletal surveys were completed in most cases where recommended by the AAP but were omitted in a substantial minority. We

routine testing should be recommended or avoided in cases of suspected physical abuse. The PECARN decision rule for neuroimaging in children younger than two years recommends imaging for those with high-risk features (4.4% risk of clinically important traumatic brain injury) and observation for lower-risk children (0.9% risk) ( ; ; ). However, PECARN is based on clinically significant outcomes, whereas some injuries identified in this study, although not clinically significant, may still carry forensic relevance. At these pediatric referral centers, skeletal surveys were completed in most cases where recommended by the AAP but were omitted in a substantial minority. We were unable to determine the reasons for omitted testing, which may include lack of recommendation, inability to complete testing, or failure to communicate results to the CAP. Completion of testing often requires coordination among CAPs, other clinicians, child protective services, and families, and practice variation and resource availability across CAPNET sites may further limit completion or result availability. Among contacts who received SS as recommended by the AAP, injuries were identified in approximately 10%, with higher completion and yield among twins. Injuries were less frequently identified when testing was completed beyond AAP guidelines. Neuroimaging identified injuries in a small number of children, most of whom were twins, younger than six months, or had findings on physical examination. Our results are consistent with previous data. The ExSTRA investigators showed that fractures were detected in more than 10% of contact children; that study specifically excluded contacts who presented with their own concerns for abuse ( ). Another retrospective single-center study of 390 contacts identified fractures in 9 of 97 SS obtained in 114 contacts <2 years old ( ). In contrast to our population, however, none of the 63 infant contacts in this study and none of the 19 eligible contacts in the ExSTRA study had abnormal neuroimaging findings. Our study has several limitations. We may have incorrectly designated some children as index or contact children; several contacts with injuries identified by testing presented with symptoms that were concerning for abuse ( and ) and might better be categorized as multiple index children who presented simultaneously. This would artificially inflate the yield of injury testing we report. Further, the presence of signs and symptoms in some children with additional injury identification implies that the injuries reported here should not be designated as occult injures. Identification of injuries in a contact child may have influenced the level of concern for abuse assigned to the index child. This influence may have varied across cases, as some CAPs assigned a final level of concern for the index child before all injuries in contact children were identified. As a result, assignment of children into “indicated” groups may have been partially circular. For this reason, we are unable to determine whether imaging was more likely to identify injuries in contacts if the index child had a higher perceived likelihood of abuse. Further, until more research is available, clinicians may choose to recommend testing for some contacts of index children with moderate concern for abuse. It is possible that recommended testing was performed at non-CAPNET centers, and the results were not known to the CAP. It is possible that contacts who did not have testing had injuries that went undiagnosed. Further, we may not have documented some injuries that were identified by outside testing but not communicated to the CAP who cared for the index child. Because we are limited to information known to CAPs, we did not identify all contacts of all children, since CAPs may not have been aware of some contacts – especially when concern for abuse in the index child was low. Additionally, our database captured a maximum of 6 contacts. However, only 4 family groups had more than 6 contacts identified. We chose to include several types of contact relationships, from siblings to daycare contacts. Different relationships may carry different levels of proximity to the abuser. Unlike prior studies, we included contact children who presented with physical exam findings or other reasons to be concerned for abuse. Taken together, these limitations reflect the challenges inherent to observational, multicenter research in our field. Despite these constraints, the findings provide meaningful, practice-relevant evidence to support clinical decision-making regarding injury testing for contact children and to inform future research aimed at refining screening strategies and thresholds. Conclusion Children who share a care environment with an abused child are at increased risk for physical abuse. Among contacts of children with high perceived likelihood of abuse, younger children, those with concerning findings on physical examination, and twins were more likely to have testing completed and to have injuries identified.

Conclusion Children who share a care environment with an abused child are at increased risk for physical abuse. Among contacts of children with high perceived likelihood of abuse, younger children, those with concerning findings on physical examination, and twins were more likely to have testing completed and to have injuries identified.

documents.title: AAP policy statement sleep-related infant deaths updated 2022 recommendations for reducing infant deaths in the sleep environment

chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Following substantial declines in the 1990s, overall sudden unexpected infant death in the USA has plateaued over the past two decades, despite expanded and updated sleep guidance. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS Provides the most recent nationally representative estimates (2016–2022) of maternal adherence to all four safe infant sleep practices using Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System Phase 8 data, demonstrating that while back-sleeping and room-sharing are common, adherence to safe sleep surfaces and bedding remains low. Identifies persistent sociodemographic disparities despite modest improvements in safe sleep practices over time. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY These findings underscore the need for comprehensive safe-sleep strategies that extend beyond back-sleeping to address sleep surfaces, bedding and bed-sharing practices. Support integrating culturally responsive safe-sleep counselling and access to safe-sleep equipment into prenatal and postpartum care, Women, Infants and Children, Medicaid perinatal services and home-visiting programmes to reduce persistent disparities. Introduction Background Sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) encompasses all sudden and unexpected deaths in the first year of life. Most SUIDs occur in unsafe sleep environments. Sleep-related SUID includes accidental suffocation and strangulation in bed (ASSB), sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) and deaths of unknown cause. A diagnosis of ASSB is assigned when a clear asphyxial mechanism is identified on scene investigation or autopsy, such as overlay, wedging or airway obstruction from soft bedding. SIDS is diagnosed when an infant death remains unexplained despite clinical history review, scene investigation and autopsy, and is further subcategorised based on information available and specific epidemiological features. Finally, deaths are classified as unknown cause, when available evidence is insufficient to assign ASSB or SIDS. The ‘triple-risk model’ suggests that SUIDs occur when a vulnerable infant encounters an external stressor, such as an unsafe sleep environment, during a critical developmental stage. In the USA, approximately 3700 infants die annually from sleep-related causes in 2022, corresponding to a rate of about 1 per 1000 live births, which remains higher than in many other high-income countries. Following the American Academy of Paediatrics (AAP) non-prone sleep recommendation (1992) and the 1994 ‘Back to Sleep’ campaign, SUID rates declined sharply from 1.3 per 1000 live births in 1989–91 to 0.8 per 1000 live births in 1995–98. A diagnostic shift between 1999 and 2001 led to fewer deaths being classified as SIDS and more being attributed to ASSB and unknown causes, resulting in relatively little overall change in the total SUID rate despite earlier declines. In response to this evolving classification pattern and emerging evidence on unsafe sleep environments, the AAP has continued to update and refine its safe sleep recommendations in 2011 and 2016, and again in 2022. The US infant mortality statistics show marked demographic disparities. Black infants experience disproportionately higher rates of all SUID categories, with especially elevated ASSB mortality around 4 months of age. Public awareness and adherence to broader AAP recommendations vary by race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status and cultural norms. Bed-sharing, for example, is deeply rooted in many communities and may conflict with recommendations for solitary sleep. Inconsistent counselling during prenatal and postnatal care further contributes to uneven adoption of safe sleep behaviours. These patterns highlight persistent gaps between evidence-based recommendations and parental practices. The Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) provides a unique opportunity to examine maternal practices related to infant sleep in a large, population-based and nationally representative sample. PRAMS gathers information on maternal demography, PNC utilisation, tobacco use, breastfeeding and infant characteristics, allowing exploration of factors that influence safe sleep practices. It also enables analysis of temporal trends in the adoption of evolving recommendations, which helps identify lagging practices and assess the need for additional interventions to promote behaviour change. Objective This study uses PRAMS Phase 8 (2016–2022) data to estimate maternal adherence to four recommended safe infant sleep practices, namely, supine sleep position, room-sharing without bed-sharing, use of a firm sleep surface and avoiding soft bedding. We also examine temporal trends and identify sociodemographic and behavioural correlates of non-adherence to inform targeted, culturally competent public health interventions that promote safe sleep recommendations and reduce sleep-related infant deaths. Methods Data source and study population This secondary analysis used repeated cross-sectional data from PRAMS Phase 8 (2016–2022). PRAMS is a collaborative surveillance system of the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and state health departments that samples recent mothers 2–6 months postdelivery using stratified birth certificate-based methods. PRAMS surveillance data, implemented in 1987, covered approximately 83% of all US births by 2018. Survey weights account for three components: (1) the sampling weight to account for different sampling rates in different strata, (2) non-response adjustment using birth certificate data available for non-responders and (3) non-coverage adjustment to account for eligible records missing from the cumulative birth certificate file. Consequently, unweighted counts represent the actual number of survey respondents,

is a collaborative surveillance system of the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and state health departments that samples recent mothers 2–6 months postdelivery using stratified birth certificate-based methods. PRAMS surveillance data, implemented in 1987, covered approximately 83% of all US births by 2018. Survey weights account for three components: (1) the sampling weight to account for different sampling rates in different strata, (2) non-response adjustment using birth certificate data available for non-responders and (3) non-coverage adjustment to account for eligible records missing from the cumulative birth certificate file. Consequently, unweighted counts represent the actual number of survey respondents, whereas weighted counts represent population-level estimates of US live births in participating states and years. Additional details of sampling design, participating states and Phase 8 release thresholds are provided in . Of 249 970 respondents, 235 410 had singleton births. The analytical sample included 125 931 women who provided definitive information on all four recommended infant sleep practices (position, location, surface and bedding). The selection flow diagram is shown in . Multiple births and respondents with missing information on plurality (3.5%) were excluded because multiple gestations differ in obstetric risk classification, and their infants may require longer hospital stays due to risks associated with prematurity and low birth weight. Respondents were further excluded if they had missing data for any of the four primary outcome variables related to infant sleep practices. Beyond item-level missingness, exclusions were required where the bedding variable contained internally inconsistent responses (eg, simultaneous negative responses to both safe and unsafe indicators) or incomplete reporting of unsafe bedding items (blankets, toys/pillows, bumper pads). These records could not be reliably classified, resulting in an additional 22% exclusion. Structural skip patterns inherent to PRAMS administration ( ) contributed approximately 12% of the missingness in the sleep-location variable. Although some skipped responses may have reflected room-sharing, we deliberately treated them as missing to avoid speculative reclassification. An additional 9% of room-sharing responses were excluded due to discordant reporting patterns (eg, no room-sharing combined with crib use), as retaining such records would lead to potential overestimation of safe sleep behaviours. These exclusions accounted for the relatively high proportion of excluded data for sleep bedding and location. Outcome variables and correlates Safe and unsafe infant sleep practices were defined according to the AAP guidelines. Dichotomous outcomes captured adherence (safe) versus non-adherence (unsafe) for: (1) sleep position, (2) sleep location, (3) sleep surface and (4) sleep bedding. provides operative definitions of safe and unsafe infant sleep practices and an overview of AAP recommendations. details the PRAMS questions on infant sleep practices and categorisation of safe and unsafe practices. Sleep position was measured using a ‘most often’ question reflecting usual practice, while all other practices were based on how the infant usually slept during the past 2 weeks. Covariates were selected based on prior literature linking their association with sleep-related infant deaths. Sociodemographic correlates included maternal age, race/ethnicity, education level, insurance type and Women, Infants and Children (WIC) registration status. Behavioural and infant-related correlates included marital status, pregnancy intention, adequacy of prenatal care (PNC) utilisation as assessed by Kotelchuck Index, infant maturity, birth weight category, breastfeeding status, current maternal smoking and postpartum depression. Broader categories were collapsed to streamline analysis, prevent overfitting and enhance statistical power. Maternal age categories, originally ranging from <20 to >40 years were collapsed into three groups (<20, 20–34 and >34 years). Educational attainment categories for high school diploma and some college education without an associate degree were similarly merged. Race and ethnicity data were consolidated as Hispanic or non-Hispanic; non-Hispanic respondents were further categorised as white, black or other, with the latter including American Indian, Alaska Native, Pacific Islander, Asian or multi-ethnic individuals. Missing data Listwise deletion was applied to missing outcome variables (46.5% of respondents), reducing the analytic sample size. Missing covariate data ( ) were excluded from individual analyses. Because excluded respondents differed from included respondents, particularly by age, race/ethnicity, marital status, depression and lack of healthcare worker (HCW) advice ( ), selection bias is possible. Although multiple imputation was technically feasible, we chose sensitivity analysis over imputation, as the substantial excluded outcome data described earlier would have required strong assumptions given the complex survey design with weighting, stratification, socially sensitive trimester-specific responses and correlated sleep-practice domains. To evaluate robustness, we compared characteristics of included versus excluded respondents and conducted sensitivity analyses for the two most consistently reported practices, namely, sleep position and sleep surface, using parallel adjusted models. Statistical analysis PRAMS provides a unified analytic dataset of single-year, single-state weighted datasets. All analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics V.25 with the Complex Samples module for weighted analyses. PRAMS-provided final sampling weights and design variables were specified in the complex samples plan (see the ‘Data availability free text’ section), allowing the statistical software to internally account

weighting, stratification, socially sensitive trimester-specific responses and correlated sleep-practice domains. To evaluate robustness, we compared characteristics of included versus excluded respondents and conducted sensitivity analyses for the two most consistently reported practices, namely, sleep position and sleep surface, using parallel adjusted models. Statistical analysis PRAMS provides a unified analytic dataset of single-year, single-state weighted datasets. All analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics V.25 with the Complex Samples module for weighted analyses. PRAMS-provided final sampling weights and design variables were specified in the complex samples plan (see the ‘Data availability free text’ section), allowing the statistical software to internally account for the survey design for variance estimation and population-level inference without generating or modifying weights. We calculated weighted period prevalences and 95% CIs for each safe sleep practice and stratified results by sociodemographic and behavioural correlates. Temporal trends (2016–2022) were evaluated using log-linear regression on Joinpoint Regression Software V.5.4.0. Average annual percentage change (APC) with 95% CIs was calculated using the formula APC=(eˆβ−1)×100, where β is the slope coefficient. Models were tested for 0–1 joinpoints due to the limited annual time points. To identify correlates of unsafe infant sleep practices, we first estimated unadjusted ORs with 95% CIs using simple logistic regression. Variables significant in unadjusted analyses were then entered into separate multiple logistic regression models to obtain adjusted ORs (AORs) with 95% CIs. In addition, unsafe location components were analysed separately to clarify whether associations were driven by bed-sharing or by infants sleeping in a separate room. A p value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Ethics statement This study analysed de-identified data accessed from the CDC PRAMS Analytic Research File portal in November 2024 (see the ‘Data availability free text’ section). We adhered to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology guidelines for reporting cross-sectional studies. Patient and public involvement Patients and the public were not involved in the design, conduct, reporting or dissemination of this research. Results Study population Of the 125 931 participants with complete information on all four sleep practices, most were non-Hispanic white (58%), aged 20–34 years (77%) and had at least a high school education (53%) ( ). Excluded respondents showed similar characteristics overall; however, a higher proportion of older, black or college-educated women were excluded ( ). They were also more likely to lack HCW advice on safe sleep practices. Prevalence of safe infant sleep practices summarises the prevalence of each practice. Approximately 80% of mothers reported placing infants in the supine position and room-sharing without bed-sharing. In contrast, adherence to safe sleep surfaces (36%) and safe bedding practices (33%) was substantially lower. Detailed distributions of specific unsafe practices (eg, non-supine positions, sleep surfaces and bedding items) are presented in . While nearly all respondents reported at least one safe practice, none adhered to all four. Trends from 2016 to 2022 All four safe sleep behaviours increased significantly over time. Improvements were modest for the safe supine position (APC=0.7%; ) and safe location (APC=0.6%; ), but greater for safe surfaces (APC=2.7%; ) and especially safe bedding (APC=11.2%; ). Patterns suggested sustained increases in safe bedding throughout the period, and an uptick in all other safe behaviours between 2018 and 2020. Maternal correlates of safe sleep practices The weighted prevalence of safe sleep practices across sociodemographic, behavioural and healthcare characteristics is presented in . The unadjusted associations (ORs) between maternal characteristics and unsafe infant sleep practices ( ) indicated that maternal age, education, race/ethnicity, insurance status, WIC enrolment, marital status, pregnancy intention, PNC utilisation, HCW advice, breastfeeding status, smoking and postpartum depression were each significantly associated with at least one unsafe practice. In contrast, infant maturity and birth weight were not meaningfully associated with unsafe sleep practices. In multiple logistic regression analyses ( ), the associations remained largely consistent in direction, although attenuated after adjustment; corresponding forest plots for unsafe position ( ), location ( ), surface ( ) and bedding ( ) illustrate these findings. Across all sleep practices, adherence increased with maternal age and education. Persistent racial and ethnic disparities were observed. After adjustment, non-Hispanic black mothers had higher odds of unsafe sleep behaviours, including unsafe position (AOR 3.4), unsafe location (AOR 2.4), unsafe surface (AOR 1.5) and unsafe bedding (AOR 3.6). Hispanic and other minority mothers also demonstrated elevated risks. Indicators of lower socioeconomic status, such as low education, Medicaid coverage or being uninsured and WIC enrolment, remained associated with unsafe sleep positioning and bedding. Inadequate PNC utilisation showed small but significant associations with some outcomes. HCW counselling was protective for most behaviours; lack of advice was associated with unsafe position (AOR 2.7), unsafe surface (AOR 1.2) and unsafe bedding (AOR 1.4). Unmarried status, smoking, postpartum depression and not breastfeeding were variably associated with unsafe behaviours, although smoking and depression were more strongly linked to unsafe surfaces and bedding.
