Sleep location: bed-sharing and room-sharing The pattern of associations observed for the composite unsafe location outcome closely mirrored those for bed-sharing ( ). Racial and ethnic disparities were less pronounced for no room-sharing and this behaviour was more strongly associated with the absence of HCW advice (AOR 1.7). Sensitivity analysis As the excluded respondents were younger, more often unmarried and more frequently lacked HCW advice, suggesting potential selection bias ( ), we compared the adjusted associations for unsafe position and unsafe surface among the included and excluded respondents. The results showed broadly consistent adjusted associations in direction and magnitude ( ). However, notable differences included a lower AOR for unsafe position among Black mothers in excluded data (2.5 vs 3.4), and a higher AOR for unsafe surface among other minority groups (2.1 vs 1.6). Discussion Principal findings This study provides one of the most recent and nationally representative assessments of maternal adherence to infant sleep practices in the USA, highlighting persistent gaps in the implementation of safe sleep recommendations. While adherence to the supine sleep position and room-sharing without bed-sharing remained high, reflecting the continued success of long-standing public health campaigns, safe surface and bedding practices remained low, consistent with earlier national reports. All practices improved from 2016 to 2022, yet gains were uneven; trends were modest for position and location but more pronounced for bedding and surface use. These findings indicate ongoing challenges in achieving widespread adoption of the full set of AAP safe sleep recommendations. Trends in context The observed improvements align with earlier PRAMS (2009–2015) and the National Infant Sleep Position study findings. The ‘Back to Sleep’ campaign rapidly increased supine sleep and halved SIDS rates, but translating expanded guidance covering sleep location, surfaces and avoidance of soft bedding has been slower. These behaviours require multiple simultaneous changes that depend on caregivers’ understanding, shifts in public health messaging and evolving guidance. Manufacturers and retailers often promote cribs outfitted with bedding and accessories, sending mixed messages to parents. Updates clarifying the distinctions between room-sharing and bed-sharing, and their intersection with breastfeeding practices, may have contributed to variability in adoption over time. Disparities Racial and ethnic disparities remained among the strongest predictors of unsafe practices, in line with previous research. These disparities mirror patterns in SUID mortality and reflect a combination of parental choices, cultural norms, systemic inequities and limited access to safe sleep resources. Pillows, blankets and bumper pads, strongly associated with ASSB, are introduced by caregivers believing they enhance infant comfort and safety. Low adherence to recommended safe surfaces and bedding is especially pronounced among black and Hispanic mothers. Thus, culturally responsive public health messaging and equitable access to safe sleep resources may support behaviour change. Sociodemographic and behavioural correlates Beyond race and ethnicity, our findings demonstrate the influence of socioeconomic, behavioural and health-system factors on adherence. Lower maternal education, Medicaid or uninsured status, unplanned pregnancy, inadequate PNC utilisation, current smoking, lack of breastfeeding and absence of HCW counselling were all associated with unsafe practices, consistent with previous studies. Healthcare providers play a central role in shaping parental decisions. Evidence suggests that parents are more receptive to counselling that promotes safer alternatives than to risk-only counselling or to receiving no advice at all. Strengthening consistent and evidence-based counselling across prenatal and postnatal care could help reduce disparities in adherence. Bed-sharing and room-sharing: context with international recommendations Our findings underscore the importance of distinguishing bed-sharing from room-sharing, as the observed associations for unsafe location were largely driven by bed-sharing rather than infants sleeping alone in a separate room. International infant sleep safety guidelines are broadly convergent regarding supine positioning, firm sleep surfaces, avoidance of soft bedding, room-sharing, breastfeeding, immunisation, pacifier use, appropriate room temperature and avoidance of smoking, alcohol and substance abuse. However, approaches to shared sleep surfaces differ. The AAP 2022 guidelines acknowledge that families may choose to bed-share for reasons such as breastfeeding facilitation or cultural practices, yet state that bed-sharing cannot be recommended under any circumstances, particularly for infants younger than 4 months; the update also reports higher risk estimates compared with the 2016 guidance. In contrast, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) on co-sleeping and SIDS guidance supports informed decision-making regarding

positioning, firm sleep surfaces, avoidance of soft bedding, room-sharing, breastfeeding, immunisation, pacifier use, appropriate room temperature and avoidance of smoking, alcohol and substance abuse. However, approaches to shared sleep surfaces differ. The AAP 2022 guidelines acknowledge that families may choose to bed-share for reasons such as breastfeeding facilitation or cultural practices, yet state that bed-sharing cannot be recommended under any circumstances, particularly for infants younger than 4 months; the update also reports higher risk estimates compared with the 2016 guidance. In contrast, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) on co-sleeping and SIDS guidance supports informed decision-making regarding surface sharing. Both guidelines recognise increased risk in the presence of prematurity, low birth weight, parental smoking, alcohol and substance use and loose bedding. While the AAP guidelines explicitly note that unintentional bed-sharing in an adult bed is safer than on a sofa, NICE guidance does not distinguish between these contexts. Counselling that clearly differentiates room-sharing from bed-sharing may help families adopt safer practices without dismissing cultural practices. Interpretation of missing-data patterns and sensitivity analysis Excluding respondents with missing or non-classifiable sleep practice data likely introduced selection bias, although sensitivity analyses showed that most associations remained stable. Excluded respondents showed characteristics associated with socioeconomic stress and lower survey completion. Slight differences in racial/ethnic associations suggest that disparities may be slightly underestimated. Nonetheless, the consistency of most adjusted estimates supports the validity of these findings. Strengths and limitations A significant strength of this study is its use of PRAMS Phase 8, a large, population-based, nationally representative dataset that provides recent and detailed information on maternal behaviours. The ability to examine four distinct safe sleep practices concurrently, apply survey weights, evaluate temporal trends and adjust for multiple covariates enhances the robustness and generalisability of the findings. However, several limitations warrant consideration. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. The data rely on maternal self-report, which is subject to recall or social desirability bias. Nearly half of the original sample was excluded due to missing or non-classifiable sleep practice information as we prioritised classification validity, but this may have introduced potential selection bias. Excluded respondents differed modestly from included respondents on key sociodemographic factors, which may have attenuated or inflated some associations, particularly racial/ethnic disparities. Conclusion In conclusion, despite the longstanding success of supine sleep messaging, comprehensive adherence to safe infant sleep remains low, particularly regarding sleep surfaces and bedding. Our findings highlight persistent racial, socioeconomic and behavioural disparities, underscoring the need for culturally responsive, family-centred and healthcare provider-driven interventions. Integrating safe sleep promotion into broader maternal and child health programmes will be critical to reducing disparities and reversing the stagnation in sleep-related infant death rates. chunks.content: Introduction Cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT) is a rare yet potentially severe neurological condition characterized by the partial or complete obstruction of the dural venous sinuses and/or cerebral cortical veins. This obstruction impairs cerebral venous drainage and may result in edema, intracranial hypertension, and hemorrhagic events [ ]. CVT accounts for approximately 0.5% to 3% of all strokes, predominantly affecting individuals under 55 years of age, with a particular prevalence among women of reproductive age due to the influence of hormonal and obstetric factors [ ]. Historically, the association between infections and CVT is well-documented, particularly in intracranial bacterial infections such as otitis, mastoiditis, and meningitis [ , ]. However, in recent decades, there has been growing recognition that non-bacterial agents, such as viruses, fungi, and parasites, may also be involved in the pathophysiology of CVT [ ]. These agents act through inflammatory or immune-mediated mechanisms, or by direct invasion of the central nervous system [ , ]. The increasing diversity of pathogens, especially in immunocompromised patients, has challenged the understanding of their pathogenic mechanisms, as well as the diagnostic and therapeutic approach to the disease [ ]. While the association between bacterial infections and CVT is well-established, and more recently, COVID-19-associated CVT have been documented [ – ], a comprehensive synthesis of CVT associated with other non-bacterial infections is lacking. Existing literature reviews on infectious causes of CVT often include bacterial without providing a detailed, pathogen-specific analysis of viral, fungal, and parasitic etiologies separately. Furthermore, there is no systematic review that exclusively focuses on these non-bacterial, non-COVID-19 pathogens to elucidate their distinct clinical profiles, imaging patterns, management strategies, and outcomes. This gap limits the ability of clinicians to recognize and tailor therapy for CVT caused by these specific agents. This systematic review aimed to summarize the evidence regarding the occurrence of CVT secondary to a wide spectrum of classical viral, fungal, and parasitic infections, excluding the distinct entity of COVID-19. The review focused on elucidating the implicated etiological agents, underlying medical conditions, predisposing factors, diagnostic methods, clinical manifestations, sites of CVT, treatment strategies, and patient outcomes. Methods Systematic review conducted according the Guidelines for the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) [ ], and registered in International prospective register of systematic reviews (PROSPERO, CRD42023445694). Search strategy The literature search was conducted in MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science (WoS), Embase, and the Latin American and Caribbean Health Sciences Literature (LILACS)/BVS. Furthermore, a snowball search [ ] was performed by screening the reference lists of all included studies to assess their eligibility for inclusion. Keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH Terms) related to “intracranial thrombosis”, “infections”, and their variations were combined using Boolean operators (AND, OR) as detailed in Table S1. The search was restricted to human studies, with no limitations on publication language or date, and was conducted up to and including July 31, 2025. Study selection Studies were selected based on the PECO framework to ensure alignment with the systematic review objectives. The eligibility criteria were defined as follows: Population (P): individuals of all age groups; Exposure (E): presence or clinical history of non-bacterial infectious diseases (viral, fungal, or parasitic); Comparison (C): not applicable for this descriptive synthesis; and Outcome (O): development or documented occurrence of cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT). Exclusion criteria comprised review articles, opinion pieces, editorials, and case reports with insufficient, incomplete, or non-extractable primary data. Additionally, studies that presented only pooled patient analyses without individual-level data, those exclusively including patients diagnosed with COVID-19 or bacterial diseases, as well as studies whose full text could not be retrieved, were also excluded. Patients diagnosed with COVID-19 were excluded because of SARS-CoV-2-associated CVT has been extensively characterized in recent specialized literature [ , , , ]. Given the disproportionately large volume of COVID-19 data, its inclusion would have skewed the analysis of rarer viral, fungal, and parasitic etiologies, which represent the focus of this systematic synthesis. We imported all retrieved records into an EndNote X9 library [ ] for deduplication. The resulting records were then exported to the Rayyan platform [ ], where a second deduplication procedure was conducted. Study selection was conducted through an initial screening of titles and abstracts, followed by a subsequent full-text assessment, performed independently by three reviewers (M.C.M., E.B.M., and G.A.C.). Any disagreements in the selection process were resolved through consultation with another reviewer (L.G). Data extraction Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers (M.C.M. and E.B.M.), who entered the information into a structured electronic form created in the Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) program, a tool designed for data management [ ], with any discrepancies being resolved by a third reviewer (G.A.C.). The extracted information included: (1) General information: study title, journal name, year, volume, issue, page numbers, language, abstract, author names, country, and their affiliations; (2) Study characteristics: design

performed independently by three reviewers (M.C.M., E.B.M., and G.A.C.). Any disagreements in the selection process were resolved through consultation with another reviewer (L.G). Data extraction Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers (M.C.M. and E.B.M.), who entered the information into a structured electronic form created in the Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) program, a tool designed for data management [ ], with any discrepancies being resolved by a third reviewer (G.A.C.). The extracted information included: (1) General information: study title, journal name, year, volume, issue, page numbers, language, abstract, author names, country, and their affiliations; (2) Study characteristics: design (case report or case series), publication type (full article, abstract/poster), country where the study was conducted; (3) Patient characteristics: age (in days, months, or years), sex at birth, race/ethnicity; (4) Documented underlying conditions and predisposing factors; (5) Diagnostic methods used to confirm the infectious disease, detailed imaging examinations; (6) CVT characteristics, including single or multiple thromboses and their specific locations; (7) Etiological agents (viruses, parasites, and fungi); (8) Clinical presentation of CVT, including symptom onset (acute, subacute, chronic), mental status (normal or altered), and the presence of focal neurological signs or seizures; (9) Detailed treatment regimens, including the use of anticoagulants, antivirals, antiparasitics, antibiotics, anticonvulsants, and any medical or surgical interventions or procedures; (10) Outcomes, including neurological disability assessed using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) [ ]; 11) Follow-up imaging results specifically concerning the CVT (recanalization, unchanged, or worsened). Quality assessment The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tools for case reports and case series [ ]. Two reviewers (M.C.M. and E.B.M.) independently assessed the quality of the included studies, and any discrepancies were resolved through consensus with a third reviewer (G.A.C.). Analysis Descriptive analyses were used to summarize the data. In categories regarding comorbidities, diagnostic workup, and anatomical distribution of thrombosis, categories were treated as non-mutually exclusive to reflect the clinical complexity of individual cases. For the categorization of infection etiologies, the following criteria were adopted: (1) Fungal infections were classified into two distinct groups: fungi associated with mucormycosis (e.g., Rhizopus spp., Mucor spp.), recognized for their specific pathogenicity and clinical relevance in invasive syndromes, and fungi not associated with mucormycosis (e.g., Candida spp., Aspergillus spp.), which involve distinct pathogenic mechanisms, clinical presentations, and therapeutic approaches. This division was based on taxonomic criteria, documented etiological associations with mucormycosis in the literature, and diagnostic confirmation within the included studies. (2) Even in the presence of opportunistic infections, HIV was not classified solely as a predisposing factor, as it is also recognized as a primary etiological agent of CVT due to its intrinsic pathophysiological mechanisms, such as chronic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction, which promote thrombus formation. (3) In cases of coinfection involving viral, fungal, or parasitic agents, both pathogens were listed as etiological, given the difficulty in clearly distinguishing between HIV-induced immune dysfunction, direct viral effects, and the thrombogenic potential of the secondary agent. Results The search strategy returned 14,127 records (flow diagram in Figure S1).After the exclusion of duplicates and application of inclusion criteria, 238 studies were deemed suitable for inclusion in this review. Forty additional studies were included after snowball search. Thus, 278 publications were included in the systematic review. Among the included studies (Tables S2a-f), 16 (6%) were case series and 262 (94%) were case reports. With regard to publication type, scientific articles accounted for 247 cases (89%), while poster presentations constituted the remaining 31 (11%). Publications yielded information from 1958 to 2025, with 42% of the publications occurring from 2010 to 2019, followed by the subsequent period from 2020 to 2025, with 28% of the publications (Figure S2). The list of articles included in this review is presented in the Supplement. General characteristics and global distribution of studies The included studies showed a significant geographic concentration, with 72% of the evidence originating from Asia and North America (Fig. ). Detailed distribution by continent and country is provided in Table S3. Of the studies analyzed, publications were identified in ten distinct languages, with the majority ( n = 247, 89%) being published in English (Table S4). Patient characteristics The studies included 322 patients. Among these, 54% ( n = 175) were male, with ages ranging from 2 to 87 years (median = 39 years; IQR: 25–55), while 147 (46%) were female, with ages ranging from 35 days to 86 years and a median age of 42 years (IQR: 23–57).The majority of cases ( n = 264/322, 82%) occurred in individuals above 20 years of age. CVT was frequent among young adults aged 30 to 64 years, constituting 56% of the cases ( n = 179/322), but was also present in pediatric and elderly populations (Table S5). Information about race/ethnicity was reported for only 41 out of 322 individuals

Information about race/ethnicity was reported for only 41 out of 322 individuals (13%), and was distributed as follows: 39% ( n = 16/41) Asian, 34% ( n = 14/41) White, 15% ( n = 6/41) Black/African American, and 12% ( n = 5/41) Hispanic. Underlying conditions, predisposing factors, clinical, methods of diagnosis, and imaging The underlying conditions and predisposing factors were categorized into 11 distinct groups. The most prevalent category was infections, which may be associated with the causative agent of CVT or act as predisposing factor for thrombosis, such as sinusitis, meningitis and orbital cellulitis ( n = 149/322; 46%), followed by the category of cardiovascular and metabolic conditions ( n = 131/322; 41%), with diabetes mellitus the most common underlying medical condition ( n = 117/322, 36%) (Table and detailed in Table S6). Among the included cases, the majority ( n = 265/322, 82%) presented a subacute onset of symptoms. An altered mental status was observed in 57% of patients ( n = 184/322) (Table ). Furthermore, seizures or focal neurological manifestations were described in 98% of cases ( n = 314/322) (Table ). The vast majority of cases (305/322, 95%) were assessed using neuroimaging via computed tomography (CT) and/or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Microbiological culture testing was performed in 46% (149/322), whereas a biopsy procedure was conducted in 39% ( n = 127/322) (Table ). Neuroimaging was nearly universal (95%), with MRI and CT being the primary modalities for diagnosis and vascular assessment (Table ). Notably, parenchymal brain lesions were absent in over half of the cohort (57%), while ischemic and hemorrhagic events were less frequent. Type of infection and etiologies A comprehensive etiological analysis of the 322 included cases of CVT revealed 352 causative agents. Viral infections (most frequent: varicella zoster and HIV) and fungal mucormycosis were the most prevalent, identified in 114/322 (35%) and 112/322 cases (35%), respectively. Other non-mucormycosis fungal infections were documented in 63/322 cases (20%); while purely parasitic infections were less common (15/322 cases, 5%). Among the mixed infections, viral and non-mucormycosis fungal co-infections were observed in 15/322 cases (5%), whereas associations between viral and parasitic agents, as well as viral and mucormycosis agents, were rare, each occurring in a single instance (0.3%). A single case was attributable to an oomycotic infection (0.3%). Table summarizes infection types and detailed etiologies. Anatomical location of cerebral venous thrombosis Thrombosis distribution was balanced between single (51%) and multiple (45%) sinus involvement. The median number of affected sinuses was 1 (IQR: 1–2), range 1–7. The cavernous sinus was the most frequently affected site (53%), followed by the transverse and sagittal sinuses (Table ). Detailed CVT lateralization is present in the Table S7. Treatment, outcome, and imaging follow-up The most frequently reported therapeutic approaches were anticoagulation, which was employed in 173 patients (54%), followed by the administration of antifungal agents ( n = 160; 50%) and antibiotic therapy ( n = 132; 41%). Interventional or surgical procedures were described in 129 cases (40%). Other pharmacological treatments included antiviral, anticonvulsants corticosteroids (15%) and antiparasitics in 69 (21%), 51(16%), 47(15%) and 14 patients (4%), respectively. Among the cases who reported use of anticoagulants, unfractionated heparin ( n = 96, 56%), vitamin K antagonists ( n = 76, 44%), and low molecular weight heparin ( n = 53, 31%) were the most cited, while only 9 patients (5%) were prescribed DOACs (detailed therapeutic intervention in Table S8). Clinical outcomes assessed by the modified Rankin Scale demonstrated that 95 patients (30%) achieved a full recovery, while 46 (14%) remained with no significant disability. Outcomes involving slight disability were recorded in 31 patients (10%, moderate disability in 7 (2%), moderately severe disability in 3 (1.0%), and severe disability in 5 (2%). Sixty-eight patients (21%) died, and the outcome was not documented in 67 (21%). Regarding imaging follow-up, 79 cases (25%) did not undergo serial imaging. Recanalization was identified in 56 patients (17%), whereas 4 (1%) exhibited no interval change on follow-up imaging studies performed after the diagnosis of CVT. Worsening thrombosis was reported in only one patient. Unknown or unreported data were recorded in 182 cases (57%). Recanalization was identified in 56 patients (17%), whereas 4 (1%) exhibited no interval change on follow-up imaging studies performed after the diagnosis of CVT. Worsening thrombosis was reported in only one patient. Unknown or unreported data were recorded in 182 cases (57%). Table presents demographic, clinical, and detailed anatomical localization of the sinus thrombosis, and outcome characteristics of 304 patients with CVT, stratified by the type of infection (fungal non-mucormycosis, fungal mucormycosis, viral, and parasitic). Viral infections were predominant in younger age groups (0–29 years), while fungal infections (both types) were more frequent in patients aged ≥ 65 years. Mucormycosis showed a predilection for the cavernous sinus (65% of cases involved this sinus). Conversely, viral infections demonstrated very low cavernous sinus involvement (4%) but a high frequency of thrombosis in the transverse sinus (76%), sigmoid sinus (78%), sagittal sinus (73%), and straight sinus (91%).Non-mucormycosis fungal infections also showed an association with the cavernous sinus (31%). The anatomical finding reinforces the pattern of single vs. multiple CVT. Mucormycosis, affecting primarily a single sinus (the cavernous), was associated with a single CVT (54%). Viral infections, affecting multiple sinuses, were associated with multiple CVT (59%).Antibiotic use was common in patients with fungal infections (45% in mucormycosis, 31% in non-mucormycosis) but less frequent in viral infections (22%). Viral infections were associated with the highest frequency of favorable outcome (mRS 0–2: 54.2%), alongside a higher rate of anticoagulant administration (63.9%). Conversely, mucormycosis was characterized by a high proportion of deaths (68.3%) and a lower frequency of anticoagulation (16.9%). Temporal trends Temporal analysis spanning 1958–2025 indicated a marked evolution in diagnostic and management standards. Early cases were often defined by clinical suspicion or post-mortem findings (autopsy: 6.8%), while the era post-2010 was characterized by nearly universal neuroimaging (95%). Documentation of anticoagulant use also shifted temporally; only 22% of all patients receiving anticoagulants ( n = 38/173) were reported prior to 2011, while DOACs were used in 5% of cases, primarily within the most recent period. Furthermore, while the overall mortality rate was 21.1% ( n = 68/322), longitudinal data demonstrated a sharp decline. Despite an equal absolute number of deaths in both timeframes ( n = 34 up to 2010; n = 34 from 2011 to 2025), the mortality rate fell from 32.7% in the earlier era to 15.6% in the modern era, as 67.7% of the total cohort ( n = 218) was published after 2010. Quality assessment Using the JBI Critical Appraisal Tool for Case Reports (Table S10), the overall methodological quality of the included case reports was high, with the majority of items scoring “yes” in over 90% of reports, while the quality of case series studies (Table S11) was variable. Discussion This systematic review of 278 studies comprising 322 patients with CVT secondary to non-bacterial infections reveals a distinct epidemiological and clinical profile. Viral infections (35%) and fungal mucormycosis (35%) were the predominant etiologies of CVT. A diagnostic gap was identified, with specific pathogen confirmation performed in fewer than half of the cases despite near-universal neuroimaging. Reported management strategies and outcomes differed drastically by etiology: viral infections were most frequently associated with favorable outcomes and with the highest reported use of anticoagulant. In contrast, mucormycosis was linked to the worst prognosis, accounting for most deaths, and anticoagulant use was infrequently reported in these cases. This stark contrast likely reflects profound differences in disease severity, anatomical involvement, and bleeding risk, which strongly confound any assessment of treatment efficacy from this observational data. Recanalization data were largely unavailable for most patients. A striking finding of this review is the male predominance (54%) and the concentration of cases in the 30–64 age group (56%), in contrast to the well-established female of childbearing age predominance in CVT [ , – ]. This shift can be explained by the replacement of hormonal risk factors with metabolic and infectious ones. Diabetes mellitus (36.3%) was the leading comorbidity, acting as a primary catalyst for mucormycosis (35% of cases), an angioinvasive infection that frequently affects middle-aged and older adults [ ]. Similarly, the significant role of HIV as an independent prothrombotic agent (12.4% of cases) contributes to this male-skewed demographic [ ], particularly in regions where the epidemic follows this pattern. Geographic patterns also play a role; with 45% of studies originating from Asia, our data may reflect regional variations in the prevalence of diabetes and specific endemic pathogens. Finally, the possibility of reporting bias must be considered. [ ]. Similarly, the significant role of HIV as an independent prothrombotic agent (12.4% of cases) contributes to this male-skewed demographic [ ], particularly in regions where the epidemic follows this pattern. Geographic patterns also play a role; with 45% of studies originating from Asia, our data may reflect regional variations in the prevalence of diabetes and specific endemic pathogens. Finally, the possibility of reporting bias must be considered. In the clinical literature, CVT in a young woman is often perceived as ‘classic,’ whereas cases occurring in males or older adults associated with rare infections are more likely to be perceived as ‘novel’ and thus reported as case studies. The absence of race/ethnicity data in 87% of cases limits the ability to analyze potential disparities and underscores methodological shortcomings in the available literature [ ]. The main etiologies described were viral (35%) and fungal (35%) infections, with varicella zoster virus, HIV, and mucormycosis being the most frequent. Mucormycosis, in particular, demonstrated a fulminant course with high mortality due to its angioinvasive nature, leading to endothelial damage, necrosis, and thrombotic occlusion of proximate vessels. This explains its predilection for the cavernous sinus (often extending from rhino-orbital disease) [ ] and its fulminant course with high mortality, particularly in immunocompromised patients [ , ]. In contrast, viral pathogens (e.g., VZV, HIV) are thought to induce CVT through indirect mechanisms: vasculitis, immune-mediated endothelial activation, or systemic hypercoagulability [ , ]. This diffuse vascular insult may explain the higher frequency of multiple sinus involvement (e.g., transverse, sigmoid) and the more subacute presentation. Parasitic infections may cause CVT through vessel occlusion by larvae or cysts, or via a severe systemic inflammatory response. Clinical presentation was heterogeneous: altered mental status occurred in 57% of cases, while seizures and focal neurological deficits were frequently reported, consistent with classical descriptions of CVT [ , ]. A subacute onset predominated, particularly in viral and parasitic infections, often delaying recognition and initiation of treatment [ ]. The cavernous and transverse sinuses were the most commonly affected venous structures, frequently with multiple sinus involvement. This pattern is clinically relevant, as it correlates with more severe disease, greater risk of complications, and poorer outcomes [ ]. Although not diagnostic in isolation, the distribution of venous thrombosis may provide useful clues when integrated with clinical and microbiological data [ , ]. Magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography were the most widely employed diagnostic modalities, whereas laboratory confirmation through PCR, culture, or biopsy were infrequently pursued. This gap impedes accurate identification of causative pathogens, driving reliance on empirical therapies and negatively influencing prognosis [ , , ]. Optimal care requires integration of neuroimaging with systematic microbiological testing to guide targeted treatment. Anticoagulation with heparin was the most frequent therapeutic approach, including in patients with small venous hemorrhages, in line with international guidelines supporting its safety and efficacy [ , , ]. Nearly half of the reported cases required surgical intervention, reflecting the severity of infection-associated CVT and the frequent need for multidisciplinary management. Complete recovery was achieved in only one-third of patients, while mortality reached 21%, markedly higher than the 5–10% typically reported in non-infectious CVT [ , ]. Empirical use of antifungals and antibiotics was common, reflecting clinical severity and diagnostic uncertainty. Although justified in selected high-risk scenarios, this practice increases risks of drug toxicity and antimicrobial resistance [ – ]. The Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) recommends restricting empirical antifungal therapy to high-risk patients, with prompt reassessment following microbiological confirmation [ ]. The observed divergence between practice and guideline recommendations underscores the need for greater diagnostic precision. Recent studies, including RE-SPECT CVT, SECRET, and ACTION-CVT, demonstrated comparable efficacy and safety of DOACs relative to vitamin K antagonists in non-infectious CVT [ – ]. A meta-analysis further supported similar effectiveness with superior recanalization rates [ ]. However, clinical trials specifically enrolling patients with active infection are lacking, and thus DOACs cannot yet be recommended as standard therapy in this context. Low-molecular-weight heparin remains the first-line option, while DOACs may be considered on a case-by-case basis, balancing infection type, bleeding risk, and comorbidities. Application of the JBI checklist revealed that only one-third of case reports documented adverse events. Nevertheless, 86% reported post-intervention outcomes, and nearly all adequately described diagnostic procedures. Among case series, all but one applied validated diagnostic criteria and 81% used appropriate statistical methods, though only 69% ensured consecutive inclusion, introducing risk of selection bias. These findings highlight the need for more rigorous reporting standards, greater adherence to CARE guidelines, and improved methodological consistency across studies [ ]. Geographic concentration of publications in Asia and North America undermines global representativeness, particularly for underreported regions such as South America and Africa [ , ]. and nearly all adequately described diagnostic procedures. Among case series, all but one applied validated diagnostic criteria and 81% used appropriate statistical methods, though only 69% ensured consecutive inclusion, introducing risk of selection bias. These findings highlight the need for more rigorous reporting standards, greater adherence to CARE guidelines, and improved methodological consistency across studies [ ]. Geographic concentration of publications in Asia and North America undermines global representativeness, particularly for underreported regions such as South America and Africa [ , ]. The substantial lack of longitudinal follow-up, which was unknown or unreported for 81% of the cohort, represents a critical barrier to evaluating long-term outcomes. Consequently, recanalization, a key biological marker of CVT resolution [ ], was documented in only 17% of cases. In non-infectious CVT, studies like the ISCVT [ ] have shown that most patients achieve some degree of recanalization, which often correlates with clinical stabilization. The absence of these data in our review prevents a robust correlation between specific treatments (e.g., anticoagulation vs. surgical debridement) and vascular recovery. It remains uncertain whether the infection-induced thrombus exhibits a different biological behaviour or ‘resistance’ to standard heparin therapy compared to traditional CVT etiologies. Furthermore, the reliance on case reports (94%) introduces significant survival and publication bias. Clinical literature is prone to reporting extremes, either ‘miraculous’ outcomes or uniquely catastrophic cases, while routine, uncomplicated cases often go unpublished. This bias directly impacts our 21% mortality estimate. While this rate is markedly higher than the 5–10% reported in general CVT populations, it likely reflects a selection of the most severe infectious presentations. Therefore, our results may overestimate the lethality of non-bacterial infections in CVT due to the exclusion of milder, unreported cases. These limitations underscore the need for prospective, multicenter registries to establish a more accurate epidemiological and therapeutic landscape for infection-associated CVT. The wide temporal span of this review (1958–2025) reveals significant shifts in the clinical landscape of infection-associated CVT. Early cases were frequently characterized by clinical suspicion or post-mortem findings, with autopsy documented in 6.8% of the total cohort. Conversely, the post-2010 era, which accounts for 67.7% of the total patients ( n = 218) is marked by nearly universal neuroimaging (95%) [ , ]. Management practices also transitioned over time; our analysis shows that only 22% of all recorded anticoagulant use ( n = 38/173) occurred prior to 2011, while the emergence of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) is a contemporary phenomenon representing 5% of cases. These temporal shifts have a profound impact on survival estimates; while the overall mortality rate was 21.1% ( n = 68/322), the fatality rate declined from 32.7% in the pre-2011 era to 15.6% in the modern era. Notably, while the absolute number of deaths was identical between the two timeframes ( n = 34 up to 2010; n = 34 from 2011 to 2025), the doubling of the patient denominator in recent years highlights that historical cases indeed inflate cumulative mortality and lower overall anticoagulation documentation. The findings of this review confirm international recommendations for the use of heparin, preferably low-molecular-weight heparin, as first-line therapy even in cases with venous hemorrhage [ , ]. However, relevant divergences are observed in antifungal management, since guidelines advocate targeted therapy, whereas published reports frequently describe empirical use without microbiological confirmation, reflecting the tension between clinical urgency and evidence-based practice [ – ]. Although guidelines recommend targeted treatment, empirical antifungal therapy was common, highlighting the conflict between clinical urgency and antimicrobial stewardship. Regarding DOACs, recent guidelines such as AHA/ASA 2024 [ ], CSBPR 2024 [ ], and the German S2k 2023/24 [ ] recognize them as maintenance options in non-infectious CVT, but no evidence yet supports their use in infection-associated CVT. With respect to follow-up imaging, the CSBPR explicitly recommend repeat venous imaging at 3–6 months; [ ] however, our review revealed incomplete follow-up and a low rate of documented recanalization. The guidelines and the findings of this review emphasize the frequent need for surgical and multidisciplinary approaches, which are essential for the proper management of these complex cases. Furthermore, the strong confounding effect of anticoagulation indication and disease severity must be emphasized. The decisions to administer anticoagulation, perform surgery, or use specific antimicrobials were based on clinical judgment in complex, individual cases. Therefore, the observed associations between specific treatments and outcomes (e.g., anticoagulation use with better outcomes in viral infections) cannot be interpreted as evidence of efficacy but rather as descriptions of current practice within distinct clinical scenarios. Our findings highlight the necessity of an etiology-driven approach. Diagnostically, a high index of suspicion for mucormycosis should be triggered by CVT involving the cavernous sinus, especially in patients with diabetes, ketoacidosis, or immunosuppression. This scenario mandates urgent imaging of the sinuses and orbits, followed by tissue biopsy for culture and PCR. Conversely, viral etiologies should be

on clinical judgment in complex, individual cases. Therefore, the observed associations between specific treatments and outcomes (e.g., anticoagulation use with better outcomes in viral infections) cannot be interpreted as evidence of efficacy but rather as descriptions of current practice within distinct clinical scenarios. Our findings highlight the necessity of an etiology-driven approach. Diagnostically, a high index of suspicion for mucormycosis should be triggered by CVT involving the cavernous sinus, especially in patients with diabetes, ketoacidosis, or immunosuppression. This scenario mandates urgent imaging of the sinuses and orbits, followed by tissue biopsy for culture and PCR. Conversely, viral etiologies should be considered in patients with multiple sinus thromboses and appropriate risk factors (e.g., HIV, herpes zoster rash), necessitating specific serology or CSF PCR. Therapeutically, management must address both the infection and the thrombosis. While anticoagulation with heparin is a cornerstone of CVT treatment, its application in active infection requires a careful risk-benefit assessment, particularly in angioinvasive fungal disease where the bleeding risk may be elevated. Antifungal therapy for mucormycosis requires aggressive, early surgical debridement combined with high-dose liposomal amphotericin B. The role of DOACs in this population remains uncertain due to a lack of data and potential drug interactions. This review exposes critical deficiencies in the evidence base, which must direct future research. Key priorities include establishing prospective, multicenter registries to overcome selection bias by consecutively enrolling patients with infection-associated CVT under standardized protocols. Such registries are essential to define true incidence, identify baseline predictors and mortality rates, and employ uniform follow-up to evaluate recanalization and long-term outcomes, thereby achieving global representativeness with crucial data from underreported regions such as South America and Africa. Furthermore, diagnostic pathway studies are needed to evaluate integrated algorithms that combine early advanced neuroimaging (e.g., high-resolution MRI) with systematic microbiological testing, including PCR, serology, and biopsy. Regarding therapeutic comparative effectiveness, multicenter trials are urgently needed to assess treatment strategies and determine the optimal duration of therapy, particularly the role of DOACs in infection-associated CVT. Finally, pathogen-specific studies to investigate biomarkers of endothelial injury, inflammation, and pathogen burden could significantly aid in diagnosis, risk stratification, and monitoring treatment response. Conclusions Non-bacterial infections represent important but complex risk factors for CVT, influencing disease presentation, management, and outcomes. The high mortality and limited rates of complete recovery underscore the need for improved diagnostic integration, standardized therapeutic protocols, and high-quality prospective studies. Strengthening the evidence base is essential to refine clinical guidelines and optimize patient care in this challenging condition. Supplementary Information Supplementary Material 1.

documents.title: AAP clinical report routine evaluation of the term newborn

chunks.content: Introduction Peri-Intraventricular Hemorrhage (PIVH) is one of the most common complications in very premature Newborns (NB) due to the immaturity and lability of the cerebral blood vessels, which are unable to provide the necessary oxygen to the brain, being frequent in approximately 13 % to 29.8 % of NBs with less than 32-weeks of Gestational Age (GA) and in 44.68 % of other premature babies , . PIVH can be classified according to the degree of severity as Grade I – limited to the area of the germinal matrix (subependymal hemorrhage); Grade II – with rupture of the ventricular cavities, without ventricular dilation; Grade III – with dilation of the ventricles; and Grade IV – reaching the brain parenchyma, causing intraparenchymal hematoma (with involvement of the periventricular white matter). The prognosis of PIVH varies according to the degree of the lesion , . Periventricular Leukomalacia (PVL) is a disorder characterized by multifocal areas of necrosis, forming cysts in the deep cerebral white matter, and can occur in more than 25 % of extremely premature NBs , . Both encephalopathies have a negative impact on the neurodevelopment of premature NBs, including hearing and language development, as they may affect the acoustic information pathway, causing changes in the brainstem, cortical areas, or both , , , . Thus, the normal functioning of central auditory structures is of utmost importance for the child to acquire perceptual skills . PIVH/PVL is one of the causes of peripheral and central auditory changes in premature infants. It is a risk factor for changes in the central auditory nervous system, potentially impairing the development of auditory skills necessary for adequate acoustic information processing and language development , . Therefore, it is essential to assess the integrity of the peripheral and central auditory system to monitor language development, especially in the first 2-years of life. The child must be able to pay attention, detect, discriminate, and locate sounds, and memorize and integrate auditory experiences to recognize and understand speech . The authors hypothesized that the central auditory pathway in premature infants with PIVH/PVL may be changed compared to infants without risk. Objectives To evaluate and monitor, through electrophysiological assessment of hearing, the integrity of the peripheral and central auditory pathways in infants with PIVH/PVL who stayed in a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU), aiming to verify the occurrence of possible neural dysfunctions in this system. Material and method This prospective longitudinal study evaluated preterm NBs and infants at the time of hospital discharge and after 3- and 6-months. Data collection procedures began only after the Research Ethics Committee of the Medical School of the University of São Paulo (CAPPesq HCFMUSP) approved the project under n° 4.408.694/2020 ‒ CAAE: 38,842,020.4.0000.0068. Following the ethical principles for human research, the mothers and/or guardians who agreed to their NBs’ and infants’ participation in this research signed an informed consent form describing all procedures. Thus, they consented to this research and the subsequent dissemination of the results, in accordance with the Brazilian Resolution 466/12. The sample was recruited by convenience sampling among NBs and infants from the nursery attached to the maternity ward at the Clinics Hospital of the Medical School of the University of São Paulo. They were evaluated at the time of hospital discharge and after 3- and 6-months. Even after the end of this study, children with a suspicion of hearing impairment or changes in nerve sound conduction continued having their auditory development assessed and monitored at the audiology department of the Teaching and Research Center of the Department of Physical, Speech-Language-Hearing, and Occupational Therapy of the Medical School of the University of São Paulo (CDP-FOFITO). The initial proposal was to monitor the hearing of infants up to 12-months old with periodic electrophysiological exams. However, several setbacks led to losing contact with children in both groups, with the COVID-19 pandemic having the greatest impact on the absence and refusal to continue participating in the research. Guardians mainly claimed fear of contagion, lack of someone to take the child to the exam, fear of losing their job (even though they would receive a medical certificate), and relevant financial issues. Thus, the initial case series comprised a Study Group (SG) with 12 female and 11 male NBs, with gestational age between 25- and 33-weeks, and a mean gestational age of 29.82-weeks at birth, totaling 23 NBs – 19 with only PIVH and four with PIVH and PVL. Their mean corrected gestational age was 41.82-weeks at the first evaluation after hospital discharge. Eleven infants attended the second evaluation after 3-months, with a mean corrected gestational age of 55.82-weeks at the time of the examination. Six infants attended the third evaluation, 6-months after discharge, with a mean corrected gestational age of 69.32-weeks at the time of the examination. It also had a Control Group

Their mean corrected gestational age was 41.82-weeks at the first evaluation after hospital discharge. Eleven infants attended the second evaluation after 3-months, with a mean corrected gestational age of 55.82-weeks at the time of the examination. Six infants attended the third evaluation, 6-months after discharge, with a mean corrected gestational age of 69.32-weeks at the time of the examination. It also had a Control Group (CG) with 26 healthy NBs without PIVH/PVL in the first evaluation after hospital discharge, distributed in 13 female and 13 male NBs, with gestational age between 27- and 33-weeks and a mean of 30.67-weeks of gestational age at birth. Their mean corrected gestational age was 41.78-weeks at the first evaluation after hospital discharge. Twelve infants attended the second evaluation after 3-months, with 57.67-weeks of corrected gestational age at the time of the examination. Only five infants attended the third evaluation 6-months after discharge, with a mean of 68.75-weeks of corrected gestational age at the time of the examination. In the fourth evaluation, 12-months after hospital discharge, no patient in either group agreed to complete the study ( ). Procedures The clinical/diagnostic equipment Navigator-Pro, Biologic brand, captured the Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR). All NBs were prepared for the tests by cleaning their skin with abrasive paste and attaching disposable pediatric electrodes Meditrace-200, Kendal brand, to the Frontal region (Fpz) and the right and left mastoids (M2 and M1), following the IES 10‒20 (International Electrode System) standard . The impedance of the electrodes was kept below 3 kΩ. The acoustic stimuli were rarefied polarity clicks, presented monaurally through a pair of insert earphones model 3A to elicit the responses, at 80 dBnHL, at a presentation rate of 27.7 clicks/s, duration of 0.1 milliseconds (ms), high-pass filters of 100 Hz, and low-pass filters of 1500 Hz to avoid excess artifacts, using a total of 2048 stimuli. The recording window had 12 ms, and the analysis approached the absolute latencies of waves I, III, V, and interpeak intervals I‒III, III‒V, and I‒V. ABR was classified as normal and abnormal, following the criteria established by Rosa et al. (2014) . The reference electrodes were positioned on the right and/or left mastoids (M2 and M1), the active electrode was positioned on the vertex-high Forehead (Fz), and the ground electrode was positioned on the mastoid of the contralateral ear to obtain the long-latency auditory evoked potentials, P1, N1, P2. The acoustic stimuli used were syllables /ba/ at 70 dBnHL. The evaluation parameters were 300 /ba/ stimuli, in a recording window of 512 ms, presentation rate of 1.1 stimuli per second, trapezoidal stimulus envelope, band-pass filter from 1 to 30 Hz, gain of 100,000, and a response analysis window of −100 ms pre-stimulus and 500 ms post-stimulus. The lead researcher and two examiners visually verified whether Cortical Auditory Evoked Potentials (CAEP) were present and analyzed their latency. CAEP latency values were marked considering the point of maximum amplitude, determined as the difference between the baseline and the maximum positive or negative point according to the component analyzed. Eligibility criteria 1 – The study included all preterm NBs – children born up to 36 6/7-weeks of gestational age, according to the World Health Organization (2014) . 2 – For SG, the presence of PIVH and/or PVL risk indicators. For CG, the absence of PIVH and/or PVL, craniofacial malformations, and risk indicators for retrocochlear changes, according to the Joint Committee on Infant Hearing (JCIH, 2019) . 3 – Bilateral presence of transient evoked otoacoustic emissions for both groups to ensure normal cochlear function. Exclusion criteria 1 – All full-term NBs – children born after 37-weeks of gestational age – were excluded . 2 ‒ NBs with conductive and/or cochlear changes and other risk indicators for hearing impairment were excluded from the sample, according to the criteria established by the JCIH. (2019) . All subjects underwent ABR with click stimuli and CAEP with speech stimuli (syllable /ba/). Each group’s results were compared using statistical tests. Statistical analysis Quantitative data analysis was initially performed by obtaining descriptive measures (mean and standard deviation) for each group, using the ANOVA statistical test with Tukey's test when more than two intra-subject variables were analyzed, at the three evaluation moments (immediately after hospital discharge, 3rd-month after hospital discharge, and 6th-month after hospital discharge). The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis was set at 5 %. Statistically significant values were marked with an asterisk (*), and a tendency towards significance was marked with a hash (#). Results The study sample initially had 23 NBs in SG and 26 NBs in CG. Two methodologies were used to analyze

The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis was set at 5 %. Statistically significant values were marked with an asterisk (*), and a tendency towards significance was marked with a hash (#). Results The study sample initially had 23 NBs in SG and 26 NBs in CG. Two methodologies were used to analyze the results, the first part consisted of a cross-sectional data analysis, and the second, a longitudinal analysis. Initially, the absolute latencies of waves I, III, V, and the interpeak intervals I‒III, III‒V, I‒V were analyzed in each group, separately for each ear, to characterize the responses of the Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR) in the study population. These analyses did not show any statistical difference between the ears in either test. Therefore, the right and left ear values were grouped for subsequent analyses, while maintaining the comparison between the Experimental Group (EG) and the Control Group (CG). shows that there was no significant difference in ABR parameters in the first assessment (immediately after hospital discharge – NB), except for interpeak III‒V ( p = 0.042), with a lower latency value in the SG. No differences in ABR parameters were found in the second evaluation (3-months after hospital discharge – 3 m), except for wave I ( p = 0.012), with a lower latency value in the CG ( ). The results of the comparison between the SG and CG described above in show a significant difference between ABR wave V and interpeak interval III‒V in the third evaluation, with lower latency values in the SG (after 6-months of hospital discharge – 6 m). below shows the minimum and maximum values of the CAEP parameters obtained in the study population, in the right and left ears. shows the percentage of presence and absence of CAEP components in the SG and CG in each assessment. Note that the N2 component was not visualized in the three periods evaluated in either group. The longitudinal data analysis evaluated how the maturation process of the ABR and CAEP parameters occurs in each group, by comparing their mean wave latency values in the first assessment after discharge (called NB), in the second assessment 3-months after discharge (called 3 m), and in the third assessment 6-months after hospital discharge (called 6 m). The results in show no significant decrease in the latencies of ABR wave I ( p = 0.292) in SG throughout the study period. There was a significant decrease in the latencies of waves III and V ( p = 0.002 and < 0.0001, respectively). Likewise, there was a significant difference in the interpeak intervals I‒III, III‒V, and I‒V ( p = 0.006, p = 0.006, and < 0.0001, respectively). There was no statistically significant decrease in the CAEP P1, N1, and P2 latencies in the three study periods. According to the Tukey test (two-by-two comparison), a significant difference occurred in the maturation of wave III between the first (NB) and third evaluations (6 m) ( p < 0.01); a significant difference occurred in the maturation of wave V between the immediately after discharge and after 3-months (NB and 3 m) ( p < 0.05), the same occurring between the first and third evaluations (NB and 6 m) ( p < 0.01) and between the second and third evaluations (3 m and 6 m) ( p < 0.05). Regarding interpeak interval I‒III, a significant difference was found only between immediately after discharge and after 3-months (NB and 3 m) ( p < 0.05); the interpeak interval III‒V matured significantly between immediately after discharge and after 6-months (NB and 6 m) ( p < 0.05); lastly, the differences in the interpeak interval I‒V occurred between NB and 3 m ( p < 0.01) and NB and 6 m ( p < 0.01), with a decrease in ABR latencies. According to the Tukey test (two-by-two comparison), no significant differences were found between the CAEP components in the three study periods. The results in show a significant decrease in CG in the latencies of ABR waves III and V and interpeak intervals I‒III and I‒V ( p < 0.0001 and < 0.0001, p = 0.002 and p = 0.0001, respectively) throughout the study period. There was no statistically significant decrease in the CAEP P1, N1, and P2 latencies in the three study periods. study periods. The results in show a significant decrease in CG in the latencies of ABR waves III and V and interpeak intervals I‒III and I‒V ( p < 0.0001 and < 0.0001, p = 0.002 and p = 0.0001, respectively) throughout the study period. There was no statistically significant decrease in the CAEP P1, N1, and P2 latencies in the three study periods. According to the Tukey test (two-by-two comparison), wave I did not have statistically significant periods, with gradual evolution throughout the study; as for wave III, a significant difference occurred in the period between the first and second evaluation (NB and 3 m) ( p < 0.05) and between the first and third evaluation (NB and 6 m) ( p < 0.01). As for the decrease in wave V latencies, a large difference occurred between immediately after discharge and after 3-months (NB and 3 m) ( p < 0.01), the same occurring between the first and third evaluations (NB and 6 m) ( p < 0.01) and between the first and third evaluations (NB and 6 m) ( p < 0.01). Also, a significant difference in interpeak interval I‒III was only evident between immediately after discharge and after 3-months (NB and 3 m) ( p < 0.05). Lastly, the differences in interpeak interval I‒V occurred between NB and 3 m ( p < 0.05) and NB and 6 m ( p < 0.01), with a decrease in ABR latencies. illustrates the evolution of the BAEP and CAEP parameters in the Control and Study groups in the three periods analyzed. Discussion Despite the setbacks that arose throughout the research, its results will hopefully contribute to advances in knowledge about the central auditory pathway functioning and neuroaudiological monitoring in infants who suffered PIVH and/or PVL due to prematurity, mitigating the impact of these problems on language development. This study included 23 infants, making up the Study Group. PIVH affected 35 % of them on the left side and 13 % on the right side; bilateral PIVH occurred in 39 %, and in 13 % there was no defined side. These findings are noteworthy when considering that the left side of the cerebral cortex is responsible for language, having been affected in the vast majority of the infants evaluated. There may be losses along the auditory pathway even after PIVH absorption. This agrees with the literature that points to peripheral and central auditory changes, also affecting the development of auditory skills, whose acquisition directly interferes with language development, school learning, and consequent social performance , , , . The presence of potentials at the cortical level signals the arrival of sound information to the auditory cortex, allowing the objective evaluation of the cortical structures involved in attention, localization, memory, and discrimination of sounds, and making it possible to relate their findings to linguistic performance. The authors of a previous study suggested that such potentials could be used during hospitalization to identify early possible central changes throughout the maturation of preterm NBs . This statement is in line with the objectives of the present research. The analysis of ABR results found absolute latencies and interpeak intervals within normal parameters in all infants in the CG, in the three evaluations. This demonstrates constant and gradual auditory pathway maturation. However, the analysis of ABR parameters in the SG verified changes in 13 % of the infants, who were referred for monitoring of auditory pathway maturation throughout their development, until around 3-years-old. A previous study verified central changes in 33.4 % of premature NBs; children with PIVH grades II, III, and IV had a higher occurrence of central changes than those with grade I. In the audiological monitoring at 6-months old, the central auditory change remained in 51.85 % of the children who already had it at birth . However, these findings did not corroborate those obtained in the present study, probably due to the difference in PIVH grades of the study population. The comparison of potentials did not show any difference between the ears, corroborating other studies whose results also indicated no difference between the ears , . However, this disagrees with studies that concluded that auditory function is asymmetrical, with a slight advantage for the right ear , . In the comparative analysis of the mean ABR absolute wave latencies and interpeak intervals between infants in the SG and CG ( to ), the parameters that most differentiated the two groups always had shorter latency times in the EG, in the three periods evaluated. Some authors attribute this shortening to changes in the morphological and functional development of the auditory system, which may characterize transient or permanent neural dysfunctions . The difference in the interpeak interval III‒V between SG and CG continued at 6-months, now at the expense of wave V, which

advantage for the right ear , . In the comparative analysis of the mean ABR absolute wave latencies and interpeak intervals between infants in the SG and CG ( to ), the parameters that most differentiated the two groups always had shorter latency times in the EG, in the three periods evaluated. Some authors attribute this shortening to changes in the morphological and functional development of the auditory system, which may characterize transient or permanent neural dysfunctions . The difference in the interpeak interval III‒V between SG and CG continued at 6-months, now at the expense of wave V, which was also significantly shorter in SG ( ). The hypothesis for this finding is that it probably shows accelerated maturation due to a rapid increase in axonal myelin density in the brainstem , expressed by the shorter latency of wave V and/or shorter nerve conduction time due to the shorter length of the nerve fibers of the auditory pathway in the brainstem, in its most rostral region, in infants who had PIVH , . This study aimed to investigate the presence of exogenous CAEP components in preterm NBs. The clinical applications of CAEP include the monitoring of auditory maturation in NBs, since research into the presence or absence of its components allows us to observe the response to sounds from the auditory pathway to the cerebral cortex. When performed longitudinally, it makes it possible to infer how the auditory system is organized in relation to sound reception at the cortical level over time . The CAEP P1 component has been established as a biological marker to assess the central auditory system maturation in children, as this robust positive response is easily identified and occurs between 100‒300 ms post-stimulus, depending on the child's age . CAEPs measure cognitive development, especially in premature babies. From birth, their capture shows the organization of cortical generators and the development of the central auditory system , . The authors of a study found that children with abnormal CAEPs during the neonatal period may have language alterations . This study named the CAEP peaks and valleys as P1, N1, P2, N2, despite having late latency times. This agrees with other studies that maintained the same nomenclature, as they attributed such an increase to the immaturity of the cortex structures , . The mean P1, N1, and N2 values ( ) were slightly shorter than those found in previous studies – whose results were, respectively: P1 – 247.93 in the right ear and 251.23 in the left ear; N1 – 395.39 in the right ear and 403.77 in the left ear;[25] P1 – 205.0 in the right ear and 201.8 in the left ear; N1 – 298.2 in the right ear and 302.8 in the left ear . In the first evaluation of this study, the absence of P1 and N1 ( ) was higher in both groups than in a previous study . It found absent P1 and N1 in 13 % ( n = 4) of the neonates in the preterm group, perhaps because they were a group with a higher GA (mean of 34-weeks), fewer complications, and/or shorter length of hospital stay. As for oscillations in the percentage of presence/absence of CAEP in the second and third evaluations, the literature consulted lacked results for comparison. However, both the SG and the CG maintained the absence of these parameters, which may indicate that prematurity is the main risk factor for changes in auditory processing at the cortical level and may be an indicator of cognitive changes or immature cortical structures in this population , . The evolutionary study of the mean ABR and CAEP latencies ( , ; ) in SG and CG showed that the ABR waves matured rapidly throughout the study period, mainly in the first 3-months after hospital discharge. This characterizes a phenomenon common to premature infants with accelerated maturation, known as the recovery period or catch-up, already observed in a previous study . However, wave I matured gradually and continuously, without significant differences between periods. The literature indicates that wave I is already practically mature at birth, even in preterm infants, as it reflects nerve conduction proximal to the cochlea , . The CAEP did not show significant differences throughout the study period, possibly due to their late maturation, beginning at birth, and completing around 14-years old , , , . It is interesting to note that the ABR parameters, especially wave V and the I‒V interpeak interval, remained shorter in SG than in CG in the three evaluations. This may indicate accelerated maturation due to a rapid increase in the myelin layer in the auditory nerve in the brainstem region, or synaptic plasticity influenced by the auditory experience (even in a NICU), capable of proliferating collateral axons and dendritic germination

. The CAEP did not show significant differences throughout the study period, possibly due to their late maturation, beginning at birth, and completing around 14-years old , , , . It is interesting to note that the ABR parameters, especially wave V and the I‒V interpeak interval, remained shorter in SG than in CG in the three evaluations. This may indicate accelerated maturation due to a rapid increase in the myelin layer in the auditory nerve in the brainstem region, or synaptic plasticity influenced by the auditory experience (even in a NICU), capable of proliferating collateral axons and dendritic germination and changing the neural response properties , . shows the maturation process of the ABR and CAEP waves in the two study groups, which developed quite similarly. Thus, it is believed that SG and CG infants would complete the maturation process at similar times. This belief could only be confirmed by monitoring these children’s maturation process until around 3-years old to ensure adequate auditory development and language acquisition and development. The etiology of prematurity is multifactorial, contributing to the possibility of numerous complications and serious consequences. One of the limitations of this study was that its sample had mostly grade I PIVH; therefore, the PIVH/PVL duration and severity parameters in SG were not considered, making it impossible to correlate the degree of involvement and the results. Another aspect that may have interfered with the analysis of the results in this study was that, because they remained in the NICU, some premature infants could only be evaluated a few weeks after their birth, having already experienced several complications during their hospitalization. These complications were not considered. Furthermore, the PIVH may have already been completely resolved by hospital discharge, which leads us to infer that the brain structures previously compressed by the hemorrhage were no longer compressed due to blood absorption, ceasing to be a preponderant factor. Thus, prematurity is a primary factor for lifelong damage, demonstrating the importance of looking at preterm children with extreme attention from an audiological standpoint, aiming at the full development of their oral and written language, as they have a higher occurrence of minimal neurological dysfunctions, such as attention deficit, hyperactivity, and school performance below expectations , . Conclusions This study found a gradual decrease in nerve conduction time towards the most central structures of the auditory pathway in the brainstem in both study groups, corroborating that neuromaturation of the auditory system occurs in the caudo-rostral direction. The comparison of brainstem and cortical potentials showed that auditory function is symmetrical in the peripheral and central portions of the auditory pathway in both groups. The present study concluded that the maturation of the ABR and CAEP waves in both groups developed in a very similar way over the six months after hospital discharge. Therefore, it is believed that hearing monitoring is necessary until around 3-years of age to ensure adequate auditory and language development. Prematurity is a primary factor for lifelong damage, demonstrating the importance of looking at preterm children with extreme attention from an audiological standpoint. In accordance with editorial policy, the authors declare that data relating to the article entitled “Electrophysiological evaluation of the auditory pathway in newborns and infants with peri‑intraventricular hemorrhage and/or periventricular leukomalacia”, should be requested from the corresponding author. documents.title: AAP clinical report DKA diabetic ketoacidosis pediatric management

chunks.content: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a progressive autoimmune disease that is often discovered upon presentation of clinical symptoms ( ). However, before clinical onset (stage 3), there are presymptomatic stages (stages 1 and 2) that are characterized by the presence of circulating autoantibodies (AAbs) ( ). Individuals with stage 1 T1D have positivity for 2 or more AAbs, are presymptomatic, and are normoglycemic. In stage 2 T1D, individuals have 2 or more AAbs and subclinical dysglycemia. By stage 3, symptoms and overt hyperglycemia are present, and individuals meet the standard diagnostic criteria for diabetes ( ). Therefore, screening for T1D-associated AAbs is a reliable way to identify individuals with presymptomatic T1D prior to clinically significant beta cell loss and the need for exogenous insulin ( ). There are several potential benefits of AAb screening ( ). First, screening that leads to early detection of T1D gives clinicians an opportunity to intervene with disease-modifying therapy (DMT) ( ). Teplizumab is the first DMT approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) that can alter the course of an autoimmune endocrine disease ( ). Compared with placebo, teplizumab was shown to delay the onset (stage 3) of T1D by ∼2.7 years ( ). The availability of teplizumab for people 8 years of age and older with stage 2 T1D is a significant development and has intensified discussions on the need for general population screening ( , ). Early detection of T1D followed by metabolic monitoring can also result in an improved clinical presentation and a reduced risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) at or around the time of stage 3 diagnosis ( ). DKA is a life-threatening condition that has short- and long-term impacts on health ( ). The T1D Exchange and SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth registries reported that up to ∼40% of youth (<20 years of age) diagnosed with T1D initially presented with DKA in the United States ( , ). An international retrospective study on DKA at diagnosis, including 10 European countries, reported DKA rates ranging from 21.6% to 43.8% ( ). Risk of DKA depends on various factors. The rate of DKA can be higher in certain geographic regions, and it was exacerbated during the early waves of the COVID-19 pandemic ( , , ). Data from the SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth study have shown that the prevalence of DKA at or near T1D diagnosis was highest in children aged 0 to 4 years ( , ). AAb screening reduces the rate of DKA around the time of diagnosis. The Autoimmunity Screening for Kids (ASK) study showed that although the DKA rate in Colorado was ∼60%, it could be as low as ∼5% in children who received AAb screening and metabolic monitoring ( , , ). While most of the evidence around AAb screening and DKA rates at presentation is from pediatric studies, rates of DKA in adults are not insignificant ( ). T1D Exchange registry data revealed that people 25 to 40 years of age showed a considerable rate of DKA at T1D diagnosis, ranging from 19% to 24% ( ). An analysis of data from the ASK study found that AAb screening could be cost-effective if conducted in an area with high rates of DKA and with screening infrastructure, such as Colorado, and where avoidance of DKA leads to long-term improvements in glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) ( ). Importantly, AAb screening can also provide people with presymptomatic T1D more time before symptom onset and insulin commencement to receive education and counseling. Diagnosis with T1D is life-altering and extremely anxiety-inducing for those affected and their families. Early detection that leads to better awareness of T1D prior to stage 3 diagnosis and the establishment of a care team and monitoring plan can reduce anxiety at the time of diagnosis ( , , ). Additionally, AAb screening is an important differential diagnostic tool. More than 40% of people over 30 years of age with new onset T1D are initially misdiagnosed with type 2 diabetes (T2D) ( ). AAb testing can be used to appropriately diagnose individuals with T1D when they are not responding well to T2D therapies or if they do not fit the typical T2D phenotype ( , , , ). Finally, AAb screening can give people the opportunity to take part in clinical trials ( ). Despite these advantages, AAb screening has mostly taken place within research-based screening programs and is done inconsistently in the clinical setting. This may be due to limited awareness among healthcare providers (HCPs) regarding the presymptomatic stages of T1D, appropriate tests to order including the existence of AAb panels, how to perform T1D screening, and the potential to reduce severity of disease at presentation. A lack of established workflow can also be a major barrier to AAb screening; therefore, screening processes that
